brief: A new launch trailer for Grand Theft Auto VI reveals more details about what's set to be the biggest game of the year.

title: AI giant Anthropic woos potential investors ahead of stock market debut
body:
AI giant Anthropic woos potential investors ahead of stock market debut
- Published
Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic has been drumming up support for its expected stock market listing as it seeks to reassure investors of its profit-making potential.
Anthropic revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands.
In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on tech.
It also emphasised safety at its event after warnings by current and former researchers of serious and even existential risks to humanity posed by AI.
Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period.
The company also told investors during the event at its headquarters in San Francisco that it had made a third quarter profit on an adjusted basis, an accounting method which ignores non-recurring costs.
Investors reportedly left the Anthropic investor event optimistic about the company's rapid revenue growth and path to profitability.
Alongside concerns about profit generation, there have also been fears about the safety of AI models.
Anthropic has been vocal about AI's risks, with its chief executive Dario Amodei calling on the pace of development to slow down.
In September one of its researchers warned of a greater than 10% chance that AI could "kill all humans" within the next decade, and a former researcher said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.
The firm itself said in September it had identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" which could support the development of biological weapons.
However, US President Donald Trump has said researchers have been "bringing up things that won't happen" and that in a race between the US and China to develop the technology, "whoever wins AI, wins".
Rival tech firm OpenAI has also warned about safety, with its chief executive Sam Altman saying in September that his company will not go public this year as it addresses concerns.
The ChatGPT-developer is also eyeing a bumper stock market listing, which is expected to value the firm at more than $1tn.
- How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections 
  - Published2 days ago
Market sentiment
Anthropic's revenue figures, along with those of rival OpenAI, are an important gauge of the AI industry's growth and ability to finance the infrastructure needed to develop the technology.
Stocks in some US technology companies dropped on Wednesday over concerns around investments in AI.
Shares in chip makers - including AMD, Nvidia and Intel - fell sharply.
In Asia, shares in Japanese tech investment firm Softbank were down by more than 9% on Thursday. South Korean semiconductor giants also dropped, with Samsung falling by 9.5% and SK Hynix 11% lower.
Shares have been falling this week after remarks by Hock Tan, the chief executive of US tech manufacturer Broadcom, over AI spending.
Tan said at a conference in Singapore on Monday that many investors have "no clue" and have set "extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino".
The falls deepened after US inflation data released on Wednesday showed price rises accelerated by more than expected in September.
Investors are concerned that higher inflation will mean the US Federal Reserve is more likely to put up the cost of borrowing.
brief: It comes as some investors have become concerned about the amount of money being spent on AI infrastructure.

title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
body:
Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
- Published
A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".
As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.
But, here's we do know so far.
Help from a chatbot
The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).
Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.
Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".
The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.
Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.
The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.
Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.
But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.
Hiding in plain toilet paper
On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.
A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.
The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.
When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.
In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".
It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."
Who is Abdulrahman Alfozan?
Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.
Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream.
"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."
Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."
On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.
The FBI investigation is ongoing.
If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine.

title: Avian flu and costs among reasons for loss of captive birds at Castle Espie
body:
Avian flu and costs among reasons for loss of captive birds at Castle Espie
- Published
Avian flu, cost-cutting and Brexit are among the reasons behind the transfer of captive birds from one of Northern Ireland's best-known wildlife sites, according to the charity that runs it.
Director of Operations at Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT) Alex Lane said avian influenza, as well as difficulties in transporting birds since Brexit, has contributed to the decline in the number of captive birds at Castle Espie.
The closure of both the site's captive bird programme and guided school tour programme is part of wider WWT cost-cutting measures.
An Assembly member has described the changes to the education offering as "disappointing".
Alex Lane said the site used to have around 500 birds in its captive collection - but, a combination of Brexit and avian influenza means today, there are fewer than 100.
Both the Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs and the UK's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs have been contacted for comment.
From November onwards, all captive birds at Castle Espie will be transferred to other WWT sites across the UK.
The centre, which is located in County Down, will also no longer offer guided school tours.
However, the centre have said they will "continue to welcome self-guided school visits".
Castle Espie, which is managed by the WWT, is located on the shores of Strangford Lough, just outside Comber.
The reserve is a safe haven for native and exotic birds, ducks and geese, and some of its collection including globally at-risk species.
It has different types of wetlands, including freshwater and sailing lagoons as well as seasonally flooded areas.
SDLP MLA Cara Hunter, who sits on the Stormont education committee, told BBC News NI that the "loss of guided educational visits is disappointing".
"Castle Espie has played an important role in introducing generations of young people to nature, conservation and the unique environment on their doorstep.
"I would be concerned that these changes could reduce opportunities for schools, particularly those with limited resources, to access high-quality environmental education."
The MLA added that "opportunities that educate, inspire and broaden horizons are quietly lost while Stormont remains distracted from the issues that matter most to families".
Alex Lane, Director of Operations at WWT, said rising costs and the challenge around income means charities like the WWT are facing "increasing pressure".
"We've got a sizeable deficit and obviously that's unsustainable in the long term," she told BBC News NI.
Lane said it is important the WWT have surplus income so that they can "do the conservation work that is part of their mission".
She said the site used to have over 500 birds in its captive collection - but, in part due to avian influenza, today there are less than 100.
Lane added that another factor in the decline in the number of captive birds is the increased difficulties in transporting birds since Brexit.
"There is no aligned system for bringing birds into Ireland from mainland UK.
"We've got a vastly reduced collection, and that's not by choice. That is the impact of avian influenza and the restrictions placed on bird movement as a result of Brexit."
It is thought that diverging post-Brexit bio-security checks has increased red tape for moving birds between Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
Under the strict mandates of the Windsor Framework, these regulatory shifts also mean heavy administrative and logistical costs.
According to the UK Government's official website, external, the movement of captive birds from Britain to Northern Ireland requires an export health certificate.
There is also a requirement for captive birds to be checked at the point of entry when transported to Northern Ireland, to protect animal health and welfare and public health.
However, Lane said there will be benefits to the decommissioning of the captive bird collection.
"The intent with the site is to reset it as this hub for wetland nature conservation.
"We're effectively opening up more space for wild birds."
Lane said the site "needs to stop" its formal education offering in part due to financial pressures WWT faces.
She added that there is also an insufficient number of schools booking guided tours at the site to cover costs.
Lane said the low number of school visits may be partly be caused by the cost of transport.
brief: Difficulties in transporting animals since Brexit has contributed to the decline in the number of captive birds.

title: Brazil sees record fall in Amazon deforestation as key election looms
body:
Brazil sees record fall in Amazon deforestation as key election looms
- Published
Brazil's government says deforestation rates in the country's Amazon and savanna regions have fallen to record lows ahead of a presidential election run-off in which the rainforest's future is a key issue.
Left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, when he assumed office three years ago, pledged to end deforestation by 2030 in the Amazon. It had surged under his right-wing predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro.
Lula will face Bolsonaro's son Flavio in the run-off on 25 October, with polls suggesting a neck-and-neck race. Flavio is expected to continue his father's policies if he wins, though he has pledged to fight organised crime in the Amazon.
Satellite data shows that in the year to July 2026, the deforestation rate fell by 41.8% in the Amazon - the biggest drop since records began in 1988. The fall in the Cerrado, Brazil's savanna region, was 23.8%.
The Amazon rainforest - the world's largest - is a crucial buffer in the global fight against climate change and 60% of it is located in Brazil.
Jair Bolsonaro promoted mining in indigenous lands in the Amazon and forest clearances soared at the same time as resources to protect the forest were cut.
During Bolsonaro's presidency from 2019 to 2022, the Amazon lost nearly 60% more in forest lands compared to the previous four years, news agency AFP reported, citing official data.
Lula reversed his policies and oversaw deforestation rates drop to a six-year low during his first year in office. Lula tightened up environmental monitoring and penalties for illegal logging.
"Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030," he said in a post on X on Friday.
Tropical rainforests like the Amazon are home to millions of species. In a healthy state, they absorb vast quantities of planet-warming carbon dioxide, helping to keep the Earth cool.
But they have come under increasing pressure from decades of deliberate land clearance for agriculture and logging, as well as climate change, which scientists warn can create conditions for wildfires.
Brazil's Environment Minister Joao Paulo Capobianco described the decline in Amazon deforestation as "absolutely stratospheric".
It was an "historic achievement" for Brazil, said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima.
It showed that "with political will, it is possible to curb deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions", Astrini said.

  - Published22 November 2025
  - Published17 November 2025
brief: The Amazon rainforest is a crucial buffer against climate change - but deforestation had expanded under former president Jair Bolsonaro.

title: Why hasn't the UK had any named storms yet?
body:
Why hasn't the UK had any named storms yet?
- Published
With November already on the horizon the UK is yet to see its first named storm of the season.
Deep Atlantic lows responsible for more turbulent conditions have been steered away by dominant areas of high pressure.
This year the headlines have been about worsening drought rather than the impact of gales.
However, could this be the calm before the storms as the Met Office predict a growing chance that late autumn and early winter will turn wetter and windier as El Niño strengthens in the Pacific.
Why has it been a quiet start to autumn?
As autumn sets in and the nights get longer temperatures around polar regions start to fall. This causes a greater contrast with the warmer tropics which can fire up a more potent jet stream - the fast moving, narrow band of fast winds high in the atmosphere.
The jet stream is largely responsible for developing and delivering our stormier pressure systems.
Typically in autumn the jet stream would be a regular visitor to the skies above the UK, steering wet and windy weather towards us.
However, so far this season it has often been sitting to the north or north-west of the UK. This has meant south or south-westerly winds bringing warmer than normal conditions and high pressure having more of an influence leading to reduced rainfall for many.
These weather patterns have therefore meant only occasional bouts of stronger winds across the north-west of the UK, with little disruption.
The heaviest of the rain has also been focused across Scotland and Northern Ireland while parts of England and Wales have continued to be much drier than normal.
Parts of Herefordshire for instance have only received a tenth of the rainfall they would normally have seen by mid-October so far this month.
Some of the biggest impacts of the dry weather have been across the southern England where exceptionally low reservoir levels have prompted the Environment Agency to declare "severe drought" in some areas.
- Is there a hosepipe ban in my area? What you need to know 
  - Published18 hours ago
The quiet before the storm?
A change in the position of that jet stream and its strength is expected through the coming week.
This will allow deeper low pressure systems to affect more parts of the UK marking a shift to a more widespread wetter and windier weather.
Forecasts will need to be monitored closely as there is potential later in the week that we could see our first spell of widely disruptive weather this season.
There are also longer term signals for increased rainfall and storminess later in autumn and early winter in the UK.
The Met Office's current three month outlook covering October, November and December forecasts a double the normal chance of wetter weather and 1.3 times the normal chance of windier weather which is consistent with the type of patterns seen with previous El Niño events.
When do we see the most named storms?
Storms are most often named when potentially damaging winds are forecast, but can also be named for flooding rain or disruptive snow.
They were first named to help bring public attention to episodes of severe weather, to help people prepare to avoid the worst impacts by planning ahead.
In Europe, there are five storm naming groups created from the meteorological agencies based in a similar geographic location.
The UK, Ireland, and the Netherlands form the western storm-naming group which started naming storms in 2015.
Weather systems are named by the the UK's Met Office, Ireland's Met Éireann and Netherland's KNMI based on expected weather impacts as well as how likely those are.
Although named storms can affect the UK at any time of the year, analysis shows they are much less common in spring and early summer. The only month with no named storms in the eleven years that we've been naming storms in the UK, is May.
The chances of seeing a storm increases from late summer and throughout autumn with the peak of the season arriving in our winter months. This increase in storminess is why the storm-naming season begins in September each year.
It is not unusual to still be awaiting the arrival of the first storm at this time of year. In about half of the years since 2015, the first storm arrived after 1 November.
  - Published1 September
  - Published3 September
brief: So far this autumn wet and windy weather patterns have been steered away from the UK. When could we see that change?

title: Evacuation orders as fast-moving California wildfire burns homes
body:
Evacuation orders as fast-moving California wildfire burns homes
- Published
Evacuation orders in California are in effect due to a rapidly growing wildfire that has already burned six homes in the southern Los Angeles area.
The Norte Fire erupted on Friday in Orange County and quickly grew to 465 acres by the evening. One firefighter suffered heat exhaustion while battling the blaze.
Officials say the fierce Santa Ana winds will blow until Saturday, bringing further risk of more conflagrations.
The US National Weather Service (NWS) has issued a red flag warning for several California counties due to strong, gusty winds combined with low humidity and dry vegetation that create critical wildfire spread conditions.
The Norte Fire is one of 13 burning across the state, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection.
In an update on Friday evening, Division 3 Fire Chief Mark Backoff said that six homes had either been damaged or destroyed by the Norte Fire, and one firefighter had been injured from heat exhaustion.
"We continue to engage in the firefight, and have additional resources coming," he said.
Footage posted online showed blazes tearing through homes in the communities of San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano.
The Bryson Fire, burning in the affluent coastal city of Malibu in Los Angeles county, has also sparked evacuation orders throughout the Santa Monica mountains and has grown to 147 acres.
More than 400 firefighters have been fighting the blaze.
Further south, the Henderson Fire in San Diego country erupted on Thursday, and has grown to over 2,000 acres, including around Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton.
The size of the blaze has twice forced officials to close the I-5 highway, an important route that runs the length of the US West Coast.
The fires are being fanned by the Santa Ana winds, which normally begin during cooler months from late September to May.
Officials say the winds peaked on Friday, but will remain dangerous into early Saturday morning.
Winds topped 40mph (64km/h) in the Los Angeles area, the NWS said, adding that motorists should watch for debris blown into roadways.
Temperatures were far above average for this time of year in southern California, further driving up the fire danger.
The NWS has issued a heat advisory, saying that the danger of heat-related illness remained high.
Forecasts expect temperatures to reach 95F (35C) in southern California on Saturday.
brief: Fanned by the fierce Santa Ana winds, the Norte Fire is one of 13 burning across the state.

title: Living with a stink? Technology might help
body:
Living with a stink? Technology might help
- Published
Milpitas, an affluent city in California's Silicon Valley tech hub, has an odour problem.
For decades, residents have had to endure rank smells wafting from industrial sites, among them a 342-acre landfill.
"When I first moved here, I could not open my window for over 10 years," says Chia-Ling Kong, an engineer for a tech firm who lives around half a mile from the dump.
While things have got better in recent years, Kong says she and her neighbours must still contend with around "two or three hours of bad smells a day".
Perhaps befitting Silicon Valley, the community is putting its hopes in technology.
The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered by local authorities to use drones and install monitors to systematically track and measure the chemicals responsible for bad odours. They have also been told to automate the collection of landfill gases responsible for smells.
Kong is optimistic a data-driven approach will make a difference. "Hopefully with this continuous monitoring, it makes it easier to pinpoint problems at the moment it starts."
The operators of the landfill say they are committed to operating it safely and protecting air quality.
Just like in Milpitas, where Kong is part of a citizen's campaign against the odours, communities around the world are raising a stink about bad smells making day-to-day life miserable. Sometimes a rubbish dump is to blame, or it might be a sewage treatment works, or a reeking factory.
When the complaints start stacking up, resolving them is not always simple. Many countries have no regulations in place dictating how to manage smells.
In the US, for example, the Environmental Protection Agency does not regulate environmental odours as a pollutant. This leaves states and local governments to take charge of the issue.
Urban sprawl is often part of the problem, bringing communities closer to stinky facilities that may historically have been kept at a distance.
This is creating more demand for technologies to monitor and prevent smells. Odour consultant Micheal Bull says people are increasingly concerned about neighbourhood stinks.
"You're getting developments being built nearer to odorous processes… as land has become more valuable, there is also infilling," Bull says. He is speaking about his experiences in the UK, but it's a similar story in many parts of the world.
The technologies used to tackle industrial pongs generally fall into three categories: they absorb odours; convert them into something less smelly through a chemical reaction; or burn them away.
Experts on fixing industrial odours say that the best technologies, when used correctly, can remove 90% or more of the target compounds responsible for smells.
But this can be expensive and some operators opt for simpler and cheaper solutions. These include masking odours from landfill or sewage processing by spraying giant quantities of deodorisers.
Odour experts contacted for this article were dubious about the effectiveness of such industrial scale air fresheners. "In my view they're not likely to change the odours," says Bull, who likens them to fabric conditioner.
Bad smells from waste sites – a common cause of complaints – are among the stinkiest and most difficult to resolve, according to Carlos Diaz, an environmental consultant based in Spain. "Landfill is difficult to treat because you have a very large surface," he says.
In some places at least, technology is making a real difference. Residents in Des Moines, Iowa, have long complained of the so-called Eastside Funk, a putrid scent that residents report drifts over parts of the city.
A study commissioned by city authorities showed that a trio of industrial meat companies were among culprits.
"Within 10 miles, there's about half a million people," says Dalton Jacobus, who works in the Department of Neighborhood Services. "If the winds are out of the wrong direction, 100,000 people can be in the middle of that odour plume."
The authorities are now paying around $240,000 (£182,000) a year on technology to track the stink, so they can take action. "What we wanted to do was build a ring of odour monitors around the facilities that we suspected of emitting odours," says Jacobus.
The monitors, which measure levels of chemical compounds in the air, work in combination with a weather station to provide real-time data on the concentrations that are coming from each facility based off the wind patterns.
This has put an end to finger pointing about who's to blame each time a smell sparks complaints, says Jacobus. "Now we can say with reasonable certainty that 'this odour event did originate from your facility, what was going on'?"
Meanwhile, some of the sites that have been blamed for causing unpleasant smells in Des Moines have spent millions of dollars to upgrade their own odour control systems.
Smithfield Foods, which operates a meat processing in Des Moines, says it has invested $2m to install a regenerative thermal oxidiser that destroys the chemicals associated with bad smells. Even so, the company says it does not believe it is the source of odour complaints.
Before installing the monitors – which some local companies help pay for – officials in Des Moines would drive out to the source of a complaint to sniff the air.
Relying on the human nose to sniff out industrial smells is still commonplace. Claudia Barrios Obregón from Kunak, the company behind the monitors in Des Moines, says: "Right now, the way that cities control or measure odours is olfactometry: a human panel measures and gives an opinion of what the odour is like. But that's not that realistic."
The Spanish company's monitors are an example of so-called electronic noses that make it easier to detect smells.
Whatever technology is used, it can be hard to keep everyone happy, as smells are so subjective. "Unfortunately, the general rule is that the nastier we perceive the odour to be, the more sensitive towards it we are," says Johan Lundström, a professor in the science of smell at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden.
Technology of Business
  - Published16 September
  - Published9 September
  - Published2 September
brief: Smells from rubbish dumps and industrial facilities are being more carefully monitored.

title: Severe drought declared and hosepipe bans in force - is your area affected?
body:
Severe drought declared and hosepipe bans in force - is your area affected?
- Published
Severe drought has been declared in parts of southern England after months of dry weather drove some reservoirs to exceptionally low levels.
Most of England and all of Wales were already under drought conditions after both nations' hottest summers on record, which has taken its toll on rivers, crops and nature.
Roughly 30 million people across parts of England and Wales are covered by hosepipe bans, as part of water companies' efforts to manage supplies.
So how is your area doing and are you in a drought?
First 'severe drought' declared
"Severe drought" - the highest category - has now been declared for parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex.
It means environmental authorities will ramp up monitoring of reservoir levels, river flows and water quality, as well as carry out extra checks on businesses withdrawing water from natural sources.
The "severe drought" classification was introduced following the 2012 drought and this is the first time it has been implemented.
The UK government says two previous events would have met the "severe drought" classification, had it been in place. They are:
- August 1976, for Devon and Yorkshire in England, and Gwent, Monmouthshire and Glamorgan in Wales
- November 1995, for Yorkshire only
Most of England and all of Wales were already in drought, following earlier announcements by the Environment Agency (EA) and Natural Resources Wales.
Parts of north-east and north-west England are in the category below drought, called "prolonged dry weather".
There are no official droughts currently in Northern Ireland.
There is no single definition of drought, but it is characterised by a period of low rainfall. As the ground dries out, crops and vegetation can begin to struggle.
If dry conditions persist, rivers, reservoirs and groundwater levels can also fall, putting pressure on water supplies.
The EA says that south-east and south-west England have experienced their driest April to September in more than a century.
Scotland does not declare droughts but monitors "water scarcity" - when there is not enough water of sufficient quality to meet demands of people and the environment.
While conditions have improved in parts of Scotland following recent rainfall, some south-eastern areas remain in the most extreme categories of "moderate" or "significant" scarcity, according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.
Hosepipe bans for millions
Both drought and water scarcity can lead to hosepipe bans - officially called "temporary use bans" - if they are not already in place.
So far, 11 UK water companies have announced hosepipe bans in 2026. This means hosepipes cannot be used for watering gardens, washing vehicles and windows, and filling pools.
Ten companies are spread across central, southern and eastern parts of England, and one is in Wales.
Rivers, reservoirs and groundwater - how are supplies?
Our three main sources of water are reservoirs, rivers and from deep underground.
A key reason why parts of southern England have entered "severe drought" is low reservoir levels.
At this time of year, the Environment Agency says it would expect England's reservoirs to be about three-quarters full, but they are just over half full on average.
Ardingly Reservoir in West Sussex and Wimbleball Reservoir in Somerset are among those at "exceptionally low" levels.
Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water says most reservoir levels in Wales are normal for the time of year.
And reservoir levels in Northern Ireland and Scotland are close to average, according to the latest available data.
Many of the UK's rivers have also been affected by the low rainfall.
Most monitored river flows in England were classed as "below normal", "notably low" or "exceptionally low" in July, according to the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH).
South-east England relies more heavily on groundwater than reservoirs. Groundwater originates as rainfall and is naturally stored beneath the surface in the pore spaces and fractures in rocks.
Groundwater levels were generally declining in September following the prolonged dry weather.
More than half of monitored sites across the UK recorded levels considered "below normal" or lower, with levels particularly low in parts of southern England.
Water can flow more slowly through some rock types than others, sometimes taking years to fully respond to current conditions.
These groundwater stores "respond more slowly to changes in the climate than rivers, which is why they provide a useful buffer during periods of drought", said Prof Alan MacDonald of the British Geological Survey.
It is why groundwater droughts in the south of England generally take a longer time to develop but can be longer-lasting if they do occur.
Is climate change to blame?
Droughts are complex phenomena, driven by a mix of natural and human causes.
The Met Office expects the UK to experience drier summers on average in future as the world warms, though there has been no clear trend so far.
But rising temperatures can play a more direct role by drawing extra moisture from the soil via evaporation.
"A warmer atmosphere is thirstier for moisture and this can mean water in the soil, rivers and reservoirs are depleted more effectively, leading to more rapidly onsetting droughts, heatwaves and wildfires," said Richard Allan, professor of climate science at the University of Reading.
But there are other factors that determine whether dry conditions lead to water shortages, including how we use water.
In a landmark review into the water sector of England and Wales, water companies were criticised for historic underinvestment in water infrastructure.
And while spring and summer were relatively dry for much of the UK, winter was much wetter than usual, raising questions about how effectively water is being managed.
As part of plans to address water shortages, the government and water companies are planning nine new reservoirs for England by 2050, in addition to one under construction at Havant Thicket in Hampshire.
But the EA has warned that measures to tackle water leaks and control water demand - potentially including hosepipe bans - may be needed in England too.
Water companies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland - which are all public bodies or non-profit - also said they were taking steps to secure future supplies.

title: Was Neanderthal life violent? This wound suggests lethal fighting was more common
body:
Was Neanderthal life violent? This wound suggests lethal fighting was more common
- Published
A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been struck through the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, archaeologists say.
They say a 15mm hole found in a shoulder blade in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan could be the earliest evidence of lethal violence involving such a weapon.
From the angle of the wound and other evidence, the researchers believe the spear entered the individual's chest and passed through the body - probably damaging a lung and major blood vessels - and exited through the left shoulder blade to leave a near-perfect hole.
The research is the latest in emerging evidence that suggests Neanderthal societies experienced more violence than previously thought.
Neanderthals were a separate species of humans that went extinct around 40,000 years ago. They lived across a large expanse of Europe and western and central Asia, and sometimes overlapped with our species, Homo sapiens.
The wounded Neanderthal's remains were found in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. As well as the left shoulder blade, the individual's right hand, three ribs and some teeth were also found.
A hole in the shoulder blade may be the earliest evidence of "lethal interpersonal violence" from a wooden spear, according to Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology.
"The fatal strike may have been an intended heart shot," she told BBC News.
Archaeologists call the remains Shanidar A, named after the cave in which they were found. Remains of at least 10 Neanderthals were discovered in excavations in the cave in the 1950s.
The wound is thought to be the first evidence for use of sharpened wooden spears in the prehistoric Middle East, according to Pomeroy.
"It is not the kind of break that you would get naturally, because it is so circular," she said. "Experiments with reconstructed wooden spears produce very similar round holes in bone."
But the interpersonal violence is by no means certain, she says. It may be a case of friendly fire, a wound caused as a result of a hunting accident.
But Prof Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum in London, who was not involved in the research, told BBC News that an attack by a rival was the more plausible explanation.
"The researchers leave it open whether this resulted from a hunting accident or interpersonal violence, but in my view the latter seems more likely, given the positioning and extent of the wound," he said.
This discovery has echoes of an earlier find in the same cave, in 1957. Those remains involved another Neanderthal who lived more recently, around 50, 000 years ago. Their ribs had evidence of a partly healed wound, which archaeologists believe was probably caused by a stone-tipped spear.
We can't tell for sure whether these Neanderthals were hurt by a companion during a hunt or murdered by a rival. But they join a small but growing body of evidence which point to the possibility that human-on-human violence was more common and goes back further than the current scientific consensus would suggest.
"I unfortunately see the growing body of evidence as an indication that interpersonal violence goes deep into human prehistory," Stringer told BBC News.
A key piece of that evidence is a study published in 2022 of very early Neanderthal skulls from northern Spain at an archaeological site called "the Pit of Bones". It suggests that deadly violence was taking place about 430,000 years ago.
Researchers found 57 healed head injuries among 20 individuals. Nine individuals had potentially fatal skull fractures. Six had similar puncture wounds at the back-left of the head. Because the wounds repeatedly occurred in almost the same place, the researchers concluded that deliberate blows were more likely than accidental damage. One skull had two wounds that had probably been inflicted with the same object.
The Pit of Bones findings do not show that everyone in this population was habitually violent, but they provide strong evidence that repeated killing occurred among these people hundreds of thousands of years ago.
For decades, many archaeologists linked the beginnings of organised warfare to farming, when people began living in permanent settlements and competing over land, livestock and food stores.
But evidence from earlier hunter-gatherers and still older human relatives has since shown that individual killings pre-date farming by a very long way.
The live scientific debate is over how common such violence was, and when sporadic attacks became organised conflict and wars between groups.
The research has been published in the journal Scientific Reports.
brief: A 75,000-year-old Neanderthal spear wound may be evidence violence shaped human life far earlier than thought.

title: £15m for zero-emission testing at Belfast Harbour
body:
£15m for zero-emission testing at Belfast Harbour
- Published
Belfast Harbour is to become a live environment for testing zero-emission transport and energy systems.
It comes after a £15m investment from UK Research and Innovation's Local Innovation Partnerships Fund.
The cluster led by Artemis Technologies, will connect electric vessels, high-power marine charging, autonomous transport and energy systems through secure digital twin technology.
Testing these technologies in an operational port will show how they work as an integrated system and help reduce barriers to commercial adoption.
Artemis Technologies CEO Dr Iain Percy said they are creating a digital network that will allow them to "optimise" both transport and energy use.
"What does that mean for most people? It means your bus turns up at the right time in terms of transport.
"But in terms of energy it means, more significantly that when the wind is blowing too hard, the network tells our boat 'take the power' and ultimately as we build up, it tells Belfast Harbour which uses a huge amount of energy 'take that energy'.
"Equally when the wind doesn't blow, it says 'don't use that energy' and what does that mean?
"It means we don't have to shut down windfarms and ultimately lower energy prices," he added.
This is the second project announced from the £30m allocation to the Belfast-Derry Innovation Corridor.
Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said: "It will be developing to try and match up the energy supply with the demands of the harbour, which is a really big user.
"We are really world leading in terms of this so it is a really good investment," she added.
It's hoped what is learned in this project could have wider applications across Northern Ireland.
Dr Percy said: "Where the real accelerator value add comes in here, what can be done on that network can be rinse and repeat anywhere else."
"We already have real buy in from Foyle Port and other regions within Northern Ireland," he added.

title: Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget
body:
Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget
- Published
Chancellor John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the bank sector, senior banking executives have told the BBC.
Healey has described banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, but leaders in the sector have said it will be "on the menu" at the Budget in two weeks' time.
The biggest four banks collectively made about £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, and trade unions have called for them to face additional taxes.
The trade body for the banking sector, UK Finance, warned "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".
Shares in banks including Lloyds and NatWest fell on Friday on expectations that the sector would be hit by tax hikes. The firms were among the biggest fallers on the UK stock market, with both dropping more than 2%.
Barclays fell only slightly and HSBC actually rose as both have large international businesses and would be less affected by a hike in UK taxes.
There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.
One option is for Healey is to reverse a reduction in the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax, from 8% to 3%, introduced in 2023, by Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt.
Critics argue this would be unfair noting the cut coincided with a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%.
Healey could also raise the bank levy - a small percentage charged on loans.
The BBC understands that the Treasury is leaning towards changing the surcharge if they were to go ahead as it is easier to change an existing tax rather than impose a new windfall tax.
Reversing the 2023 surcharge rate would raise around £2bn. However, the last government was persuaded that adding 8% on top of corporation tax of 25% would leave UK banks struggling to compete with European and US rivals - so it may be that it is raised, but not all the way back to the 8% level.
Speaking to the press in Bangkok, Healey praised the role banks play in the British economy.
Adding that he has "decisions to take in the Budget", he said: "My observation on the banks is that people too often see them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects."
In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.
Sir Philip Augar, an author and former banker in the City of London, told the BBC's Today programme there was "room for a moderate increase" in taxes on the sector that could raise up to £3bn a year.
He said lenders were enjoying "booming conditions", benefiting from higher interest rates which boost their profits.
Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which banks lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.
Sir Philip added that when the banking sector "hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out - when it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment".
He said banks cannot simultaneously be "too big to fail and too big to tax".
Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, which represents trade unions, said Britain's four biggest banks are making a billion pounds a week, with bonuses at post-financial crash records. "These are bumper profits - driven by high interest rates and households' mortgage misery," he said.
"Now it's time to make sure banks pay their fair share," he added.
"But if the chancellor does ask the Banks to pay a fairer share of tax in the Budget, that's 100% the right call," he added.
- Burnham announces scheme to help first-time buyers onto housing ladder 
  - Published27 September
- Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget 
  - Published1 day ago
- Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget 
  - Published2 days ago
Banks were pleased to have avoided being targeted at the last Budget, given the large profits they have made in recent years.
There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since.
Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive.
It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.
However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business.
A Treasury spokesperson said: "As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals."

title: Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?
body:
Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?
A new version of Tesla's Roadster electric sports car, equipped with thrusters which apparently allow it to hover and turn in mid-air, has been unveiled in Texas.
"You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," the car firm's CEO Elon Musk said as he presented the vehicle at a facility owned by his SpaceX company, which helped develop the model.
Musk said an audience was needed to prove the car "is not AI", before showing a demonstration of the Roadster driving up and off a steep ramp, spinning in the air, and landing using air jets.
But there are several reasons we're unlikely to see a flying car on our roads anytime soon, as the BBC's technology editor Zoe Kleinman explains.

title: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
body:
I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
- Published
Jess Bacon does all her clothes shopping online.
As a plus-size woman, she finds the size ranges available in stores unreliable. "The sizing in store is notoriously bad. I find it quite demoralising in store," she says.
"The average size woman in the UK is a size 14 or a size 16. I think a lot of people just don't feel seen or represented," says the 29-year-old from Peterborough.
Jess, a culture journalist and author, finds shopping online "much quicker than going into a store, paying for parking, trying things on".
And she feels posting back items that don't fit is less hassle than returning in store, while frequent visits to her local post office give her "more of a community connection".
Jess notes Primark is one of the few High Street retailers where plus-size people can shop. In her experience, Primark stores usually stock up to a size 22.
But soon she'll have the option of staying home even for this - as, after years of holding out, Primark now plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain.
Even throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, when shops were closed, Primark didn't offer the ability to shop online. In 2022 it launched a click-and-collect service, but shoppers still had to travel for their purchases.
The retailer has not said when it expects to launch the service, but has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes.
Analysts say the decision shows Primark is facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein.
Online shopping had been on the rise even before the surge seen during the pandemic.
Online accounted for 27.3% of all retail sales in August this year, according to the Office for National Statistics, up from 18.1% in August 2019.
Internet shopping has also been boosted by the decline of the High Street in many parts of the country, something which Jess has noticed in Peterborough. "We don't have John Lewis [anymore]. There's kind of not that much of a reason to go into town."
'I basically never go into clothes shops'
Like Jess, Julia Mitchell, who lives near Chichester, doesn't enjoy in-person clothes shopping. She finds it overstimulating and thinks there are better bargains to be had online.
"I basically never go into them [clothes shops]. It's not really something I enjoy," the 32-year-old says.
"I guess some people might be able to see stuff and pick it up and look at it, but for me, being able to get the best price is more important."
Julia, a content creator, tries to shop ethically and most of her purchases are second hand from Vinted.
The one thing she never shops online for, though, is books. "The thing about bookshops is that they are cultural spaces and community spaces."
Sandra Davies does all her shopping online. She has had three strokes and finds walking to and around stores too much physically.
"I've tried it on two occasions but on both times, standing in a queue for over 10 minutes was too much for me and I collapsed."
The 61-year-old from Sheffield says waiting for deliveries can be taxing as well, as she worries about missing the postie and having to reschedule.
Returns policy can 'make or break'
Julie Palmer, a retail analyst, is not surprised that Primark has finally moved into home deliveries as it has evidently recognised that "online sales bring scale".
However, she says a shop's returns policy for online purchases can "make or break" it. Many brands offer hassle-free returns, which Palmer says Primark must match in order to compete.
"Shoppers want them to be free, simple and quick. That means a generous window, lots of drop-off options and refunds that land within days, not weeks.
"When a policy is clunky or slow, customers remember it and shop elsewhere next time."
But returns are expensive for retailers. Some, like Asos, have started charging a fee if customers make frequent returns.
This is a balancing act, Palmer says, "because a fee can easily push a customer to a competitor".
"Most retailers that charge still offer free returns in store, which is a deliberate way to get people through the door and hopefully spending again."

  - Published28 September
- Primark finally set to launch home deliveries 
  - Published10 September
