title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
body:
Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
- Published
The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.
Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.
Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.
As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.
BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.
Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.
Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.
The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".
Two crew missing after one of Sunday's attacks
The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.
The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.
Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.
Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".
Oil shipments stall
Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen.
About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day.
The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.
Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.
These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.
So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships.
Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day".
"The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added.
The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media.
Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman.
A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard.
Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said.
Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship.
Additional reporting by Becky Dale
Graphics by Tom Shiel and Mark Edwards
brief: BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows 12 vessels were struck in a week.

title: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
body:
Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
- Published
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division.
Nandy said there were reasonable grounds to believe the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.
Sky said it would "carefully consider" a letter from the culture secretary and "engage constructively" with the review into the deal.
"We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's media and entertainment business together will create a stronger British media," it said.
ITV welcomed the letter and said the deal would help it "compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries".
The two companies announced in July that Sky had agreed to buy ITV's broadcasting business, including its free-to-air TV channels and the ITV X streaming service.
The deal does not include ITV's production arm, ITV Studios, which makes popular programmes such as Love Island and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.
It would give Sky access to millions more viewers, while bosses hope it would help both compete with streaming giants such as Netflix.
- What Sky buying ITV could mean for your favourite shows 
  - Published6 July
But Nandy has told Sky and ITV that she is considering issuing a public interest intervention notice (PIIN) to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) and regulator Ofcom, forcing an investigation into the tie-up.
In a letter to both companies, she said she was minded to order the probe to address public interest considerations including:
- The need for free expression of opinion in news media
- The need for a range of views in news media across the UK
- The need for a range of people controlling the media across the UK
- The need for a wide range of programmes to be offered across the UK
The letter said Nandy recognised Sky News and ITV News were two of the most prominent sources of television news in the UK, with a joint 26% share of those viewing news on linear TV.
Consumers would still have access to other sources of news such as the BBC and Channel 4, it added.
But Nandy believes that, over time, the tie-up could undermine the range of views available to viewers, with 86% of the linear TV news market controlled by the BBC and Sky/ITV.
The North of England could be particularly hard hit as well as nations of the UK other than England and those from lower socio-economic backgrounds, the letter argued.
This is because their main source of news is broadcast news, it added.
Sky and ITV have been given until 20 October to respond to the culture secretary's concerns.
A Sky spokesperson said: "We have already made clear commitments to protect ITV's identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices."
An ITV spokesperson said: "We welcome the publication of the secretary of state's 'minded to' issue a public interest intervention notice letter as was expected and look forward to fully co-operating in the process.
"This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries."
Nandy's intervention would be made under a new public interest consideration.
This would need legislation to be brought forward, given that current laws do not cover the effect of a merger on streaming or on-demand programmes.
She said: "If I decide to intervene on the basis of this new public interest consideration, I will bring forward legislation... to extend the application of the public interest consideration relating to the availability of a wide range of broadcasting to on-demand programmes."
brief: The culture secretary says the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.

title: Living with a stink? Technology might help
body:
Living with a stink? Technology might help
- Published
Milpitas, an affluent city in California's Silicon Valley tech hub, has an odour problem.
For decades, residents have had to endure rank smells wafting from industrial sites, among them a 342-acre landfill.
"When I first moved here, I could not open my window for over 10 years," says Chia-Ling Kong, an engineer for a tech firm who lives around half a mile from the dump.
While things have got better in recent years, Kong says she and her neighbours must still contend with around "two or three hours of bad smells a day".
Perhaps befitting Silicon Valley, the community is putting its hopes in technology.
The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered by local authorities to use drones and install monitors to systematically track and measure the chemicals responsible for bad odours. They have also been told to automate the collection of landfill gases responsible for smells.
Kong is optimistic a data-driven approach will make a difference. "Hopefully with this continuous monitoring, it makes it easier to pinpoint problems at the moment it starts."
The operators of the landfill say they are committed to operating it safely and protecting air quality.
Just like in Milpitas, where Kong is part of a citizen's campaign against the odours, communities around the world are raising a stink about bad smells making day-to-day life miserable. Sometimes a rubbish dump is to blame, or it might be a sewage treatment works, or a reeking factory.
When the complaints start stacking up, resolving them is not always simple. Many countries have no regulations in place dictating how to manage smells.
In the US, for example, the Environmental Protection Agency does not regulate environmental odours as a pollutant. This leaves states and local governments to take charge of the issue.
Urban sprawl is often part of the problem, bringing communities closer to stinky facilities that may historically have been kept at a distance.
This is creating more demand for technologies to monitor and prevent smells. Odour consultant Micheal Bull says people are increasingly concerned about neighbourhood stinks.
"You're getting developments being built nearer to odorous processes… as land has become more valuable, there is also infilling," Bull says. He is speaking about his experiences in the UK, but it's a similar story in many parts of the world.
The technologies used to tackle industrial pongs generally fall into three categories: they absorb odours; convert them into something less smelly through a chemical reaction; or burn them away.
Experts on fixing industrial odours say that the best technologies, when used correctly, can remove 90% or more of the target compounds responsible for smells.
But this can be expensive and some operators opt for simpler and cheaper solutions. These include masking odours from landfill or sewage processing by spraying giant quantities of deodorisers.
Odour experts contacted for this article were dubious about the effectiveness of such industrial scale air fresheners. "In my view they're not likely to change the odours," says Bull, who likens them to fabric conditioner.
Bad smells from waste sites – a common cause of complaints – are among the stinkiest and most difficult to resolve, according to Carlos Diaz, an environmental consultant based in Spain. "Landfill is difficult to treat because you have a very large surface," he says.
In some places at least, technology is making a real difference. Residents in Des Moines, Iowa, have long complained of the so-called Eastside Funk, a putrid scent that residents report drifts over parts of the city.
A study commissioned by city authorities showed that a trio of industrial meat companies were among culprits.
"Within 10 miles, there's about half a million people," says Dalton Jacobus, who works in the Department of Neighborhood Services. "If the winds are out of the wrong direction, 100,000 people can be in the middle of that odour plume."
The authorities are now paying around $240,000 (£182,000) a year on technology to track the stink, so they can take action. "What we wanted to do was build a ring of odour monitors around the facilities that we suspected of emitting odours," says Jacobus.
The monitors, which measure levels of chemical compounds in the air, work in combination with a weather station to provide real-time data on the concentrations that are coming from each facility based off the wind patterns.
This has put an end to finger pointing about who's to blame each time a smell sparks complaints, says Jacobus. "Now we can say with reasonable certainty that 'this odour event did originate from your facility, what was going on'?"
Meanwhile, some of the sites that have been blamed for causing unpleasant smells in Des Moines have spent millions of dollars to upgrade their own odour control systems.
Smithfield Foods, which operates a meat processing in Des Moines, says it has invested $2m to install a regenerative thermal oxidiser that destroys the chemicals associated with bad smells. Even so, the company says it does not believe it is the source of odour complaints.
Before installing the monitors – which some local companies help pay for – officials in Des Moines would drive out to the source of a complaint to sniff the air.
Relying on the human nose to sniff out industrial smells is still commonplace. Claudia Barrios Obregón from Kunak, the company behind the monitors in Des Moines, says: "Right now, the way that cities control or measure odours is olfactometry: a human panel measures and gives an opinion of what the odour is like. But that's not that realistic."
The Spanish company's monitors are an example of so-called electronic noses that make it easier to detect smells.
Whatever technology is used, it can be hard to keep everyone happy, as smells are so subjective. "Unfortunately, the general rule is that the nastier we perceive the odour to be, the more sensitive towards it we are," says Johan Lundström, a professor in the science of smell at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden.
Technology of Business
  - Published16 September
  - Published9 September
  - Published2 September
brief: Smells from rubbish dumps and industrial facilities are being more carefully monitored.

title: 'I paid thousands to a company for jobs that never came'
body:
'I paid thousands to a company for jobs that never came'
- Published
A company has been accused of promising jobs in the healthcare sector which never materialised, leaving people thousands of pounds out of pocket.
Registered in 2025, Synetal Solutions Ltd says it offers career-focused training programmes in the healthcare and IT sectors.
But the BBC has spoken to a number of people who claim they were promised training and support to secure sponsored healthcare jobs that never became available to apply for.
London Citizens Advice says it has seen an increase in recruitment-related scams since the government stopped overseas recruitment for care workers, external. The charity described the firm's practices as "unethical".
Synetal Solutions says it "takes these concerns seriously and disputes the broad allegation that its services or candidate outcomes are fictitious".
'Miserable'
Apurv Patel, who has been in the UK on a Skilled Worker visa since 2023, said he paid Synetal Solutions £3,600 across February and March for healthcare training after he and a friend were verbally promised guaranteed sponsored jobs.
Eight months later he has received no job offers, interviews or meaningful employment support, he said.
"I'm frustrated. I paid money, I wasted my time. I did whatever they wanted without any result," he said.
"It's had a miserable effect on my family and finances."
Patel said he did receive some training but described it as poor quality and ultimately "worthless".
Having previously worked for two years as a healthcare assistant, he said he became concerned when a trainer was unable to answer routine questions about care work.
"She didn't give us any answers and we realised she didn't have any experience of healthcare," he said.
The company disputes claims that training was ineffective.
He also alleged communication with the company deteriorated after he made his second payment, with responses sometimes taking several days.
Patel has since complained to his bank and sought help from Citizens Advice.
The BBC has seen emails from the company advertising a "three-month recruitment programme" offering "training and placement with sponsorship" for £5,500.
Home Office guidance, external states agencies may charge for services such as training or CV-writing assistance, but cannot charge fees solely for finding, or attempting to find, employment.
Responding to questions about its marketing, Synetal Solutions said: "We acknowledge the 'guarantee' wording in the emails supplied and recognise that contractual terms alone do not resolve concerns about those assurances."
As part of its programme, Synetal Solutions created accounts for trainees on iHasco, a health and social care training platform.
The BBC contacted iHasco, which confirmed the company was a customer. However, it said its terms did not permit customers to resell its training content to individuals who were not employees.
The company said it was reviewing Synetal Solutions' account and would take appropriate action if necessary.
Synetal Solutions said it had acted in accordance with its agreement with iHasco.
The Care Quality Commission said there was no single qualification that automatically qualified someone to work as a care worker. Instead, providers are responsible for ensuring employees are appropriately trained and competent for their roles.
The BBC also contacted a number of healthcare organisations whose logos appeared on Synetal Solutions' website as examples of employers where graduates had worked.
Those organisations that responded said they had no links to the company. Some also said they had not authorised the use of their branding, and some said they would not accept certificates provided through the company's training.
Daniel Blake, director of London Citizens Advice, described the company's approach as "exploitative".
"The promises that were made are impossible promises," he said. "They are targeting people with vulnerable immigration status.
"This company is asking for large sums of money upfront without any reputable standards, without any reputable evidence of success, and yet when it goes wrong they are refusing to take any responsibility.
"For us, it seems a very unethical way of conducting business."
He added that no reputable recruitment agency would guarantee a successful outcome without first assessing a candidate and matching them to a suitable role, and urged anybody asked to pay large sums upfront to seek independent advice.
"If it seems too good to be true, it probably is," he said.
The company's website stated: "Synetal Solutions provides the right support, guidance, and guaranteed job placement to help you succeed."
But since the BBC contacted Synetal Solutions mentions of job guarantees were removed from the website.
Its social media channels also promoted healthcare as "one of the most reliable paths" for people seeking visa-sponsored work in the UK.
Sarah and Rahul, whose names we have changed, said they paid £3,000 to Synetal Solutions while seeking sponsored employment before the expiry of their student visas.
Rahul, a former dentist in India, could remain in the UK on a graduate visa for longer, but Sarah's immigration status was close to expiring.
To pay the fee, the couple said they borrowed money from a family friend and took out a loan.
Rahul said he was shocked by the quality of the training.
"The mentor didn't know anything about healthcare," he said.
The couple said they were also shown the names of established healthcare providers, including Bupa, as examples of potential employers. Bupa told the BBC it had no connection with the company.
Synetal Solutions says some of their candidates "told us they had secured employment with Bupa" and the reference was "not intended to suggest a formal partnership with Bupa".
It says it had not verified those outcomes and "cannot attribute the recruitment decisions to our training".
Rahul said he secured one or two interviews, but prospective employers rejected the certificates he had received through the programme.
The couple said Synetal Solutions had since stopped responding to their messages.
"We're desperate," Sarah said. "We don't see any other way out."
Amisha, whose name has also been changed, said she signed up with Synetal after being told that both a placement and visa sponsorship were guaranteed.
Her student visa is due to expire soon.
She said the training consisted of three sessions lasting around 90 minutes each.
After paying an initial instalment of £1,800, she became reluctant to make a second payment because she felt she had received little in return. She said the company warned her that her contract would be cancelled if she failed to pay, prompting her to transfer a further £1,800.
"I was waiting for interviews for two or three months. They were ignoring me," she said.
According to Amisha, the company applied for only a handful of vacancies advertised on job-search website Indeed. She eventually secured an interview for a healthcare assistant role, but said the employer told her the certificates she had received were not recognised.
The BBC also identified what appeared to be at least a couple of stock photographs or AI-generated images used as testimonials on the company's website.
The company said it had not authenticated the two reviews identified, and removed them after we contacted them.
Teni Shahiean, an immigration lawyer at OTS Solicitors, said it was "particularly concerning" where individuals facing visa deadlines were being asked to make substantial payments on the understanding that jobs, sponsorship or immigration outcomes were seemingly guaranteed.
She urged caution, adding that a job offer alone does not guarantee someone will be able to remain in the UK.
"The outcome can depend on the role, the sponsor, the individual meeting the relevant immigration requirements and, ultimately, any decision by the Home Office," she said.
'Go to the police'
Blake told the BBC: "If it seems good to be true, it probably is. If you are considering handing over money upfront then seek advice."
He said that "if people have given money and haven't received the service that they were entitled to they should seek redress".
"First of all, make a complaint directly to the company, then to Trading Standards.
"If people feel a criminal offence has happened, we would encourage and support them to go to the police."
A government spokesperson said: "We know how much distress scammers cause to their victims, which is why we will do everything in our power to protect hardworking families and vulnerable customers.
"Our reforms have provided Companies House with new and improved powers to prevent companies from acting unlawfully and to query, remove and share suspicious information."
Synetal Solutions said: "We provide training and employment assistance and maintain supporting records. Recruitment, sponsorship and visa decisions depend on employers and the Home Office."
The company said it had records of genuine candidates who had secured jobs and sponsorship through its services.
Get in touch
Have you been affected by issues covered in this story? Share your experiences.
brief: Apurv Patel is one of several people who say they were promised job opportunities that did not appear.

title: How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections
body:
How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections
- Published
A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. 
Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings with staff to track their impact and working on new legislation aimed at curbing their rapid expansion across the country.
"This happens sometimes, something starts slow and then it goes fast," the senior policy adviser to the Democratic senator told the BBC. The person spoke on condition of anonymity as they are not permitted to speak to the press.
The 180-degree turn in this senator's attention was driven almost entirely by a growing wave of public backlash that has seen politicians across the country scramble to keep up. Public sentiment has turned against the expansion of data centres, the large warehouses that store processing power needed for internet activity.
Packed with rows and rows of computer chips, sometimes seven-feet high, data centres have turned into more than infrastructure for the internet. They are now the physical embodiment of the recent and explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and the varied fears people associate with it.
"I don't want to be the guinea pig for this," Indiana resident Angelita Soriano told the BBC.
A new Amazon data centre is being built directly across the street from her home. When complete, the 26-building structure will take up more than a square mile in her neighbourhood and maintain 782 diesel-powered generators.
Some data centres are even larger. In Ohio, a joint effort between OpenAI, Nvidia, SB Energy and the US Department of Energy is set to build a data centre complex that will stretch for roughly six square miles, the same size as most townships in the US.
There are about 3,000 data centres currently operating in the US, with that number potentially doubling in the next few years, according to a report by, external Pew Research Center.
Data centres are built through very local rules and permits, meaning federal lawmakers like US senators have little say in the process.
Yet, opposition has become so strong so quickly in the US that suddenly, politicians at all levels are now all but required to take a stand.
"This isn't just an issue on the left, there is huge pushback among conservatives to data centres," Chloe Autio, an AI policy adviser, said. "Whoever articulates a clear position and sticks to it, in either party, really stands to benefit."
Her analysis was echoed by the adviser to the US senator working on data centre legislation.
"There is a clear policy need here that we're looking to fill," he said. "This is a major backlash across the country - constituents are seeing the impacts of data centres and they do not like them."
That has put many on Capitol Hill - even Republicans - in direct conflict with President Donald Trump, who has championed the unrestrained growth of AI technology.
Trump has dubbed the backlash to data centres a "sick conspiracy" and said people and towns working to keep the buildings out are "backwards and poor".
His ire has been used as a boon to Democratic politicians looking to draw midterm votes from unhappy or undecided constituents.
The BBC spoke to residents of Indiana, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon, all of whom have been organising locally against the development of data centres. They expressed concerns about many aspects of the buildings, including their size, construction and operational noise, their impact on air, water and energy resources, as well as the speed at which they seem to be approved by local authorities.
During the first few months of this year, community groups organising against data centres more than doubled to 833, cropping up in almost every US state, according to research from Data Center Watch. The firm collects data for AI industry stakeholders and is part of an AI startup 10a Labs.
Stephanie Maldonado, the political director of LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, referred to the pushback against data centres as "a David and Goliath story" that began several years ago.
"People have been ready to put a stop to it," Maldonado added. "Now, people are angry."
New national polling, external shows that AI regulation and data centres are among some of the top issues for voters this election cycle, behind the ongoing Iran war and various aspects of the economy.
Proponents of building data centres often argue the projects will create more, and better paying, local jobs.
Yet, recent research, external from the Brookings Institution, a non-partisan policy research group, found that a new data centre creates between 100 and 200 local jobs, which is "fewer than industry advocates claim". The projects also have essentially no impact on local wages.
Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs was one such proponent - until public pressure pushed her to the other side of the issue. In July, she enacted a three-year pause on any new tax break given to a company for a data centre project.
Arizona is far from the only state to see politicians react to data centre backlash.
Abdul El Sayed, a Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, made new rules and regulations for data centres a clear part of his successful primary campaign for Senate.
In the race for governor of Georgia, a Democrat who is calling for a pause on data centre development is in a dead heat with a Republican who disagrees.
Republican Senator John Husted of Ohio, who is fighting to keep his seat against Democrat Sherrod Brown, has also had to shift his position. Recent polls, external have found that the majority of Ohio voters oppose data centres. He has softened his support, saying that their arrival should be up to local citizens and elected officials.
Meanwhile, Brown has stumped on his opposition to new data centres. He leads Husted in recent polls.
Husted's trouble in Ohio led the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the major fundraising arm for conservatives in the Senate, to write in a private memo, external that Republican politicians needed to entirely reframe how they spoke to voters on data centres.
"This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle," the NRSC added.
Texas is perhaps the most clear cut example of how backlash has turned into an undeniable issue for even the most pro-business politician.
The state currently has almost 300 operational data centres, with another 170 planned for development, according to Pew data.
At the end of last year, Republican Governor Greg Abbott had boasted of Texas as "the epicentre of AI development" because of the number of data centres it housed.
Within months he was backtracking, citing concerns of "safety and quality of life".
It could play a part in the state's upcoming Senate race too.
Democrat James Talarico's campaign is pushing for an end to "sweetheart tax deals" for Big Tech. He's now seen as a frontrunner for the historically Republican seat, where he is facing off against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Paxton said in a late September interview that there was still "plenty of open space in Texas that we can put data centres".
Many of the actions or proposals that have come from politicians looking to appease or address these voters are temporary. Most of the moratoriums, for instance, will end in one to three years.
It is possible that the political winds will have shifted by the time such moratoriums expire, leaving Big Tech and AI firms to build as they wish.
For now, people's feelings toward them are strong.
Balaji Tammabattula, the chief executive of Barupon, is developing a roughly 700-acre data centre and technology campus in Liberty, Texas. Despite the buildings being designed to use rain capture for water and supply its own energy needs, an increasingly common design for major data centre projects, Tammabattula told the BBC that people in the community oppose the project out of hand.
"There's just such a high level of tension from the jump that you can't really even break through with the facts," he said.
During a recent community event, Tammabattula said he tried to speak one-on-one with a woman who was vociferously opposed to the project.
"She just looked right at me and said, 'Get the hell out of my state.'"
brief: Democrats and Republicans alike are coming out against data centre development, amid growing backlash across the US.

title: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
body:
Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
- Published
Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery.
The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.
The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing green vestments while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital.
Pope Leo "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said.
- Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next 
  - Published2 days ago
Also on Friday, the Pope phoned Russian President Vladimir Putin from hospital to urge a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where access to food and water has been cut off for thousands.
"The fact that he accepted the call and spoke with the Pope may, I hope, be a sign that the Pope's request will indeed be carried out," said Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's secretary of state.
Without mentioning a ceasefire, the Kremlin said: "The Vatican's intention to help create the conditions necessary to ensure the safety of the town's population and to organise vital supplies has been supported".
"It has been agreed to cooperate on this matter," it added.
The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Turk, made a similar plea to address what he described as a "desperate" situation in Oleshky.
The Pope's doctors said on Friday tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his surgery.
His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung".
The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.
"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital.
Pope Leo first announced that he would be having the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
The Vatican has stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure.
Additional reporting by Joel Guinto
Related topics

  - Published2 days ago
brief: The pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after having surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday.

title: Russian man linked to deadly London hospitals hack arrested
body:
Russian man linked to deadly London hospitals hack arrested
- Published
German police have detained a Russian man accused of being part of a cyber-crime gang which caused chaos at London hospitals and contributed to a patient's death.
The hack of blood testing company Synnovis in 2024 led to disrupted pathology services across several London hospitals and was the first cyber attack in history to be directly linked to a death.
The BBC can confirm German detectives are now including the incident in their investigation into the detained Russian and his associates.
Separately, the BBC has learned that British police are examining whether its own inquiry may lead to an unlawful killing case - potentially a world first in cyber-crime.
The detained suspect is a 28-year-old Russian man named by German press as Vladimir K.
He was arrested in Japan in May when he travelled to the country for a holiday.
According to German officials, the suspect's holiday plans were intercepted and he was arrested by Japanese police when he entered the country.
He is accused of being one of the core members of the Qilin cyber-crime gang - which has allegedly hacked more than 4,000 organisations since 2024 and extorted more than $140m (£105m) from victims.
Vladimir K was wanted in Germany for hacking into a logistics company in September 2024, encrypting data on its systems and extorting it for around $160,000 in cryptocurrency.
While his extradition was first reported in early October, external, the BBC can now confirm German police are including the Synnovis hack in their investigations.
Synnovis hack
Synnovis is diagnostics and pathology service which operates as a partnership between the hospitals and German company Synlab.
A critical incident was declared at some London hospitals after the provider was targeted by Qilin on 3 June 2024, with blood transfusion services severely disrupted, operations cancelled and emergency patients diverted elsewhere.
King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, one of two trusts heavily impacted, confirmed a year after the hack that one patient had also "died unexpectedly".
A spokesperson for the trust said a number of contributing factors led to the patient's death including "a long wait for a blood test result".
"The patient safety incident investigation identified a number of contributing factors that led to the patient's death," they said at the time.
A similar attack in 2020 by a different hacker group on a hospital in Düsseldorf in Germany led to a negligent homicide investigation being opened after an elderly patient died.
It was later dropped after medical experts concluded the patient's condition was so severe that they would have died regardless of the issues caused by the cyber-attack.
Prosecutors could also not definitively prove that it was the direct cause of death.
In total, the Synnovis hack in 2024 disrupted more than 10,000 appointments and caused weeks of disruption.
The hackers also threatened to publish the data on their dark net website unless Synnovis paid a ransom.
The criminals eventually published the highly private data online after no ransom was paid.
At the time, they told the BBC the hack was not just for the money but to protest the UK's lack of help in the Russian war on Ukraine.
But the hackers did not say if they were from Russia or Ukraine, and their claims were dismissed as an attempt to distance themselves from the cyber-crime extortion tactics Qilin were known for.
The group, which has been tracked since 2022, is behind a string of criminal hacks targeting schools, hospitals, companies, councils and health organisations.
It was also behind the high profile and disruptive hack on Japanese beer maker Asahi in October 2025.
It is very rare for hackers to be arrested in Russia as its government refuses to co-operate with Western law enforcement requests.

  - Published25 June 2025
  - Published14 January 2022
brief: The 28-year-old detained by German police is accused of being part of the cyber-crime gang that hacked blood-test firm Synnovis in 2024.

title: Covid vaccine compensation scheme set for overhaul after Inquiry criticism
body:
Covid vaccine compensation scheme set for overhaul after Inquiry criticism
- Published
The government has committed to reform of the scheme that provides financial support for those injured or bereaved by vaccines.
It was a key recommendation of the UK Covid Inquiry, and has been a focus for campaigners.
One campaign group has welcomed the recognition that vaccine injury and bereavement is real and that the current scheme is not fit for purpose.
But it says it wants a clear commitment to action by ministers, rather than simply saying they will look further at what needs to be done.
Urgent reform
The benefits of vaccination are well documented. The AstraZeneca Covid jab is credited with saving millions of lives worldwide. But some people have experienced harm.
In her fourth report, the chair of the Covid Inquiry, Baroness Hallett, called for better support for those affected.
She said while this was a minority, the way they are supported needed urgent reform.
More than 24,000 people have made Covid-related claims to the Vaccine Damage Payment Scheme (VDPS), a form of financial support paid by the government, but just over 1% have resulted in one-off tax-free awards of £120,000.
The report called for "urgent" reform of the scheme, saying that it is "not sufficiently supportive".
It said the current system, in which those affected must show they have been at least "60% disabled", does not work effectively for Covid vaccines.
In its response to the report, the government says, external it is committed to reviewing the scheme to ensure it is "fit for purpose and delivered effectively."
Ministers in England have promised to work closely with the other nations of the UK as well as those injured by the Covid vaccine and their families.
Campaigners want action
One of the main campaign groups for those who were injured by the Covid vaccine is Vaccine Injured and Bereaved UK.
The group welcomed the government's acknowledgement that vaccine injury and bereavement were real and that the VDPS is not fit for purpose.
But in a statement it said that was not the same as committing to action.
"After more than five years of campaigning, and with the Covid-19 Inquiry explicitly calling for reform as soon as possible, we had hoped the Government would finally come forward with a clear commitment to action, not simply say it would look further at what needs to be done.
"We understand that work may be needed to develop the reforms, but there is a real difference between saying you will look at something and committing to deliver it.
"Today, we have no clear timetable, no certainty about what will change and no assurance about when families will finally see meaningful progress."
Running costs of scheme
The Government response also said it recognised there were concerns about the running costs of the scheme.
Last month it was revealed that the VDPS has cost £83m to run since April 2022.
The amount spent on administration costs and medical assessments was more than double the £32m paid out in financial support to victims so far.
Ministers say they will ensure the scheme is working properly.
brief: Ministers promise to reform the scheme that provides financial support for those injured or bereaved by vaccines in the UK.

title: Ten-year-old Willow among children to benefit from pioneering same-day test to spot infections
body:
Ten-year-old Willow among children to benefit from pioneering same-day test to spot infections
- Published
A pioneering same-day test has been used to detect hidden and drug-resistant infections among children in intensive care.
Respiratory samples from more than 100 critically ill young patients at London's Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH) were sent for what is known as metagenomic testing., external
It can identify bacteria, viruses and fungi from a single sample, which in many cases influences what doctors prescribe.
Metagenomics can detect infections that standard tests miss, meaning better outcomes for some critically ill patients.
'The test... saved her life'
In March, 10-year-old Willow Crowther became dangerously ill with pneumonia, which triggered a seizure and multiple cardiac arrests.
Willow, from Kent, was admitted to intensive care at GOSH. Her mum, Stacey Moore, was told she had a 50% chance of survival.
"The consultant said... we should bring our family up to say goodbye to her. This is how critical and in how much danger she was of passing away."
The team at GOSH used metagenomics - a diagnostic test that works by sequencing all genetic material present, in contrast to conventional methods where clinicians need to decide in advance what they're looking for.
The test identified that Willow had a drug-resistant bacterial infection which needed a different antibiotic to the one she had been prescribed.
"The fact that they had a test there available to her was paramount. It saved her life," said Stacey.
"It's a miracle she's here and we're extremely grateful for that," added Willow's dad, Russ.
With the right treatment, Willow was eventually able to recover from her infection, but needed several months in hospital.
She is one of many patients at the children's hospital to benefit from the new type of testing.
During a study in 2024-5 metagenomic testing was used on 122 critically ill children in the paediatric intensive care unit (ICU) at GOSH.
The results have now been published in the Lancet Microbe.
Metagenomic testing analyses all genetic material in a sample and can detect thousands of different pathogens.
By contrast, the most common method of identifying bacteria is by trying to culture them in Petri dishes, a technology that has been used since Victorian times.
Another test, PCR, can identify viruses and some bacteria, but doctors need to specify what they are trying to detect.
Metagenomics testing at GOSH was able to identify around nine in 10 bacteria and viruses and all fungi in samples.
In a quarter of cases, the results influenced prescribing decisions, including starting, stopping or changing an antibiotic.
Dr Sam Ray, consultant in paediatric intensive care medicine at GOSH and co-author of the study said traditional testing required clinicians to make an educated guess about which infection they were looking for.
"The study has helped us to spot infections we would have missed, get children on the right treatment and stop antibiotics when we know they aren't going to work.
"Removing unnecessary treatment is incredibly important for the fight against growing antimicrobial resistance."
Metagenomic testing at GOSH also detected 50 organisms not identified by routine diagnostics, meaning it could play an early warning role against new infections.
Dr Julianne Brown, head of the GOSH Metagenomics Service and co-senior author of the study said the new testing was being gradually rolled out to around 30 intensive care units across the UK treating both adults and children.
"It could be a powerful tool for identifying new infections that pose a pandemic threat," she added.
"In the future, if there was to be a new mystery pathogen that could be a cause of the next pandemic, we would detect that very quickly and put the right measures in place."
The project at GOSH builds on trials at Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Trust which first used metagenomics to test for respiratory infections in adult patients.
- Boy with rare condition amazes doctors after world-first gene therapy 
  - Published24 November 2025

title: Trans people should use hospital spaces according to biological sex, NHS England says
body:
Trans people should use hospital spaces according to biological sex, NHS England says
- Published
Trans patients should be cared for on single-sex hospital wards or bays that align with their biological sex rather than their gender identity, according to new NHS England (NHSE) guidance.
It says when this is not "clinically appropriate" then alternative arrangements should be made and the dignity and safety of all patients should be maintained.
The guidance also says staff facilities should be used by people based on their biological sex, while trusts should ensure enough alternatives to single-sex facilities, such as single-occupancy toilets, are offered.
Previous NHSE guidance suggested patients and staff could be accommodated on wards or use facilities based on their gender identity.
That meant that a trans woman – a biological male who identifies as a woman – could have chosen to be on a women's ward, or a trans man – a biological female who identifies as a man – could have opted for a men's ward.
That guidance was withdrawn following the Supreme Court ruling in April 2025 that under equality law the term "sex" means biological sex and "woman" refers to a biological woman.
The judgment said for a space or service to be single sex it should only allow those of the same biological sex to use it.
Also under the new guidance issued on Thursday, NHSE emphasised that in order to avoid discriminating against trans people they should be offered gender neutral spaces.
But the guidance also says decisions may have to be made on a case-by-case basis and must ensure clinical needs are met.
It also makes clear that there are circumstances where clinical need is the overriding priority, including on emergency units and urgent care settings.
In addition to the patient document of the guidance, NHSE has published advice for trusts on how to organise changing rooms, toilets and other single-sex facilities for staff.
Again, it says they should be used by people based on their biological sex, not their gender identity.
The document encourages NHS trusts in England to carry out an audit to ensure they are offering enough alternatives to single-sex facilities, for instance, gender neutral or single occupancy toilets.
Pressures on hospitals mean many have already struggled to keep wards single sex.
NHSE data shows that the number of breaches of the previous mixed-sex accommodation guidance has been growing every year since 2021- where members of the opposite sex were placed on a single-sex ward.
The most recent figure for August 2026 shows there were 5,520 breaches, compared to 3,853 in June 2025.
Sex-based rights charity Sex Matters has welcomed the guidance as a "momentous shift back to reality", but is concerned about how it will be applied.
"NHS patient data is a mess, with potentially thousands of trans-identifying people recorded as the opposite sex," CEO Maya Forstater said.
Trans rights organisations TransActual and Trans+ Solidarity Alliance have said they are concerned NHS staff will be unclear on how to safely look after trans patients.
"This guidance will not survive contact with reality in resource-strapped hospitals and will create unworkable operational challenges," they said.
The NHS has been at the centre of a number of high-profile arguments over the interpretation of equality law and workplace regulations.
In January 2026, Darlington Memorial Hospital was found to have violated the dignity of a group of nurses who complained about a transgender colleague - a biological male who identified as a woman - being allowed to use the female changing rooms. The nurses were told they should change somewhere else if they objected.
The tribunal concluded that the trust had indirectly discriminated against them.
The nurses are currently seeking £400,000 from the NHS to cover their legal costs.
One of the nurses who brought the action, Bethany Hutchison, who is now president of the Darlington Nurses Union, says they welcome the "clear and necessary guidance" from NHSE, but the test will be whether trusts follow it.
"The Darlington nurses should never have had to take their own employer to court to secure privacy, dignity and lawful single-sex facilities," she said.
"Enforcement cannot continue to depend on the courage and personal sacrifice of individual nurses."
In Scotland, another employment tribunal found, in December 2025, that a nurse, Sandie Peggie, had been harassed by NHS Fife over its interpretation of rules on single sex spaces.
Peggie had complained about a doctor, who was a trans woman, using the female changing rooms.
She was suspended after raising concerns. The tribunal dismissed her other claims of discrimination and victimisation.
An appeal is under way and expected to reach the courts next year.

brief: New guidance says trans patients should be cared for on single-sex hospital wards or bays that align with their biological sex.

title: I'm 12 and I want to try protein powder - should I?
body:
I'm 12 and I want to try protein powder - should I?
- Published
Twelve-year-old Ben is desperate to try protein powder but there's one hurdle: me, his mum.
"I've asked about 20 times and you just keep saying no!", he says, claiming it would make him "fitter and bigger" and that his male friends use it.
In recent years, there's been an explosion of products marketed as "high protein", including milk, yoghurt, breads, cereals, bars and powders.
Social media is flooded with adverts for various supplements, including protein powder.
As a health journalist, I'm sceptical and think at Ben's age he must be getting enough protein through his diet.
So, do experts think it's safe for pre-teens and teenagers or is a big, juicy steak just as good?
My sport-obsessed son, who already eats a healthy balanced diet, asks me about protein powder on a regular basis.
His friend Louis, 12, has been using protein powder once or twice a week for nearly a year, after a workout and on top of whole foods. His parents are aware of this.
"I think it's helped, it gives me more energy and it's helped me grow, probably," he says.
But Ben's other friend Otis, who is 13, is not keen on the idea and feels there is pressure on young people to take protein supplements.
"They might just start using them without thinking about the consequences or what effects it may have on them."
Why do we need protein?
Proteins break down into amino acids that help the body grow and repair.
But your body can't make all the amino acids it needs on its own, so you need to get more - known as essential amino acids - through your diet.
For an adult with a healthy weight, the recommended daily amount of protein you should be eating is 0.75 grams per kg of body weight, according to the NHS.
A good rule of thumb is that the amount of protein you have for each meal should fit into the palm of your hand.
If you exercise a lot, and when you get older, you need more protein so you could have up to 2 grams per kg of body weight.
But do teens really need it if they're eating well?
For teenage boys and girls "you can get all the protein that you need from food alone", says registered dietitian Nichola Ludlam-Raine.
It is important that teenage girls, especially, get enough iron and calcium, so Ludlam-Raine says not to become overly focused on protein at the expense of other nutrients.
Protein shakes, powders or bars can be useful for some, including high-level athletes and those who have certain allergies, but they should not replace a healthy diet.
There can also be some unwanted side effects from using protein powders such as bloating, gas, cramps, and diarrhoea.
Those with pre-existing health conditions should not use it unless they have been told they can by their doctor.
Ludlam-Raine points out that the protein powder market is not as tightly regulated as medicines.
"Of course, you can get reputable companies who do third-party testing and make sure that what you see on the label is what is in the inside, but that's not always the case," she says.
"And ultimately you can't just have a shake and your biceps grow."
Some protein powders contain high amounts of added sugar, artificial ingredients, and hidden stimulants.
Dr Ramnik Mathur is a consultant paediatrician from West London.
He explains that we need micronutrients like zinc, calcium and magnesium, which are found in whole foods.
So, if meals are replaced with protein shakes, those nutrients are lost.
Experts suggest spreading out protein across the day and aiming for 20-25g per meal. If you're keen to up your intake, try some of these recipes.
During puberty when children have growth spurts, they do need more protein because their body is growing rapidly, building new muscle and bone mass.
But Mathur says there are risks to eating too much protein.
"If you look at social media, they'll say you need to eat a lot of protein, but your body can handle only so much."
He explains that if you eat too much, it has to be excreted by the kidneys and liver which can become overloaded and have serious health implications.
The key takeaway from Mathur: "If a 12-year-old child is eating a healthy balanced diet then they shouldn't need any more protein."
Ludlam-Raine's advice is to get teens to improve their diet first before taking any protein powder, especially regularly.
If they still want to use it, speak to a registered dietitian or nutritionist first.
Now off I go to tell my son the answer is still no - and the experts say the same.

title: Cut screen time in classrooms to avoid long-term health issues, clinicians urge
body:
Cut screen time in classrooms to avoid long-term health issues, clinicians urge
- Published
The amount of time children in England spend on screens at school could be harming their "physical and developmental health", a group of more than 150 clinicians has warned.
GPs, paediatricians and other specialists said in an open letter to Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Health Secretary Yvette Cooper that tablets and laptops are being used without a full understanding of their long-term health impacts, including on eye health.
The clinicians said they are prescribing glasses, hearing aids and speech therapy to children "for a problem that is unintentionally being made worse in our schools".
The government said it was consulting on screen time guidance for children aged five to 18 but that technology could be a powerful learning tool if used properly.
The group of clinicians said nearly one million children are using screens in most lessons, despite studies suggesting a rise in short-sightedness.
They pointed to an analysis of 276 studies covering 5.4 million participants around the world.
That analysis, they claimed, found a rise in short-sightedness among children and adolescents from around 24% in 1990 to almost 36% by 2023, warning the condition is associated with an increased risk of a range of eye health problems.
Many children now spend longer on screens in the classroom than is recommended in a 24-hour period, the letter said, adding: "As a country, we need to wake up to this now, and start rolling back screen use in schools before the damage compounds further."
One of its signatories was Dr Becky Foljambe, an NHS GP and founder of Health Professionals for Safer Screens. She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme parents had not been given the chance to "opt out" of the "excessive" use of screens in schools, which risks children "just not thriving" in education.
She said an "explosion" in short-sightedness "cannot be put down to genetics alone".
Foljambe said it was a "lazy argument" to advocate for screen use to prepare children for a digital world, adding: "They also need their sleep, their eyesight, they need rest, they need ability to critically think and appraise."
- WhatsApp introduces optional parental controls for teenagers 
  - Published30 September
"We are conscious that some of this evidence is still surfacing but the direction of travel is consistent across multiple, independent, and in some cases very large, bodies of research," the letter continued.
It also warned that children with special educational needs are "disproportionately" directed to screen-based learning.
Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said education technology can provide schools with "very effective learning tools".
But he said such technology was only part of an "overall learning strategy", which also includes classroom discussion and interaction, and that the school day also has "plenty of non-screen time such as PE, sport, and break times with classmates".
"We would welcome the development of practical, evidence-based guidance to support the work of schools in the use of education technology," he added.
Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said it was "important that a healthy balance is struck", adding that "greater clarity is needed from the government on this".
A Department for Education spokesperson said the government was developing new screen-time guidance for children aged five to 18, and will consult on the safety of artificial intelligence and educational technology in schools.
They said: "Used well, technology can be a powerful tool to support learners who need it and free up teachers to deliver the excellent education every child deserves."
It comes after a ban on smartphones in schools in England came into force in June, making individual schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day.

brief: A group of clinicians warns technology use in English schools is driving a rise in health problems like short-sightedness.

title: I lost my hair to chemo - now my wigs are worn by A-list stars
body:
I lost my hair to chemo - now my wigs are worn by A-list stars
- Published
When Antonia Okonma Shittu was told she had multiple sclerosis (MS) and would be using a wheelchair within the year, she was in denial.
The 26-year-old, who was in between acting jobs and working in a call centre, said the diagnosis was a "massive turning point" in her life.
"It does really make you think about what you want to do in life," she said.
She looked back to what she enjoyed doing as a child - styling hair - and decided to use the shock of the diagnosis to spur her on to turn her passion into a business.
Antonia, who grew up on a council estate in west London, bought two wigs and went door to door selling them from the boot of her car.
Almost two decades later, she is now a multi-million-pound brand owner, with current and past high-profile clients including tennis icon Serena Williams, actress Niecey Nash and model Naomi Campbell. She even won a Black British Business Award last week.
Antonia, now 44, still struggles with her health, having also received diagnoses of Graves' disease - an autoimmune condition - and heart failure, but hopes her experience running a hair empire while fitting in hospital appointments can inspire other women.
'I didn't feel like myself after losing my hair'
Antonia says she saw a gap in the market when she was surrounded by "terrible" wigs while working in TV and film, including in the ITV series Bad Girls two decades ago.
"Women wanted natural-looking wigs and they just weren't available. They looked like helmets!"
Antonia set up a Facebook page and began advertising on Gumtree. "I had very limited resources. I didn't have any investors behind me. I come from very humble beginnings."
Her experience dealing with MS has helped her success, she says. Antonia lost her hair when she underwent chemotherapy following a bone marrow transplant, so she knows what it is like to be "completely bald".
This made her relate more deeply to her customers, she explains, as she understands the loss of control some women feel when they lose their hair.
"I didn't feel like myself," she says, "but being able to put on a wig that looks something close to how your hair was, or the look you used to have, it's as though you can feel like yourself again."
When she sees a woman put a wig on and her "whole face lights up", it can be "very, very rewarding".
"When we feel good about ourselves...we're more confident, we can achieve more. I felt like I was changing the world, one person at a time."
Balancing health and business
While Antonia's business, A-List Lace Hair, has grown from strength to strength, with salons in London and New York, she has been dealing with the impact of her health conditions.
She struggles with fatigue due to her MS and uses a wheelchair, but says this has not stopped her success. Instead, it has simply changed the way she has run her business.
"I used to feel that being a good entrepreneur was being able to do as much as I can myself," Antonia said.
"Due to my health challenges, there are days where I literally can't feel my legs, they feel like jelly, there's days where I'm completely exhausted after sleeping, I wake up completely shattered."
This has forced her to "trust other people and gain strength in building a team".
As a woman in business, being in a wheelchair can sometimes make Antonia feel "smaller" as people often have to look down at her at industry events.
"People are often surprised when I start speaking about my business, as though they're thinking 'how have you accomplished all of this in a wheelchair?'"
Antonia, who has three young children, says that being underestimated can be a good thing, and she wants to remain open about her health to inspire other women.
She says she used to feel "weak" because of her disability, but now feels she has gained "so much strength" from sharing her experience online.
Asked what she would say to another woman who may fear her age, disability or health could get in the way of success, she says: "I would encourage them to just start."
"You might not have control over your health, you might not know what tomorrow is going to bring, and you might not have all the resources. But start with what you do have, and let's see what could happen next."
