title: Pakistan rules out unconditional talks with Afghanistan
body:
• Demands verifiable mechanism to end terrorist attacks from Afghan soil
• FO says no formal Russian mediation initiative currently under discussion
• Warns India that any future aggression will be met with a stronger response
ISLAMABAD: The Foreign Office on Friday said that talks with Afghanistan could not be unconditional, while rejecting suggestions that Islamabad was unwilling to engage with its neighbour and saying it would welcome sincere efforts by friendly countries to help resolve the dispute.
“Pakistan is not shying away from discussions or dialogue, including with representatives of Afghanistan. Pakistan would welcome any sincere efforts by friendly countries that could help address our legitimate security concerns and promoting regional peace and stability,” Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said at the weekly media briefing.
The statement came as Russia recently renewed its readiness to mediate between the two countries, although Islamabad denied the existence of any such initiative.
“At present, I am not aware of any separate, formal Russian mediation initiative being under discussion,” Mr Khan said, adding that Pakistan remained open to engagement that produced tangible results.
Russia, the only country to have formally recognised the Taliban government, has recently renewed its offer to facilitate a settlement if both sides request its involvement.
Moscow’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, had earlier this month made this suggestion after the latest round of the Moscow Format consultations on Oct 5 ended without a joint communiqué because of differences between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban delegations over references to terrorist networks operating from Afghanistan.
Mr Khan said the absence of an agreed statement at the Moscow Format meeting reflected the Afghan delegation’s unwillingness to accept language on terrorist networks that had been agreed in the previous year’s document.
“The fact that no joint communiqué was issued after the Moscow Format is self-evident that Afghanistan did not accept the formulation which had been acceptable until last year particularly about presence of terrorist network in Afghanistan. This shows that there is reluctance on the part of Afghanistan that terrorism is originating from its soil,” he said.
The failure to get a joint communique highlighted the central obstacle to normalising relations, which is Pakistan’s demand for action against the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and other terrorist groups it says are using Afghan territory to launch attacks across the border.
The Taliban authorities have avoided taking a categorical position on the TTP and other groups, while rejecting Islamabad’s allegations that Afghanistan is being used as a base for attacks against Pakistan.
The dispute has frustrated international efforts to reduce tensions. Qatar and Turkiye last October helped broker a ceasefire, but subsequent round of talks failed to reach a lasting settlement. Saudi Arabia separately hosted discussions, while China held talks between the two sides in Urumqi in April. None of these efforts could resolve the disagreement over terrorist groups and the measures needed to prevent cross border attacks.
Pakistan’s position, Mr Khan said, was that dialogue would need to be backed by an arrangement that could verify whether terrorist activity against the country had stopped.
“The talks will not be unconditional. Pakistan has been raising the issue of terrorism emanating from Afghanistan at different forums. Unfortunately, the Taliban regime has been taking one step forward and one step backward,” Mr Khan emphasised.
“Pakistan has only one demand that there should be a verifiable mechanism to ensure complete cessation of terrorist activities emanating from Afghan soil against Pakistan,” he said.
‘Stronger response’
Mr Khan reminded India of the response it faced during last year’s military confrontation and warned that any future aggression would be met with an even stronger response.
FO reaction came after Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh a day earlier threatened a bigger strike in the event of any future terrorist attacks.
Singh, while speaking at National Defence Conclave 2026 in Delhi, recalled Operation Sindoor and said that it marked a decisive response to terrorism. He also referred to earlier Indian military operations.
“We reject and condemn the Indian Defence Minister’s provocative remarks entailing a threat of Indian aggression against Pakistan. Such reckless statements reflect India’s hegemonistic mindset and the risks its belligerent posture poses to regional peace and stability in South Asia,” Mr Khan said.
“We wish to remind India of the consequences of its military aggression in May last year, when Pakistan demonstrated both its capability and resolve to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and gave a fitting reply to Indian aggression,” the FO spokesperson said.
Mr Khan urged New Delhi to draw lessons from the previous confrontation and avoid further escalation.
“India should draw an appropriate lesson from the last year’s experience and abandon its belligerent posture and dangerous rhetoric and act with responsibility for lasting peace in the region,” he said.

title: Imran being forced into Benazir, Nawaz-style deal, claims Achakzai
body:
• Demands authorities disclose whereabouts of Sohail Afridi
• Mengal says those claiming to be framers of Constitution are ‘trampling it’
• TTAP alliance challenges governor’s rule, emergency before Peshawar High Court
PESHAWAR: PTI founder Imran Khan is being forced into an agreement, similar to those given to former prime ministers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto, Leader of the Opposition in the National Assembly Mahmood Khan Achakzai claimed on Friday.
The opposition leader was referring to the arrangements whereby the two former PMs went into self-imposed exile following their respective ousters.
Mr Sharif, who was ousted and imprisoned following a military coup by then-army chief Pervez Musharraf, left the country in 2000 following a deal negotiated by Saudi and Lebanese leaders.
Benazir, meanwhile, voluntarily went into self-exile after her party lost the 1997 general elections following her dismissal by then-president Farooq Leghari. At the time, her husband Asif Zardari was imprisoned over corruption charges, and was finally released in 2004.
“The same is happening today with the PML-N and PPP in government,” Mr Achakzai said at a news conference at the Peshawar High Court (PHC).
He was accompanied by Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) leaders Sardar Akhtar Mengal and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas.
He said they were in contact with all opposition parties and would soon convene a multi-party conference. Resigning from the assemblies was also an option, he said, adding that they had submitted their demands in response to the offer of negotiations.
“Nowhere in the world is a prisoner denied meetings,” he said, calling for the withdrawal of the “wrong amendment”, empowerment of parliament and the formation of an independent commission to ensure transparent elections.
He said no problem could be resolved until parliament was empowered. Expressing concern over the whereabouts of the KP chief minister and other lawmakers, he demanded that the authorities disclose the chief minister’s whereabouts, calling it their constitutional right to know.
“We stand with the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The people of this province have the first right over its minerals. Regardless of political affiliation, everyone must unite for the homeland,” he said, adding that they would be safer if the country survived.
Mr Mengal said those claiming to be the framers of the Constitution were trampling on it. He questioned the imposition of governor’s rule in KP on the grounds of terrorism, asking whether military operations had improved or worsened conditions in Balochistan.
He said KP’s elected chief minister had been removed, while the provincial assembly speaker and a minister were missing. Those who had won the general elections on Form 47 had become members of the National Assembly, he alleged, adding that the system could not continue this way.
Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in the Senate, said lawlessness had reached its peak. “You cannot run a country, yet you have occupied a province,” he told reporters, adding that a cabinet member had himself acknowledged that the system had collapsed.
TTAP challenges governor’s rule
Meanwhile on Friday, TTAP leaders challenged the proclamation of emergency and imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa before the
PHC, seeking to have the measures declared unconstitutional and illegal.
The constitutional petition was jointly filed by TTAP Chairman Mehmood Khan Achakzai, Vice Chairman Senator Raja Nasir Abbas, Balochistan National Party-Mengal chief Sardar Akhtar Mengal and Sindh Taraqi Pasand Party leader Syed Zainul Abideen through Advocates Muazzam Butt and Baseem Ahmad Siddiqui.
The court was requested to declare the Oct 11 proclamation of emergency, issued under Articles 232(1) and 234 of the Constitution, unconstitutional and without lawful authority, arguing that the required constitutional conditions had not been met or that the measures exceeded the powers conferred by the Constitution.
They challenged the purported transfer of the KP Assembly’s legislative powers to parliament and the displacement of the elected chief minister and provincial cabinet. They also sought the annulment of executive orders and notifications that depended on the validity of the proclamation.
The petitioners also challenged the establishment of the purported KP Advisory Council and Area Development Secretariat, arguing that these bodies could not exercise powers beyond those conferred by the Constitution or replace established provincial institutions.
They questioned any purported suspension of constitutional provisions, including Article 175(3), unless expressly authorised by the Constitution.
The petitioners sought annulment of the Oct 11 notification concerning the deployment of armed forces in the province to the extent where it violated Article 245, failed to meet constitutional requirements or exceeded the scope of the provision.
They also sought directions to ensure that elected representatives and constitutionally established institutions in KP were not unlawfully prevented from performing their functions and that no elected representative was detained or restrained except in accordance with the Constitution.
Pending a final decision, they sought interim relief to suspend or restrain the impugned measures to prevent the displacement of elected institutions, transfer of legislative authority, creation of parallel executive structures or other irreparable harm, subject to the court’s assessment of constitutional requirements and public safety.

title: US says Iran barred from maritime trade as pressure campaign targets oil revenue, military funding
body:
US says Iran barred from maritime trade as pressure campaign targets oil revenue, military funding
Strait of Hormuz transits remain 70% below pre-conflict levels: UK maritime agency
US Central Command (CENTCOM) Commander Admiral Brad Cooper claimed Friday that Iran has been cut off from maritime imports and exports as Washington intensified its campaign against Tehran's oil revenue and military funding.
In a video message, Cooper said US efforts focused on three areas: restricting Iranian oil exports, disrupting digital financing and weakening the ability of Iran's security forces to pay their personnel.
"As a point of emphasis, with the exception of the humanitarian assistance we've allowed in, Iran has no exports and no imports by sea," Cooper said.
He said US forces have prevented Iran from exporting at least $25 billion worth of crude oil in recent months.
"CENTCOM has also supported US interagency partners in freezing nearly $350 million in digital cryptocurrency assets, further constricting Iran's ability to fund terrorism or replace weapons and factories that we destroy," he said.
Cooper claimed that Iran-aligned groups operating across the region had begun withholding payments to their fighters to redirect funds to the IRGC, which he said was also struggling to pay its personnel.
Read: Iran president says conflict in Mideast amounts to 'ecocide'
According to Cooper, the IRGC was also struggling to pay its personnel.
"The Islamic regime is clearly feeling the economic pain, and the IRGC is increasingly showing signs of greater desperation as a result," he said.
US claims Strait of Hormuz remains open
Despite the restrictions on Iranian maritime trade, Cooper said commercial shipping continued through the Strait of Hormuz.
He accused Iran of attacking commercial vessels and said US forces were working with regional allies and shipping industry partners to strengthen maritime security.
"Let me be clear: the Strait of Hormuz is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran, and it remains open for business," Cooper said.
He said approximately 400 merchant ships had transited the strait over the previous seven days.
He added that US forces had assisted Gulf partners in transporting more than 100 million barrels of crude oil through the waterway during the same period, bringing the total volume shipped with US assistance in recent months to more than 1.3 billion barrels.
Strait of Hormuz transits remain 70% below pre-conflict levels: UK maritime agency
Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained about 70% below pre-conflict levels as attacks on commercial vessels continued, a UK maritime agency said Friday.
In its weekly overview, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) reported 125 outbound and 129 inbound transits over the past seven days.
The figures marked a decline from 129 outbound and 146 inbound transits recorded the previous week, according to the agency.
UKMTO reported 12 attacks on vessels during the week, including 10 in the Strait of Hormuz, one in the Gulf and one in the Gulf of Oman. Six vessels continued or reached port, one was lost, two were disabled or not under command, and three have unconfirmed outcomes.
Container ship sinks after projectile strike
UKMTO said a container ship was struck by an unidentified projectile near Ras Shaykh Masud on October 13.
The vessel caught fire and sank the following day, according to the agency.
All crew members were evacuated, UKMTO said.
The agency warned that it was struggling to establish the actual number of attacks because most targeted vessels declined to report incidents.
UKMTO said it had recorded 84 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began in late February.
The reported attacks came amid continued tensions between Iran and the US over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
The waterway is a major route for global energy and commodity shipments and remains a key issue in negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
Iran says oil tanker hit naval mine in Strait of Hormuz
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said Friday that an oil supertanker struck a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, triggering a massive explosion and fire.
The vessel was carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil when it attempted to transit the strategic waterway, according to a statement carried by the semi-official Tasnim News Agency.
The IRGC Navy described the vessel as a "rogue" tanker that had switched off its navigation and radar systems.
It claimed the tanker had attempted to exploit US military support to transport goods through the strait.
The statement did not identify the vessel, its owner or flag.
It also provided no information about possible casualties or the extent of the damage.
The conflict began with US and Israeli attacks against Iran on February 28, followed by a ceasefire in April.
Clashes between Washington and Tehran later resumed as negotiations stalled, although the two sides signed a framework agreement in June.

title: Two terrorists killed in Balochistan IBO: state media
body:
Two terrorists killed in Balochistan IBO: state media
Sources say terrorists were involved in harassing passengers along the Quetta–Taftan Highway
Security forces killed two terrorists during an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in the Dalbandin area of Balochistan’s Chagai district, Radio Pakistan reported on Saturday, citing security sources.
According to the sources, security forces effectively targeted the terrorists’ hideouts during the operation.
The killed terrorists were involved in harassing passengers travelling along the Quetta–Taftan Highway and spreading fear and panic in the area, the sources added.
On October 15, security forces killed five terrorists belonging to the Indian proxy, Fitna al-Hindustan, during an IBO in the Washuk district of Balochistan, the military’s media wing said.
“During the conduct of the operation, a terrorist hideout was busted by security forces through swift and decisive action,” ISPR said, adding that five Indian-sponsored terrorists were neutralised.
Read: 49 terrorists killed in Balochistan, K-P IBOs
On October 14, security forces also killed five terrorists and injured four others during an IBO against Fitna al-Hindustan in the same district of Balochistan. During the operation, advanced weapons and ammunition were recovered.
Pakistan has witnessed a surge in terrorist activity over the past three months, with a series of attacks across the country resulting in the martyrdom of security personnel and civilians.
Last week, 12 people were killed and 35 others injured when a blast struck a joint checkpoint near Aman Mela in the Darazinda area of Dera Ismail Khan, with the TTP claiming responsibility for the attack.
On September 19, 23 people, including 15 police personnel, were martyred in a blast at a mosque in Kohat’s Police Lines during Friday prayers. Eight terrorists were also killed during a subsequent search and clearance operation. Later, the Ittihadul Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), led by Afghanistan-based Hafiz Gul Bahadur, claimed responsibility for the deadly bombing and rampage involving multiple attackers.
In a separate incident, a captain and a lieutenant were among six security personnel martyred in an exchange of fire in Hangu district, while eight terrorists were killed.
On September 1, six personnel, including two officers, and a customs department official were martyred as security forces thwarted an attempt to breach the Customs House in Balochistan.
In July, at least 30 people, including 27 police personnel, were martyred when terrorists identified by the state as the Indian proxy Fitna al-Hindustan ambushed police personnel deployed in the Kach Mangi Phase III area of Ziarat, triggering hours-long gun battles. title: Opposition unites against governor's rule in K-P
body:
Opposition unites against governor's rule in K-P
Vows joint resistance, keeps resignations option open
PESHAWAR:
Opposition parties on Friday vowed a joint struggle against the imposition of governor's rule and emergency in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), demanding constitutional supremacy, parliamentary sovereignty and free and fair elections, while keeping open the option of resigning from the assemblies.
Opposition Leader in the National Assembly Mahmood Khan Achakzai said he would contact opposition parties and convene an all-parties conference (APC).
He said the option of resigning from the assemblies remained open, but stressed that the opposition favoured a peaceful, constitutional struggle and was ready for talks.
Speaking at a news conference at the Peshawar High Court, Achakzai said he had come to express solidarity with the people of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, alleging that the federal government had acted unconstitutionally by removing the elected provincial government.
He said the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) had won seats in the elections but the government had been handed to another party. He also cited the disqualification of lawmakers and alleged irregularities in the electoral process.
Achakzai said no one should be prevented from meeting a prisoner and alleged that PTI founder Imran Khan was being pressured into an agreement.
He said former prime ministers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto had faced similar treatment in the past, adding that the same was happening under the current governments led by the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP).
He questioned the whereabouts of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and said information about him should be made public. He also expressed concern over reports that provincial ministers, lawmakers and party workers had gone missing.
"This is not the time to remain silent but to stand up for the people's rights and constitutional protection," Achakzai said. "We will neither throw stones at anyone nor resort to violence. We will pursue a peaceful struggle."
He said the opposition was willing to negotiate if the government was serious about dialogue. Policies should be made in parliament, he added, and all institutions should operate within their constitutional limits.
Achakzai said the opposition had set out its demands in response to the government's offer of talks. These included upholding the Constitution, withdrawing controversial amendments, restoring parliament's role as the principal centre of decision-making and establishing an independent commission to ensure free and fair elections.
The country's problems could not be resolved unless parliament became the primary forum for decision-making, he said, adding that contacts with opposition parties were under way and all would be invited to the proposed APC.
On provincial rights, Achakzai said the people of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa had the first claim to the province's mineral resources. He called for unity across political lines to protect the country and safeguard public rights.
He also cited the merger of the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas (Fata) with Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, saying decisions of national importance should be made through constitutional and democratic procedures.
Akhtar Mengal, head of the Balochistan National Party, criticised those who claimed to be the architects of the Constitution while, he said, violating its provisions.
He alleged that the imposition of governor's rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa amounted to blaming the entire province for terrorism. Counterterrorism operations had also been under way in Balochistan for years, he said, but insecurity continued to affect the province.
Mengal questioned whether such measures could resolve the country's problems. He also alleged that the elected chief minister of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa had been taken away and cited reports concerning the whereabouts of the provincial assembly speaker and ministers.
He said people elected through what he called "Form 47" were occupying the assemblies and argued that such a system could not endure.
Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, opposition leader in the Senate, said lawlessness had worsened and accused the government of taking control of a province because it could not manage the existing system. Government ministers had themselves acknowledged the system's failure, he said.
He alleged that those who had stolen the public mandate were seeking to silence dissent and protests. Citing rising poverty, he said remaining silent about the country's situation was inconsistent with patriotism. He pledged to continue his struggle regardless of the circumstances.

title: Pakistan to chair IMF, WB boards in 2027
body:
Pakistan to chair IMF, WB boards in 2027
WBG Corporate Secretariat briefed Cheema on the responsibilities associated with the chairmanship
ISLAMABAD:
Pakistan will chair the Boards of Governors of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group (WBG) in 2027, marking the country's first return to the leadership of both institutions since 1953, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said on Friday.
Economic Affairs Minister Ahad Cheema, who also serves as Pakistan's governor to the World Bank, was formally announced as the incoming chairman during the plenary session of the 2026 WBG-IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok.
The annual meetings, being held from October 12 to 18, brought together policymakers, central bank governors, business leaders and other participants from around the world to discuss the global economy.
The ministry described the appointment as a historic milestone, saying the chairmanship would provide Pakistan with an opportunity to contribute to international economic and development discussions and facilitate constructive dialogue among member countries.
Following the plenary session, the WBG Corporate Secretariat briefed Cheema on the responsibilities associated with the chairmanship. He also met WBG Vice President and Corporate Secretary Aradhana Kumar-Capoor to discuss institutional support and coordination during Pakistan's tenure.
Cheema separately met outgoing chairman Carlos Carvallo Spalding, governor of Paraguay's central bank, congratulating him on completing his tenure and commending his stewardship. The two discussed the responsibilities of the office and priorities for the coming year.
During the meetings, Cheema reaffirmed Pakistan's commitment to strengthening the voice of developing countries, improving coordination among multilateral development institutions and promoting effective and predictable development financing.
He emphasised the importance of mobilising private investment to support sustainable and inclusive growth. He said Pakistan would work closely with the WBG, the IMF and member countries to encourage constructive dialogue and contribute to a more responsive multilateral development and financial system.
Separately, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb met World Bank Group President Ajay Banga at a dinner hosted by the Thai prime minister on the sidelines of the annual meetings in Bangkok, according to state-run Pakistan Television.
Pakistan remains engaged with the IMF under a $7 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and a $1.4 billion Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF). Earlier this month, Pakistan and the Fund reached a staff-level agreement following the fourth review under the EFF and the third review under the RSF.

title: PHC to hear challenge to emergency on 20th
body:
PHC to hear challenge to emergency on 20th
PTI Chairman approached the PHC on October 14, challenging imposition of emergency and governor's rule in K-P
PESHAWAR:
The Peshawar High Court (PHC) has listed for hearing the petitions challenging the federal government's October 11 decision to impose emergency and governor's rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P). The court will take up the pleas on October 20.
PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan approached the PHC on October 14, challenging the imposition of emergency and governor's rule in K-P and seeking the annulment of the presidential proclamation issued on October 11. National Democratic Movement (NDM) leaders Mohsin Dawar and Bushra Gohar also separately filed similar petition in the court.
In his petition, filed through Advocate Ali Zaman, Gohar termed the measures unconstitutional and discriminatory, arguing that terrorism cannot be used as a pretext to curtail the powers of an elected provincial government.
The PTI chairman contended that terrorism had affected different parts of the country in the past without elected provincial governments being removed on that basis.
He cited the security situation in Balochistan, where terrorist attacks and casualties had been continually reported, arguing that governor's rule had not been imposed there despite the serious law and order challenges.
He referred to the period between 2007 and 2015, when K-P and the former tribal areas experienced a severe wave of militancy, resulting in substantial casualties among civilians and security personnel.
The petitioner argued that the elected provincial government had not been removed through governor's rule during that period and urged the court to examine the constitutional justification and alleged motives behind the current measures.
Gohar maintained that the PTI opposed terrorism and supported action against militant elements and efforts to restore peace. He rejected allegations that the party's provincial government had failed to take effective action against terrorism or had shown leniency towards militants.
He stated that such accusations were being used to exert political pressure and weaken the mandate PTI secured in the 2024 general elections.
The petition argued that the party had won a two-thirds majority in the province and that the federal government could not curtail the powers of an elected government because of political differences.
It also questioned the use of the failure of negotiations as a justification for action against PTI, maintaining that the party had not planned any unlawful activity during its long march and that peaceful political protest could not, by itself, justify suspending an elected government.
Invoking Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, the petition asked the court to examine whether the requirements for imposing an emergency and invoking governor's rule had been met.
Article 232 deals with emergency powers in specified circumstances, while Article 234 provides a mechanism for a presidential proclamation where a provincial government cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
Separately, NDM President Mohsin Dawar and Bushra Gohar filed a constitutional petition through Advocate Yousaf Orakzai, challenging the October 11 presidential proclamation as unlawful, unconstitutional and beyond the president's authority.
The NDM leaders asked the high court to declare the proclamation unlawful and set it aside. They have also sought interim relief suspending its implementation until the petition is finally decided.

title: DISCOs seek Rs2.6/unit hike for Sept
body:
DISCOs seek Rs2.6/unit hike for Sept
NEPRA to hold public hearing on Oct 29 to consider request
ISLAMABAD:
Distribution companies (DISCOs) have sought regulatory approval to recover an additional Rs2.5624 per unit from consumers through electricity bills under the September 2026 fuel charges adjustment (FCA). The proposed increase is also expected to apply to K-Electric consumers under the government's uniform tariff policy.
The Central Power Purchasing Agency-Guarantee (CPPA-G), on behalf of DISCOS, has filed an application with the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (NEPRA), seeking approval for the monthly adjustment. The regulator has scheduled a public hearing on October 29.
According to the application, the reference fuel cost was Rs7.4596 per unit, while the proposed adjustment of Rs2.5624 per unit reflects the difference between the reference cost and the actual fuel-related charges incurred during September.
The data submitted to NEPRA shows that total electricity generation stood at 13,217 gigawatt-hours (GWh) during the month, while net electricity supplied to DISCOs amounted to 12,760 GWh after accounting for transmission losses and electricity sold to independent power producers (IPPs).
Hydropower remained the largest source of electricity generation, contributing 4,834 GWh, or 36.58% of the total. Nuclear power plants generated 1,893 GWh, accounting for 14.32%, while imported coal-fired plants produced 2,155 GWh, or 16.31%.
Imported coal generation cost Rs37.142 billion, translating into Rs17.2329 per unit. Meanwhile, liquefied natural gas (RLNG)-based generation produced 804 GWh, or 6.08% of the total, at a reported cost of Rs39.37 billion, equivalent to Rs39.7372 per unit.
High-speed diesel was the most expensive major fuel source listed in the September data. It generated 213 GWh at a cost of Rs13.262 billion, translating into Rs62.1381 per unit.
Furnace-oil-based plants contributed 263 GWh at a cost of Rs11.812 billion, or Rs44.8613 per unit, while gas-fired generation accounted for 1,066 GWh at the reported rate of Rs13.0414 per unit.
Local coal-fired plants generated 1,327 GWh at Rs5.9946 per unit, while nuclear generation was reported at Rs2.9045 per unit. Wind power contributed 464 GWh, while bagasse-based plants generated 35 GWh.
The data also indicates a continuing rise in nuclear generation costs over recent months, although the figures provided in the application would need to be compared with previous monthly filings to establish the extent of the increase.

Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah on Friday hinted that the federal government could consider foregoing interim governance in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) if the PTI agreed to support law enforcement agencies in their fight against terrorism.
Speaking to a private news channel, Sanaullah said the government wanted all political parties to reach a consensus on counterterrorism, arguing that growing security challenges required a unified response from the federal and provincial governments.
He said the government's primary demand from the opposition was that it stand with Pakistan, its law enforcement agencies and armed forces. The fight against terrorism had cost the country precious lives, including those of military personnel, he added.
Sanaullah maintained that political differences should not undermine ongoing counterterrorism efforts, stressing that the strategy adopted to combat terrorism should not be questioned or made conditional on political demands.
Responding to questions about why the government was pursuing negotiations despite parliament's ratification of the emergency measures and governor's rule, Sanaullah said the administration continued to seek consensus among political parties on matters of national security.
He argued that the evolving security situation demanded cooperation rather than confrontation, adding that the federal and provincial governments needed to adopt a common strategy to counter the threat. title: Fazl draws ire over K-P governor's rule remarks
body:
Fazl draws ire over K-P governor's rule remarks
Naqvi alleges JUI-F chief upset over not being offered governorship
LAHORE:
Federal Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Friday took a swipe at JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman without naming him, saying a political party chief was upset over being left out of the proposed imposition of governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) and not being offered the governorship.
In remarks circulated in the media as an informal interaction with journalists in Lahore, Naqvi was quoted as saying that the politician had relied on the establishment for decades and had even secured his party's tickets through it.
He said such politicians were in no position to point fingers at others, adding that political differences should be debated through arguments and facts rather than abusive language and allegations.
However, no formal media interaction took place.
Naqvi also questioned why some political leaders had only recently begun expressing concern over the rights and resources of the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA), asking why they had remained silent when the merged districts were allegedly denied their due share.
He said the rights of former FATA residents should be treated as a matter above political interests.
Saying that K-P was facing serious security challenges, the interior minister urged political leaders to help restore peace and eliminate terrorism rather than fuel confrontation and unrest. He said the province needed peace, stability and collective efforts instead of political confrontation.
Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz Sharif and her information minister also joined the chorus against Fazl, accusing him of supporting those backing terrorism.
Fazl, one of the most vocal opponents of governor's rule in K-P, has rejected the move and blamed the government for the failure of talks, countering its claim that PTI's negotiating team repeatedly changed its position on the chief minister's cues.
In a statement on X, Maryam said she had not expected a senior politician who had himself been a victim of terrorism to support those allegedly backing terrorism.
She said it was regrettable that, instead of holding accountable those responsible for K-P's deterioration through incompetence, corruption and poor governance, he was speaking in their favour.
Maryam questioned whether the people Fazl was defending had attended the funerals of martyrs during their 13 years in power in the province. She accused them of providing terrorists with shelter, resources, safe havens and land from which to launch attacks against Pakistan.
She further criticised the use of provincial resources for sit-ins and protests, alleging that years of PTI rule had been squandered through corruption and incompetence.
Referring to Fazl's remarks about the military leadership, Maryam said his comments about the field commander who had led Pakistan to a historic victory had hurt patriotic Pakistanis.
Maryam argued that Fazl's position was particularly difficult to understand given that his own party had suffered losses to terrorism and that his associates had been killed in attacks.
She also pointed to the personal attacks and abusive language directed at him in the past by those whose cause he was now defending.

title: "In every study that considered the question"
body:
“In every study that considered the question”
I spent most daylight hours yesterday driving in torrential rains in pretty bad visibility, and I was astonished how many cars didn’t have their lights on.
It looked something like this. The cars with tail lights on were somewhat visible, but the cars without them didn’t stand a chance:
I read up about it, and it turns out that the issue wasn’t as much forgetfulness or carelessness. Rather, it all might have to do with iconography.
Cars have two main settings for lights:
- “regular driving,” meant to be used at night and during limited visibility – like in heavy rains,
- “parking,” which activates only front lights, at half brightness, and (for some reason) leaves the tail lights off.
The UI for lights seems to typically look like this:
Without knowing, can you figure out which setting is which?
The left icon with two lights facing away from each other means the parking lights. The far-right icon with one light pointing slightly down (“low beams”) is regular driving lights. The latter is the right thing to do in the rain, but the assignment feels kind of arbitrary to me, and I could totally see the icons going the other way.
Also, the above is a somewhat gentle situation. In my rental car, the lights were on a stalk, and the setup looked more like this:
Here:
- the lightbulb on the left is a meta indicator for “this is the main light setting” (you can see it above too, on the dial),
- the middle part with the wavy line is fog lights,
- the arrow-heavy thing on the right informs of two things: pull on the stalk for high beams (another mode), or rotate the stalk left or right for turn signals.
That’s a lot of stuff going on, and many similar icons that do not appear immediately understandable. The whole interface seems optimized for motor memory, but harder to approach at first.
In both modes, the feedback from inside the car is exactly the same – you see the interior dashboards illuminate, and the front lights go up. At night, you might spot the difference in the front light intensity. But in the daytime rain, it’s less likely – especially if it’s a rare intense rain you don’t encounter often. Most importantly given the beginning of the story, you simply can’t see what your tail lights are up to.
From reading up on it, I believe what happened was the confusion between the two modes – people were driving with the best of intentions, actually turning on the lights… except the wrong kind of lights.
(Many cars have an AUTO option now, but would you trust it to choose the right thing? I didn’t, being unsure if it properly accounted for daylight rain driving.)
Lost perhaps amidst the recent conversations about icons in menus and app icons was another subtle change: Apple started embracing more iconography on buttons, too.
You can see it on keyboards, where the U.S. models followed in the footsteps of international ones, now showing symbols instead of legends for Tab, Caps Lock, Shift, Fn, Enter, Return, and Delete. Here’s the previous generation and the 2026 one:
The shift also happened on screens. Below are examples from the last three versions of iOS (18, 26, and 27), side by side.
When starting a new note, it’s not just the keyboard’s ↵ that replaced Return. The back icon also lost its legend, and Done became a checkmark:
Here might be the best case scenario, with Cancel and Done swapped with icons:
In this AirDrop screen, Done became a close box:
Elsewhere, Cancel morphed into ×, in an unfortunate position next to a different ×. Plus, Search on the keyboard became a loupe:
When screenshotting, Done was splintered into a checkmark and an ×:
And here, Done transformed into a checkmark, while Edit became a new kind of a paint icon:
Seeing all this, I was reminded of this old post from Dmitry Fadeyev, titled “False simplicity”:
Sometimes, what appears on the surface to be simple is actually far from it. For example, there’s a trend in Twitter clients to use icons instead of text labels for buttons. Just icons, no text at all. These icons don’t take much space, look elegant and maintain that simple feel of Twitter, except…they’re actually just confusing.
Fadeyev also quoted Jef Raskin’s take on icons:
In every study that considered the question, icons were demonstrated to be more difficult to understand than were labels, especially at first viewing, which contradicts one of the most frequently cited reasons for using icons, namely, comprehensibility for beginners. […] Although it is true that tiny icons can take less screen space than labels, you have to ask: At what cost? The smaller a button, the longer it takes to operate it, and the more difficult it is to find; also, it is difficult to make a small icon distinctive.
I like that take.
Here’s my personal go-to cheat sheet when it comes to iconography:
- icons are compact, allowing you to squeeze in “more UI,”
- people probably understand only a few icons (close box, checkmark, plus, some chevrons), and can learn others – but the learning process will be harder than you think,
- many icons are never understood, but people can still to some extent use them without ever understanding them,
- icons can break the monotony of an all-text interface,
- well-made icons make the interface look more attractive in a way type can’t.
I don’t believe Apple is doing it all just for aesthetical reasons. My guess is that it’s more about the first bullet point above: liquid glass added so much chrome and padding that Apple simply ran out of room for text labels encased in glass.
At the first glance, Apple is avoiding the car light problem by using popular icons. However, there’s a new challenge: most of these icons are too popular, and overloaded with meaning:
- checkmark: “commit” or “to do item/checkbox”?
- ×: “close” or “clear”?
- loupe: “search” or “zoom”?
The only outlier is the edit icon, relatively new and likely unknown. With the extra challenge that on-hover tooltips don’t exist on touch devices, the way forward would be to use the paint icon consistently to teach it to people, but it seems Apple isn’t yet doing a great job at that. The below screenshots are all iOS 27, where you can see the leftover Cancel and Done labels in place, and a missed opportunity to put the new edit icon next to Customize to help people connect the concepts:
I wish I could peek inside Apple to see how these efforts are faring, and what’s in store.
To go back to keyboards, I am curious why Apple didn’t consistently apply text and icons for all the affected keys, like they did for the bottom row a while back. Here there was enough room:
And how could we solve the car problem, if iconography is indeed the culprit? I could imagine a similar idea here as well:
But the funny thing is that most modern cars have a digital dashboard, so for the first time, tooltips are an option. You could imagine turning the stalk and seeing this kind of a message appear for a few seconds, the description and the icon side by side to help the user connect one to the other:
Perhaps seeing the word “parking” would help some people realize their mistake.
Of course, introducing a tooltip means “now you have two problems,” but let’s save that for a different post.

title: Flexport Is Hiring a Biz Ops Leader in Office of CEO
body:
employees worldwide
2K+
Global trade touches every industry, and most of it still runs on phone calls and spreadsheets. We're building the AI-powered, autonomous platform that runs the entire supply chain. 
Our mission is to make global trade so easy there will be more of it. Come help us build. 
WHY FLEXPORT
Containers get stuck. Ports back up. Customs rules change overnight. These are physical problems with real goods on the line, so AI here doesn't replace the people doing the work. AI gives them Iron Man suits, and we've already cut 80% of the emails our teams used to send.
Proven at scale
Our team continues to grow while raising the bar for excellence, innovation, and technology.
Global logistics is the circulatory system of the world economy. Back pressure here prevents every other industry from reaching it's potential. We will be the absolute leaders in applying AI and machine learning to this vital industry.
offices around the world
45+
Global network
Flexport runs 45+ offices worldwide and we're still opening more. Our teams speak over 70 languages. Between relocations, Marco Polo, and global summits, you'll have multiple opportunities to travel the world.
Our customers
Help customers solve their hardest problems with the best technology and experts in the industry.
Core values
Customer obsession is the foundation of our culture. We are successful only when our customers are winning consistently.
There are no shortcuts. We operate with integrity, putting safety, compliance, and long-term customer trust ahead of short term gains.
We are principled entrepreneurs who live in reality but are never satisfied with the status quo. We are endlessly curious and constantly seek to create meaningful change.
We turn complexity into clarity. We challenge assumptions, eliminate unnecessary steps, and streamline processes to create reliable, scalable solutions. We communicate clearly and concisely and celebrate simplicity.
We solve problems for our customers as one global team. We break down silos, collaborate across departments and time zones, and never let hierarchy or bureaucracy stand in the way of doing what’s right.
LIFE AT FLEXPORT
Use Tab or arrow keys to navigate slides.
Flexport.org
Flexport.org uses logistics as a positive force for good - enabling organizations to deliver global aid and meet their sustainability goals with greater ease and lower costs.
FAQs
Absolutely. One of the keys to our success is bringing hard-working, talented technologists into the world of global logistics and giving them the opportunity to impact this massive, antiquated industry. There's tremendous opportunity in showing people that something that appears boring like global shipping is actually incredibly interesting. And there are few industries with a starker contrast between the complexity of the problem at hand and the sophistication of the companies attempting to solve it. Where competitors see cardboard boxes that need to get moved, and opportunities to buy low and sell high, we see a world of fascinating network economics, supply and demand elasticity questions, complex coordination challenges, routing optimization, and a huge array of other problems that are best solved with technology than any amount of industry experience. Don't get us wrong, we value domain experience and are blessed to have hired so many of the smartest people from global logistics to work on our team. But we absolutely require new approaches and innovation that almost always comes from outside the sector.
It all begins with the first step: Find a role that looks right and apply online. You can filter your search by either location or team.
We recommend only applying for one role at a time, so pick the best fit and send in your application.
Once you apply, our recruiters will be in touch if it’s a good fit and we'll begin the process of getting to know each other.
They may ask you for things like work samples, but more than anything they will be listening and sharing more about what makes Flexport such a great place to work.
Our straightforward hiring process is designed to give you all the information you need to make an informed choice about your next career.
First, apply. Then, one of our recruiters will be in touch. If it’s a good match, you’ll be invited to meet with a diverse interview panel, including the manager and members of the team, structured in such a way as to mitigate bias.
By the end of the process, you will have a very real feel for what life is like at Flexport. We look forward to meeting you.

title: FLUX 3 Image Klein
body:
- Models
- News
- Research
FLUX 3 Image Klein
Today we are releasing FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6B parameter open weights model for text-to-image generation, image editing and multi-reference generation with up to 10 reference images. It shares core capabilities with the full FLUX 3 Image model: native 4K generation, pixel-perfect editing, and bounding boxes that control where elements are placed or confine edits to a defined area.
FLUX 3 Image Klein builds on FLUX 3's shared learnings across images, video and audio. Images contribute spatial detail, video adds motion and physical dynamics, and audio provides information about events and interactions. Together, these signals help the model generate images that feel grounded in the real world.
The release includes a base model for fine-tuning and a step distilled model for low-latency generation, along with FP8, INT8 and NVFP4 builds developed with NVIDIA support, under the FLUX Kommunity License.
Try it in the BFL API · Download the weights
Leading open weights quality with fewer parameters
In internal evaluations, FLUX 3 Image Klein ranks first in text-to-image, multi-reference generation and image editing, ahead of larger open weights models. It also rates above the closed models in the comparison, Ideogram V4.5 and FLUX.2 [pro]. At 5.6B parameters, it is the smallest open model in the comparison, against 7B for Qwen-Image 2.1 and 12.9B for Krea 2. Compared with FLUX.2 [klein] 9B, it gains 91 Elo in text-to-image and 70 in image editing, with 38% fewer parameters.
FLUX 3 Image Klein was also optimized for consumer GPUs. Fewer parameters make it practical to run locally and cheaper to adapt, and teams with data sovereignty or local deployment requirements can evaluate and adapt the model on their own infrastructure. This is also key for on-device image editing, allowing consumers to edit images directly on their favorite laptops. The generator weights require 11.2 GB in BF16 and 5.6 GB in FP8. With the INT8 build, FLUX 3 Image Klein runs on NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM, through ComfyUI or Diffusers, extending what FLUX.2 [klein] started to even smaller hardware. With the distilled model and the INT8 build, it generates a 1MP image in about 4 seconds on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 and under 9 seconds on an RTX 4070 through ComfyUI.
The base checkpoint is built for fine-tuning: Diffusers and Ostris's AI Toolkit support LoRA training from day one, and NVIDIA's NeMo AutoModel ships recipes that work directly from the released checkpoints.
For even faster production workloads that need lower latency, we also work with teams on specific customizations that get you there. Get in touch.
On the speed–quality frontier
FLUX 3 Image Klein also extends the speed–quality Pareto frontier. Through the BFL API, it delivers lower latency than Qwen-Image 2.1, FLUX.2 [pro], Ideogram V4.5 and Krea 2, and the highest rating at its latency and above. In the charts below, the violet line traces the highest rating available at each latency and the gray line shows the previous frontier.
Latency is measured end to end, from request submission to the finished 1 MP image, including queueing. FLUX 3 Image Klein was timed on our servers. Other models were timed from the client, which includes polling and network time. Krea 2 was timed on its Medium tier; its Large tier took 31.1 seconds for text-to-image.
Get started
FLUX 3 Image Klein is available today as open weights and through the BFL API.
Try it
- BFL API: the distilled model is available as flux-3-image-klein, with prompt upsampling and pixel restoration, which preserves unedited regions of an image exactly. Pricing starts at $0.009 per 1K image.
- Playground or Hugging Face.
Build with it
- Weights on Hugging Face: base and distilled.
- Reference inference code, including a Gradio demo for bounding-box control.
- Try it out on Hugging Face Spaces.
- Day-one support in ComfyUI, Hugging Face Diffusers, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang Diffusion and vLLM-Omni.
- LoRA training with Ostris's AI Toolkit and recipes in NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel.
- Trained on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and optimized for NVIDIA's accelerated computing platform, serving through NVIDIA TensorRT LLM, vLLM-Omni and SGLang Diffusion.
- On NVIDIA GB300, the distilled model generates a 1MP image in under 0.6 seconds in NVFP4. Serving a LoRA adds around 5% to generation time.
License
The weights are available under the FLUX Kommunity License, which allows free commercial use for individuals and companies with annual revenue under $5M, alongside research and non-commercial use. Larger organizations can deploy commercially through our self-hosted licensing options or API.
Safety
In an effort to make AI technology both open and safe, we implement multiple safeguards throughout the model development lifecycle to combat misuse. These include dataset filters during pre-training to limit exposure to harmful content, and targeted fine-tuning during post-training to suppress harmful behaviors, making it progressively harder to elicit harmful content. Ahead of the release, the FLUX 3 Image Klein checkpoints were rigorously red teamed internally and evaluated by our external safety partner Cinder, demonstrating substantially fewer vulnerabilities than other popular open weights models. More on our safety methodology is available here.
FLUX 3 Image Klein is the second open weights release from the FLUX 3 family, following FLUX 3 Action. More will follow.
Learn more
- FLUX 3: Real World Models, the research behind the FLUX 3 family
- FLUX 3 Action, our open weights 7B model for robot control
Citation
If you use FLUX 3 Image Klein in your work, please cite:
@misc{bfl2026flux3imageklein,
  author       = {{Black Forest Labs}},
  title        = {{FLUX} 3 Image Klein},
  year         = {2026},
  url          = {https://bfl.ai/blog/flux-3-image-klein},
}

title: How the Claude Code team does code review
body:
How do you review code at the volume agents produce it? On the Claude Code team, once we had high coverage and deep reviews, we started optimizing for the minimum amount of human review time that doesn't raise reverts or incidents.
We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it?
This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent.
We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes.
When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September this year.
Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible.
Code review does two jobs:
This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end.
We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"
Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.
Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.
We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily.
Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second.
So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it.
A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review.
Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can run—like tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the design—and ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide.
Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines.
Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator."
When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as:
CLAUDE.md tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date.REVIEW.md, written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix.
Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else?
On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code, is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally.
When we launched the research preview, the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time.
Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them. What's left shows up as inline comments sorted by severity. Each is tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a bug the PR didn't introduce doesn't look like the author's fault.
Every finding has to be answered. You either fix it or resolve the thread with a reason. Often an agent picks up the fix overnight, so the author comes back to a PR that's already been through another round.
Security gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive.
If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own. You can set up the same thing with the open-source security review GitHub Action or the /security-review command. Setup is covered in automated security reviews in Claude Code.
The usual: lint, type checks, tests on every platform, and a build. (We wrote about scaling CI for this volume here.) A typical CLI pull request may run dozens of checks before anyone looks at it. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to undo it. Claude can fill that in, but the person who asked for the change signs off on it.
A docs fix and an auto-updater change carry different risk, so they get different review.
The change sets the tier, not the author. A classifier reads the change and picks its risk tier. A second classifier asks whether this particular change needs another person even when its tier says it doesn't. Some paths always need a person, anything owners have listed as sensitive and any CI workflow file.
Only trusted authors get the lighter paths. Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve. An agent's approval never counts as a person's, either. Automated review can clear a low-risk change, but it can't fill a slot that calls for a human.
Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it. On an agent-written PR, the person directing the agent counts as one of the required reviewers, the same as if they'd typed the code themselves.
An approval covers one specific commit. If new commits land that the system can't vouch for, like an agent's push or a merge someone resolved by hand, the approval has to be given again.
The merge queue re-runs every check against main with the change applied, so two PRs that pass separately can't combine into a broken main. New behavior usually ships behind a flag to Anthropic employees first, and our heavy use often surfaces regressions before users do. Public releases go to the latest channel first. The stable channel trails it.
Some mistakes will still get through, so the last layer is about catching them fast. Flags turn off without a deploy. Claude Code has a weekly on-call rotation, and incident reviews ask which layer should have caught the issue.
Noticing a bad merge still depends on the author and on-call as well as the revert and incident dashboards. We don't yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges.
One colleague said slowing down does lower your error rate, but mostly because you're doing less of everything. We'd rather get faster at noticing and fixing problems.
Our code review process is constantly improving in a loop.
Any incidents are now an eval. The team collected past PRs that caused incidents, with their fix-forwards and reverts, and had engineers who know that code confirm each bug and where it lived. The reviewer runs against that set daily.
We measure noise by watching what people do with the comments. It's easy to catch more bugs if you don't mind flagging a lot of non-bugs, so we need a check on that. We sort every comment the reviewer leaves by how the person on the PR responded: they fixed it, said it was wrong, said the behavior was intentional, or decided it didn't matter. We also run the reviewer on PRs we know are clean and count how often it reports something that would have led someone to make a harmful change. Our priority, written down, is catching real bugs first and cutting review rounds second.
Noise costs more when the author is an agent. A person can wave off a nit in seconds. An agent fixes it, which means another commit and another round of review.
Review has to converge. An agent author and an agent reviewer can keep each other busy indefinitely. One CLI PR went through more than fifty rounds of review and fixes overnight before its author stopped it.
When we ran git blame on what the reviewer kept flagging, about 59% of it was code that had been there since the reviewer's first pass. The reviewer was rarely finding new bugs, it was finding a few more old ones each round.
We made it worse ourselves. We'd gotten used to running several rounds by default, since each pass catches something new. This can be worthwhile on a risky change, but not on every PR. The team now tracks rounds-to-pass alongside recall, and changed re-review:
Review agents also run nightly over existing code, helping us catch old bugs before they show up somewhere else.
Pulling a senior engineer out of deep work to catch a routine mistake costs far more than an automated review. At Anthropic, our jobs have moved from reading every diff to the decisions machines are bad at:
Code review's second job has always been to spread codebase understanding. Reading a teammate's diff is how you learn what changed and how the pieces fit. If machines do most of the reading, how does anyone learn the code?
We don't have a formal process for this. Nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code in their head, and we don't think anyone needs to. When someone wants to understand a part of the codebase, they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice. It takes minutes and reflects the code as it is today.
Some of us go a step further and have Claude build a small artifact that visualizes that part of the code and teaches it the way that person likes to learn.
If the goal is to spend human attention well, this beats reading trivial diffs line by line. A one-line copy change teaches you almost nothing. An explainer for the module you're about to change teaches you a lot. Our culture of defaulting to working on open Slack channels helps too, since you see what others are building while they build it.
If you land a small or medium change and something still goes wrong, it's a team norm that you usually fix it. A few things keep this from going badly:
Ownership is also shared. Much of the team works in open channels where anyone can see what others are building, pick up a thread, or point a Claude at a gap, and feedback comes from people who don't own the code too. That openness is a big part of how quality stays high without a gate on every line.
Agents make it cheap to start things, so some work shouldn't land. Usually someone in the channel asks why, points at an earlier decision, or suggests a simpler route, and the author closes or reshapes the PR.
Since the code was fast to write, closing the PR doesn't feel like a loss. The trick is to raise a different direction in the thread early, not as a blocking comment on a finished PR.
Most of the pieces to do this with your team exist today.
/code-review and /security-review locally, or a fresh-context subagent review.
Code Review's announcement said approving a pull request is still a human call; the product posts findings, not approvals. Our own repos go further, letting owners decide which low-risk changes merge on automated checks alone, and that line keeps moving.
When a review misses something, we ask what the model didn't have in front of it and put the fix into a CLAUDE.md, a skill or a new check. The goal hasn't changed: less human time per change, and no more reverts than before.
If your team lets agents open pull requests, we'd like to hear which checks you've automated, which still need a person, and what you think we have wrong.
With thanks to Emma Webb, Michael Segner and Amie Rotherham for their reviews.
