title: ‘I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am’ – the spooky secrets of Last One Laughing: Halloween
body:
What could be more disorientating for a comedian than not being able to laugh – for nine hours! – nor elicit laughter from anyone else in the room? I’ll tell you. Try all of the above on a sunny summer weekend while pretending it’s Halloween. Then force the comics to return to the scene of what one of their number, Phil Wang, calls “a cross between a gameshow and a psychological experiment”, and relive the whole ordeal for a man from the Guardian. Is it any wonder Wang, Lou Sanders, Tom Allen and others come across as a little punch-drunk 24 hours after emerging from televised captivity on the smash comedy hit Last One Laughing?
It’s the day after filming, at Elstree Studios, the show’s Halloween special which sees a unique tweak to its winning formula: contestants must not only refrain from laughter but from screaming. “Which I thought might be a non-event,” says Wang, “but it’s actually harder. I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am.” The participating comics – including paranormal obsessive Daisy May Cooper and that maestro of comedy-horror, Reece Shearsmith – seek not only to amuse each other but spook them too. Which makes sense, says host Jimmy Carr. “Laughs and screams come from the same place. There’s surprise in a joke, and there’s surprise in a jump scare. Comedy and horror mess around in the same area. It’s the same bit of your brain.”
Not that Last One Laughing is making serious moves into chiller territory: after all, why tamper with a format that’s given Prime Video such a huge hit? With over 2m people tuning in per episode, series one was the platform’s biggest ever UK launch. The show later won a Bafta for Best Entertainment Programme. “I don’t want to overplay the jump scares,” says Carr – who first persuaded the channel to develop a UK version of what was originally a Japanese hit. “There’s nothing that would trouble anyone. It’s not that kind of show. It’s just fun. It’s ‘event TV’ – especially when it’s tied around something like Halloween – that’s great for bringing people together.”
And for bringing comedians together too – the more so now LOL has joined Taskmaster as the shop window par excellence for standups making the leap from fringe to mainstream. Alongside national-treasure veterans (Bob Mortimer in series one; Mel Giedroyc in series two), Last One Laughing reserves places for up-and-coming acts – see recent Edinburgh comedy award winner Harriet Dyer here. Getting involved, she says, was “a whirlwind, to be honest. But it was a dream come true.” All the participating comics agree, mind you, that you can’t treat LOL like a career opportunity. “You can’t play it like that,” says Tom Allen. “You have to engulf yourself in the moment. And that reveals people’s true character. There’s something very vulnerable about laughing. We feel very open when we do it.”
Few comics are more oversharingly their own self than Lou Sanders, a late casualty (red-carded by Carr in episode six) in series one, now returning for series 2.5. There’s a strict embargo on spoilers today, but when I ask Sanders if previous experience gave her an advantage in the Halloween outing, her response does not suggest a triumphant comeback. “I thought I would be better,” she says. “But I was immediately on the back foot. And Reece got into my head early on.” Then there’s the knowledge that millions are watching. On series one, “Joe Wilkinson said to me ‘no one’s going to watch this,’ and I believed him. And then it did well. This time, you know there’s going to be eyes on it.”
Sanders has been charged with giving me a tour of the LOL house, a bar cum living room cum art deco theatre, like a prefab 1920s ocean liner constructed in a ginormous Elstree hangar. Here is the fruit machine that’s used to prompt new challenges. There the stage on which contestants perform their ‘joker’ party pieces – around which more strictures circulate than you’d expect. (“I thought it would be funny to have a fire on my head,” says Harriet Dyer. “But I was told: no fire. Then I wanted long arms, but I wasn’t allowed them … ”) There are also creepy dolls, just for Halloween. Does it get claustrophobic in here, I ask Sanders? “I wasn’t in here long enough to know” comes her doleful reply.
But if Sanders’ tactics proved inadequate, others enter Last One Laughing with sophisticated strategies all mapped out. “My tactic was to channel Dame Maggie Smith in Downton Abbey,” says Tom Allen. “Very aloof, very lofty. So I channelled everything through my eyebrows, rather than a lot of people, who try not to laugh by biting the inside of their mouth.” Wang had a more attacking approach. “My mantra was: a good defence is a good offence. Get on the front foot, try to get to people. Focus on those you know at first, because you know what makes them tick. And while doing that, watch the people you don’t know, to see what makes them laugh.”
Dyer entered the house with an idea of what not to do. “I think Sam Campbell said on series two that he thought about, like, kids dying to stop himself laughing. So I thought: should I focus on the worst thing that’s ever happened to me? But I’m not sure watching someone be traumatised with what life’s thrown at them makes for very good telly.” Campbell is the maverick Aussie comic who tested the show’s conceit to breaking point last time around, by staying po-faced from start to finish. He eventually lost in a tie-break to David Mitchell. “We nearly broke David,” says Jimmy Carr. “At the end he was going, ‘I don’t think I’ll ever laugh again. I’ve lost that part of myself for ever’.”
Series two’s other breaking point was reached when – great controversy, this – the comic Amy Gledhill was red-carded by Carr for smiling rather than laughing. My own household can’t have been alone in its outrage at this disregard for the show’s core conceit. But Carr is unrepentant. “I mean, we’d got to that stage of the day,” he says: something had to give. “And it’s that water cooler thing: as long as people are arguing about it and having fun, so much the better.”
To Carr, the show is as much sports as entertainment: the key, he thinks, to its success. “There’s a narrative to sports, whereby you’ve got to watch to the end because you don’t know what’s going to happen. And that’s the same thing with this show: it’s competitive, and you want to know who’s going to win.” “And each episode ends on a really effective cliffhanger,” adds Phil Wang, “which is quite hard to achieve with comedy.”
The other clincher, for Carr and the comics, is how rigorously LOL is produced. Says Carr, “the other countries don’t do the set pieces we do”: the guest appearances, the challenges, the props and tricks contestants can bring to the table – much to Lou Sanders’ dismay. “Reece Shearsmith is Mr Halloween, isn’t he? He’s got all that stuff at home! It’s not fair. I haven’t got a severed hand at home, have I?”
According to Wang, “shows that prepare more than they need always prosper. And this show definitely prepares more than it needs.” Every contestant has a camera trained on them throughout, and a dedicated “spotter” hanging on their every smirk. “I presented it in the room yesterday for nine hours,” says Carr. “But I haven’t seen it all yet. When you get in the edit, there’s a whole other show there. There’s all the conversations people have on the screens I’m not watching. I remember on series two discovering all these incredible moments with Diane Morgan we just didn’t know were there.”
The lineup has already been announced for LOL series three, which broadcasts next year. Harry Hill, Katherine Ryan and Lee Mack all feature. What advice – or warnings – would the Halloween participants impart? “You end up in there for so long,” says Wang – lucky for some! – “that your mood goes from giddy and excited to paranoid and nervous. I was doing a lot of pinching, a lot of breathing, a lot of meditation and mindfulness.” It was, says Tom Allen, “an intense experience, trying to withhold two emotions and not let them out of the bag. It’s exhausting.”
But it’s all in the service, says Allen, of something much needed in our not-always-joyful times. “The series speaks to a childlike sense of play, one that reminds us of being in assembly or in class at school and not being allowed to laugh. There’s nothing more exquisite than that burning desire to laugh while having to keep a lid on it, the steam cooker pressure that brings. Last One Laughing returns us to that youthful joy. I think it’s something people really crave.”
Last One Laughing: Halloween is on Prime Video from Friday.

title: ‘I need to prove my family’s sacrifice was worth it’: how pop auteur Shygirl slogged her way to the top
body:
Leaving the important stuff to chance isn’t Shygirl’s style. First aid kit, wind-up radio, batteries: earlier this morning, the singer filled her online shopping basket in preparation for impending disaster. She had read a news article advising households to put together an emergency kit. “I’m that kind of person,” she says, grinning. She woke her boyfriend, who was asleep in bed next to her. “I was like: babe, we’re sorted! I’ve got the water purifying tablets, everything!”
It’s a sticky September afternoon in east London, and the singer, whose real name is Blane Muise, introduces herself as “Shy” and slides into the booth opposite me at an Italian trattoria. She first burst on to the club scene with the naughty, pulsating Want More in 2016, and in the decade since, the singer, rapper and DJ has applied the same rigour to her career as she has to her emergency prepping, going from cult underground artist to rising pop star, opening arenas for Beyoncé and Charli xcx, winning a Mobo award in 2024, and appearing in Madonna’s recent Confessions II – The Film, in which she shared a toilet stall with Arca and Richard E Grant.
She has also grafted hard at falling in love and entering a long-term relationship, which is the subject of her forthcoming second album, Swallow!. An epic, soaring rock record, with more than a touch of William Orbit-era Madonna, it is an ode to intimacy, vulnerability and mutual devotion. Love, she says, is “scary, exciting and big”. The 33-year-old’s particular mix of hard and soft, of brash swagger, blunt humour and slippery feminine desire has found an exhilarating new form of expression.
In December 2022, Shygirl was preparing to go on tour. Her debut album Nymph had received rave reviews and she was finally earning enough money from music to rent her own place. “I felt good about the reception, but there’s always that anticlimactic feeling when you get what you wanted. You’re like: OK, now I have it. Now what?” she says, tossing her tangerine corkscrew curls. “Then I met George.”
Go on, I say, tell me the story. “It was on Raya,” she says conspiratorially. She was hungover from a night out while browsing the members-only dating app. When they matched, she asked him to send a voice note: “I don’t like meeting up with people unless I can hear what they sound like and their cadence.” Satisfied, she invited him over to watch one of her favourite films, Alien. “Then we got Thai takeout and hooked up,” she says matter-of-factly.
She was leaving for Australia later that week, but they kept talking for almost two months. When she decided to extend her trip and add a visit to Japan, “I was like: fuck it. Do you wanna come to Tokyo?” She flew him out – “in economy”, she says, laughing – and she and actor George Smale have been together ever since. “We had 10 days there and one other date in London when I got back before saying, ‘I love you.’” By the summer, they’d moved in together. Unlike previous relationships, she says, “I didn’t feel like I was all of a sudden so enamoured with someone that I didn’t know where my footing was.”
That contentment and calm was a source of inspiration. “When I made Lucky, I sat in the room with the mic. I didn’t write anything down, I just said how I felt,” she says of the album’s lead single. “It’s me saying: I am an active participant because of the choices that brought me here.” Like many of the tracks on Swallow!, Lucky[Hymn] is an indie song. “It had more of a classic tone to it because I felt like I was in a classic part of my life,” she says.
With its dreamy, moody guitars and anthemic, crashing drums, Swallow! is a different sound for an artist whose previous records have flirted with hyperpop, UK garage and electronica. As a millennial, Shygirl came of age when guitar-driven pop music was dominating the charts. “It was very prevalent in all the pop I grew up listening to: Keane, Madonna, random shit like the Rasmus,” she says. In the 2010s, when she was a teenager, musical discovery was serendipitous: “We had HMV, where you could just walk in and put the headphones on.” Her curiosity, she says, was encouraged by her parents. “I’m not from a family where they would just give you answers.”
Shygirl is the eldest of three children born to young parents in south-east London, and spent her early years bouncing between Downham, Catford and Lee Green. “My life has shown me that you are never entitled to anything,” she says. “You can be deserving but not receive.” When has she felt like that? “I grew up with that experience. My parents worked really hard. They didn’t have everything.”
Her dad, who is of Grenadian origin, worked for the UK government’s Welsh office and later as a club promoter in Notting Hill. She didn’t see him much when he was working nights. Meanwhile, “my mum used to work as a cleaner, a toilet attendant, a receptionist, a dinner lady,” she says. “She’s always had a job.” So has Shygirl, who as a teenager worked at a restaurant her mum managed.
Her parents are no longer together, though she is quick to clarify that hers was a happy childhood. “I wanted for nothing,” she says. “But I’m of the mindset that if you want something, you have to go get it. I’m only the one to blame if I don’t.” That determination runs through new songs such as Live the Life You Like, a stomping, Prodigy-esque anthem. “And then I’m pushing / It’s not enough,” she purrs.
In Amsterdam, in 2018, she booked her first show before her debut EP, Cruel Practice, had even been released. “I was like: I don’t even have any music out and someone’s taken a chance on me,” she remembers. Soon afterwards she handed in her notice as a booker at a modelling agency. “I’m about to quit a day job that had holiday pay, sick pay, and I’m gonna go be a musician? But because I used to do contracts with the model agency, I knew how to push a rate up.” She negotiated requests from brands who wanted to use her music in their adverts, until one came in from Rihanna, for Fenty Beauty, and she got overexcited – “not as sharky as I usually am” with making the deal. She got a manager, the money came in and Shygirl paid off her credit card. She likens herself to a gambler: “My money was up from being, like, two grand in debt. I’d owed my housemate money for rent.”
She signed a record deal in 2020; this year, she bought a house. She hadn’t even entertained owning one, “because I was so busy thinking I need to pay my rent and bills. My dad still doesn’t own a house. My mum just got one.” Her drive to make music, she says, “has always been to make my life better than my origins, and to prove to my family that their sacrifice is worth something”. But “living an experience they have never lived” has been accompanied by a dose of “mad guilt”.
She played New York’s Madison Square Garden with Charli xcx and Troye Sivan as 2024’s Brat summer raged on into Brat autumn. Seeing how Charli, a peer and friend, was able to maintain her sense of self even as everything became “as big and stressful as it gets” made pop domination feel more achievable. Although, “we definitely have different intentions for our day to day”. Charli, she stresses, works incredibly hard. “I work hard, but I really prioritise chilling,” she laughs.
Spending an afternoon hanging out with Shygirl, as she radiates self-possession, grace and plenty of gossipy wisdom, one gets the sense that she is something of a girl’s girl. “All of us are trying to open doors for each other – all the female artists that I’ve worked with.” Being a woman, she says, is her biggest barrier as an artist. “In my experience, that is the most prevalent block at the moment.” She gives the example of Beyoncé’s Grammy win for best country album with Cowboy Carter, which prompted the Recording Academy to create two separate categories for best country album: traditional and contemporary. “The rules shift, and the doors’ locations change,” she says.
Realising there might be a ceiling for her ambition, one imposed on her by others, has meant she is now “only interested in working with people who want different-ness. Who are not comfortable with the status quo, because I can’t relate to that. It’s not an experience I’ve had in any avenue of my life.” And, she adds, “it’s usually men” upholding that status quo. “Not to be a man hater: I love my boyfriend!”
Shygirl and Smale have been collaborating creatively, too. He provided background vocals on album opener Alyse and they have worked together on the interconnected videos for the new album, which she co-directed and which form an elliptical thriller narrative based around a kidnapping. “You’re dropped into a situation the same as The Bourne Ultimatum or Tell No One. You may have been an ordinary person; you’re now in extraordinary circumstances: what do you do?” she says. Her character ends up tied to a chair. She seldom even thinks of not acting in any situation, she says, so it was a challenge to play someone barely able to move.
But her character screams, shouts, cries and thrashes as she’s held captive, giving Shygirl an outlet for emotions she didn’t realise she needed to express. “I never raise my voice,” she says. “To shout at someone who has made you angry? To show that you’re affected by them in that way? I would never do that.” An eldest daughter, she describes herself as a protector who feels responsible for everyone else in her life. “I feel like every child gets to a point where they see their parents as human beings, not just as their caregivers. That happened for me when I was very young.” How young? “Ten, 12.” It meant she never had idols. “I don’t really look up to anyone in that way,” she says. “I see everyone with faults.”
In the video’s final shot, Shygirl looks directly into the lens, “accepting that this is a contrived environment”. She wanted to break the fourth wall, even if that movie trope is a bit of a cliche: “Sometimes cliches are cliches for a reason, you know?”
Of course, falling in love is the biggest cliche of all, I add. “Exactly!” Once you’ve said “I love you” a million times to your partner, she says, “you’re looking for other ways to express it”. Her smile is beatific thinking about it all. Playing the new album to her boyfriend made her cry; the delicate, intensely vulnerable ballad Real allowed her “to revisit the memory of when we were in Japan, and recognise that now as falling in love”. It has an incredulous, awestruck quality, as though she can’t believe her own good fortune. “We’re always choosing each other,” she says. “I’m always choosing what’s happening in my life.”
brief: Adored by Madonna and Charli xcx and buoyed by finding true love, the Londoner is branching out into rock and breaking the mainstream. She explains how her working class upbringing made her so fearless Leaving the important stuff to chance isn’t Shygirl’s style. title: Some Woman review – Anne-Marie Duff is wholly believable but this twisty drama is not
body:
Opposing forces tug against each other in this new drama as Anne-Marie Duff is magnificent amid playwright Helen Edmundson’s implausible plotting. The result is a failed suspension of disbelief yet a convincing central performance.
Duff plays Julie, a mother, ex-wife and working woman whose already over-burdened life is turned upside down by an incident at a tube station when an 11-year-old boy randomly and aggressively insults her. She challenges him, reasonably, and in a series of unconvincing plot turns, winds up facing a legal battle and potential prison sentence.
As a story of an ordinary middle-aged woman being buffeted by patriarchal forces around her, this play is stuffed full of important issues. We hear stories of casual sexual abuse, laughed off by those around Julie. Now we see her life virtually destroyed by the boy’s allegation.
There is mention of CCTV footage and you wonder if an Adolescence-style video reveal is to come. But the plot makes clear that there is no incontrovertible evidence against her, yet she stands to lose everything.
The points about everyday misogyny come through loud and clear, especially that the legal system is rigged to distrust women and believe men (or an 11-year-old boy in this instance). The West End drama Prima Facie, recently adapted for the screen, showed us just that in relation to sexual violence against women. But this is not a courtroom drama and the alleged crimes on which it turns are simply not believable.
Directed by Blanche McIntyre and staged without an interval, there is potential brilliance here, if only the plot were better crafted and so many unfocused issues not thrown at us – from the eating disorder of one daughter (Grace Doherty) to Julie’s difficult relationship with another (Hannah Onslow), both barely explored, as well as Julie’s experience of infidelity and divorce. Each of these issues gets its moment, briefly, with characters around Julie too flimsy to feel true.
The structural failings of the script aside, there are many individually moving and harrowing scenes. They culminate in a confrontation between Julie and the boy’s father (Stephen Wight). Again, this plot-turn challenges the bounds of believability but this time you can brush that aside because the forces of threat, anger and fear feel horribly, sadly real.
Julie seems pushed towards victimhood yet she refuses this foisted powerlessness in a society where toxic masculinity is chillingly in plain sight: men openly express loathing of women, boys spit obscenities at female strangers. Truth is all Julie has and upholds, whatever the legal repercussions. She is not only the everyday victim of misogyny but an everyday female hero too. This message has its own power, however bad the plotting may be.
- At the Dorfman theatre, National Theatre, London, until 21 November
brief: Dorfman theatre, London The far-fetched plot turns and some underdeveloped characters undermine the powerful messages about prejudice in Helen Edmundson’s play Opposing forces tug against each other in this new drama as Anne-Marie Duff is magnificent amid playwright Helen Edmundson’s implausible plotting. title: Sweet nothings, urinal cakes and headless dogs: 10 artworks worth seeing at Frieze
body:
Ella Fleck at Ehrlich Steinberg
The raised platform in the middle of British artist Ella Fleck’s installation vibrates under your feet to the sound of a male voice. He’s whispering sweet nothings, intoning sexual fantasies. It’s all based on third-party agencies that manage OnlyFans accounts, interacting with users, creating fictional relationships that horny guys spend thousands on. It’s a greasy, gross, uncomfortable exploration of sex work on an industrial scale.
Yuli Serfaty at Xxijra Hii
Yuli Serfaty’s headless metallic dog sculptures guard this booth, their claws sharp, their heavy teats dragging on the floor. It’s a surreal symbol of femininity pushed to an extreme, a body devalued and exploited. A video shows the creature trying to escape the booth, and succeeding. The whole installation looks like HR Giger meets Wolfenstein 3D, but with a nasty, satirical edge.
Rirkrit Tiravanija at David Zwirner
Finally, something to help you get through Frieze. Thai artist Rirkrit Tiravanija’s sculpture here is a robotic arm that carefully hands visitors a little red-and-white ibuprofen pill. If you don’t reach out, it just drops it on the floor. The robot does its job, over and over, regardless of if you’re there to receive it. It feels futile, obscene, repetitive, meaningless. Quite the comment on modern life.
Carolyn Lazard at Trautwein Herleth
It might look like a display of pens, and that’s because it is. But each one is a promotional item from a pharmaceutical company, given out as gifts to American medical professionals. Lazzard bought them in estate sales from real doctors. They become a portrait of selling out, of how healthcare in the US can be bought by corporations. There are pens with branding for antidepressants, ADHD meds, Viagra: corporations are keeping you going, keeping you productive. When it clicks, it’s an incredibly grim conceptual vision of how our bodies are treated as commodities.
Gray Wielebinski in the toilets
The urinal cakes in the Frieze bogs this year aren’t just there to keep whiffs at bay – they’re art. This is urinal cake as sculptural intervention, thanks to artist Gray Wielebinski, who has designed each one with a custom scent and encased them in metal cages. They sort of look like little chastity devices, glistening lumps of odorous chemicals for you to wee on. They’re weird, almost erotic sculptures. You can hear the anguished cry of thousands of artists wishing they’d thought of it first.
Miriam Cahn at Galerie Jocelyn Wolff
There is such an overwhelming amount of (usually very bland) painting at Frieze that it really takes a special painter to stand out. But Swiss artist Miriam Cahn’s installation is a proper diamond among the swill. It’s a whole booth filled with 26 years’ worth of self-portraiture. Each one plumbs new depths of anxious, monstrous introspection. She grins and screams, stands and falls, all in blurred, messy washes of colour. Psychologically intense, overwrought, emotional stuff.
William-Adolphe Bouguereau at Stair Sainty
My love for 19th-century French academic painter William-Adolphe Bouguereau verges on a sickness. I mean, I have a Bouguereau tattoo. So finding this little gem among the Dutch flower paintings and Egyptian busts of Frieze Masters was a genuine thrill. It’s a weird, yellowed little thing – based on a Tintoretto – of a man lying prostrate on the ground. The ropes that bind him have been snapped, wood is splintered. Here is the aftermath of violence, the shocking silence after a traumatic event. This is one of the great things about Masters: getting to spot art historical gold hidden away on the back wall of some booth. This gallery also had a gorgeous James Tissot portrait. It’s 19th-century art nerd heaven.
Luce Turnier at Harlesden High Street
There are some amazing narratives to discover in the Frieze Masters spotlight section, especially the work of Haitian modernist Luce Turnier, who lived between Paris and Haiti but has largely been forgotten by art history. This small display of stark portraits – like a more sombre Alice Neel – and vitrines is a little glimpse into a lost period of international modernism from an artist who feels ripe for a museum show.
Camarasaurus supremus skull at David Aaron
You eventually go antiquities and Flemish art blind walking around Frieze Masters, so finding the fossilised dino skulls that David Aaron Gallery has lugged to the tent is always a bit of Jurassic relief. This year they’ve brought an enormous triceratops skull and an awesome camarasaurus supremus with the tooth of an allosaurus embedded in it. Absolutely brutal, and possibly the only thing my four-year-old would like in either fair.
Sohrab Hura at Experimenter
There’s death and fear written into all of Sohrab Hura’s paintings here. They’re grotesque expressionist scenes of everyday violence: a man kicked to the ground, a crow pecking at a bleeding carcass above a figure staring aghast at a newspaper. It’s like Edvard Munch but with way more blood and guts. The painting of the woman in the dust storm isn’t good, but the rest are great, angry things.
brief: There’s plenty that stands out at Regent’s Park this year, from antidepressant pens and an ibuprofen-dolling robotic arm to Miriam Cahn’s 26 years’ worth of self-portraiture and a 150m-year-old dinosaur skull – still with embedded tooth Frieze review – you’ll see more avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tent The raised platform in the middle of British artist Ella Fleck’s installation vibrates und

title: An open book: how to make a great film adaptation, from The Shining to Trainspotting
body:
It is always fun to join in a craze, like a Victorian going mad for penny farthings. Which is probably why, against my better judgment, I went to see Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster The Odyssey this summer, buying my ticket into the popular conversation along with everyone else. This year’s other divisive adaptation, Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights, had the world and his wife arguing about it before they had even watched the film. No doubt the makers of the recent Sense and Sensibility movie were also hoping for lots of people to go and see it to discover whether they hated it.
After all, very few of us leave the cinema saying: “That’s exactly how I pictured it in my head.” Or even less likely: “That was better than the book.” We’re more likely to shake our fists at how they ruined the ending, dumbed it down, unforgivably cast somebody with the wrong hair, or betrayed a beloved character, as with last year’s Thursday Murder Club debacle.
But what makes a good adaptation? Like Odysseus himself, and as every Nancy Meyers fan knows: it’s complicated. I have just written a book about the towering heights and profane depths of adaptation, The Book Was Better, for which I subjected myself to some of the worst viewing experiences possible, including the soft rock opera musical Heathcliff; 1996’s freakishly bad The Island of Dr Moreau; and a horrible three-part version of Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged. But I also saw plenty of masterpieces that equalled or sometimes surpassed the originals. Here’s what I learned.
The first thing to say is that the quality of the source is irrelevant. I went into my research with some pretty fixed ideas: for instance, that “the brilliant adaptations are nearly always of fiction of the second or third class”, as Anthony Burgess wrote; that some works are “unfilmable”; that classics have more “room to breathe” on TV. Soon I realised none of these were true. Yes, sometimes workmanlike novels, such as the late 60s and early 70s triumvirate Jaws, The Godfather and The Exorcist, can be tuned to a level of genius on screen. But great books can make great films, too: Trainspotting, The Go-Between, The Leopard and Burgess’s own A Clockwork Orange are just a few examples. And sometimes, in the case of The Da Vinci Code and Fifty Shades of Grey, a deeply silly book becomes a deeply silly film.
It is true that certain books lend themselves to the screen more readily. Jane Austen’s immaculate plots of love impeded are templates that can be dressed up in the clothes of any age, like the computer template Cher Horowitz uses to plan her outfits at the start of Clueless – the ne plus ultra of free-handed adaptations. Austen’s novels contain the DNA of all romcoms, just as Robinson Crusoe is found in The Martian, the gothic novel in horror films, or A Christmas Carol in every single Christmas movie. Short stories, with their twisty shocks and rush towards the end point, seem made for cinema; my favourite film, Don’t Look Now, is based on a Daphne du Maurier novella. The murky origins and elasticity of myths and their close cousins, folk and fairytales, make them ceaselessly adaptable, because they leave gaps for a film-maker to fill with their own imaginations.
Being unfaithful is usually helpful. Some of the best adaptations flirt with the source material, taking frightful liberties and then abandoning it like a tabloid love rat. “Steal the parts that you need, and then run as fast as you can,” advised Paul Thomas Anderson; Hitchcock claimed he read The Birds once before making his version, and never thought about it again. (One screenwriter I spoke to told me he was once asked not to read the novel he was adapting as the production company thought it would be a hindrance). Books and films are entirely different beasts, “apples and giraffes”, as author-screenwriter Dennis Lehane once said. Adaptation is an act of translation from the verbal to the visual. A film-maker needs to find their own language.
One of my most beloved unfaithful adaptations is Alfonso Cuarón’s 2006 Children of Men, and not just because it stars Clive Owen at the peak of his physical perfection. It manages to transform a cerebral, theological novel by the Conservative peer PD James into a dystopian thriller about populism, terror and how we treat immigrants, one which – although now two decades old – feels fresher each year. (James was delighted with it.) Cuarón used the novel as a jumping-off point, then left it behind to follow his own adventure. What remained was the central conceit: what if we lived in a world without children? The “what if” high concepts of science fiction and speculative fiction are perfect for playing fast and loose with: a vessel into which a film-maker’s own preoccupations, and the anxieties of their age, can be poured.
When writer-director Sally Potter reinvented Virginia Woolf’s time-travelling fantasia Orlando, she treated it “as if the book never existed”, turning it into a lavish nose-thumb to a UK establishment that had just passed section 28. She was, she said, cruel to the novel to be kind to the film. It’s the destruction-as-creation mantra. In the hands of the right writer and director, a source can, and should, be made to submit to their will: Stanley Kubrick betrayed Stephen King’s vision of The Shining but made a tour de force. Heart of Darkness mutated into a war epic with Apocalypse Now; Red Dragon became, well, a Michael Mann film, the hypnotic Manhunter. An adaptation should never be a hollow greatest hits album. Being too reverential towards a literary source can kill it, which is why I suspect films such as The Hunger Games and The Road, lovingly and stylishly made with few changes, felt slightly bloodless on screen to me.
Can anything really be faithful anyway, and to what? No story is 100 per cent original. (As Alien screenwriter Dan O’Bannon said: “I didn’t steal from anybody. I stole from everybody!”) I don’t even think you can be “true to the spirit” of a text, because the spirit is different for everyone. We all have our own little films running in our heads when we read. Many see The Great Gatsby as a death knell for the US; adapters tend to think: “parties!”. I think Heathcliff is a psychopath who likes to hang little dogs; successive directors clearly didn’t. I loved discovering that Jodie Foster lobbied hard for the part of Clarice Starling in The Silence of the Lambs because, for her, the novel was about a woman saving the life of another woman while “all these fucking men” get in the way. An adaptation may just be a glimpse into another mind’s eye, but their pictures seldom match the ones we had imagined.
Perhaps the most obvious example of this is casting. As sure as night follows day, Hollywood casts a better-looking actor than strictly necessary, although not always reaching “Denise Richards in hotpants as a nuclear physicist in The World is Not Enough” levels. This can be deliberate: in Robert Bloch’s novel Psycho, Norman Bates is physically repellent; Hitchcock wanted the sweet-faced Anthony Perkins for the part to wrongfoot the audience. More often it’s because, as the critic Roger Ebert observed, cinema is a machine for generating empathy, so the thinking goes that leads should be “likable” – which backfired horribly when Bruce Willis was cast as a desiccated English journalist in the notoriously disastrous adaptation of Tom Wolfe’s The Bonfire of the Vanities. But sometimes an actor who is wrong on paper can make a role their own, whether it’s Margaret Rutherford as Miss Marple, Renée Zellweger as Bridget Jones or Michael Caine as Harry Palmer in The Ipcress File (in Len Deighton’s novels he’s a northerner and doesn’t have a name). Charisma goes a long way.
Perhaps in the end, adaptation all comes down to emotions and sensations. “You’ve drunk the drink, and the taste that’s left in your mouth is what you go with,” as Anthony Minghella described adapting The Talented Mr Ripley. Irvine Welsh said you must smell the books. Hossein Amini, who reinvented The Wings of the Dove as “noir in costume”, wanted to recapture that ecstatic moment when “nobody else in the world understood or experienced that book exactly like I did”.
Returning to The Odyssey, I wonder why, even though Nolan did the right things, subordinating it to his worldview and faithlessly reinventing it for our age by turning a wily trickster into a traumatised veteran, the film just made me feel as if I’d been in a war: long periods of boredom and waiting punctuated by violence. Perhaps, ultimately, he overthought it and should have felt it instead? Or maybe, as the late Hilary Mantel said of adaptation, you must “put down the text, and dream it”.
brief: Not every great novel makes a great movie, and sometimes the opposite is true. But regardless of the source text, or how beloved characters are treated, there is more than one way to write a successful adaptation It is always fun to join in a craze, like a Victorian going mad for penny farthings. Which is probably why, against my better judgment, I went to see Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster The O

title: Sod’s law: what can two turf swaps 40 years apart tell us about Britain’s biodiversity crisis?
body:
In 1983, an open-topped truck unloaded an unusual cargo in Kensington Gardens: 83 hunks of turf cut from Cae’n y Coed, a wooded hillside in the Ffestiniog valley. The ring of turf measuring eight metres in diameter that was removed from the park beside the Serpentine Gallery in west London to make space for the Welsh sods was then trucked from London to north Wales.
So began Sod Swap, a piece of sculptural defiance by David Nash, which has had an unexpected and epic afterlife. More than 40 years later, photographic artist Mike Perry restaged the work as Reverse Sod Swap, exchanging exactly the same amount of turf between Springfield Park in Hackney, east London, and pastureland in Pembrokeshire, with strikingly different results. With twin works acquiring new relevance in a time of extinction and climate crises, the sod swapping is now the subject of a new book.
It all began, says Nash, who is 80 and still working with wood and trees, with his own “bloody-mindedness”. He was invited to contribute to a new Serpentine gallery show of British sculpture. He submitted an idea of some wood sculptures for an indoor gallery because he felt too many outdoor sculptures were “like UFOs, they came and they went”, as he puts it. “But the gallery said: ‘Oh, David, you’re an outside artist, so we’d like you to participate in the outdoor space.”
Nash, who made his very outdoorsy Ash Dome and Wooden Boulder a few years before, bristled. He’d actually created an outdoor piece for a Serpentine show when he was a postgrad student at Chelsea Art School in 1970. When he tried to secure it in the ground he was told he couldn’t touch the Kensington Gardens turf because it belonged to the queen.
So this time, he plotted to rough up the manicured London park’s immaculate lawns by installing a ring of wild grassland from north Wales while also challenging definitions of “sculpture”. There was a lot of “bright red metal” around in the early 80s, says Nash wryly. “I wanted to create something that didn’t need to be cleaned.”
Sod Swap, he says, was a declaration of his identity. “I was very keen that what I put in had a sense of where it came from, which was where I was, which was north Wales.” When he realised he would have to dig up a load of Kensington turf, he decided to take that back to Wales. “That became the swap, and I liked the connotation of being a sod. It was nothing to do with the environment, really, but it turned out to be.”
Nash was anticipating a reaction and he got one. After several worried meetings about the dig, and head-scratching from council officials about the risk of “invasive” Welsh plants contaminating Kensington Gardens, Sod Swap went ahead. “He’s very subversive, David,” says Perry. “He doesn’t look it, but he is. The Serpentine expected him to bring in a big wooden sculpture. And he said: ‘No, I’m going to cut up your lawn.’ He wanted to show who he is as a person but also what sculpture could be – it doesn’t have to be a solid object on a plinth. It can be an ephemeral piece of organic material.”
In 2023, when Perry started a rewilding and art project on 4.9 hectares (12 acres) of farmland in west Wales, he wondered if he might revisit Nash’s concept, four decades on. Slightly nervously, he contacted Nash, and was relieved when the sculptor gave an enthusiastic “yes”. A week later, Perry drove over to north Wales, where Nash took him to see the site of the Kensington Garden sods. Amazingly, 40 years on, they could still detect a faint circle in mossy grass now punctuated by mature trees.
The Welsh turf hadn’t lasted so long in London. After the show ended, the gallery planned to simply to remove the turf but, thankfully for Nash, the “archangels of art outside”, Sue Clifford and Angela King, stepped in. The two co-founders of environmental arts charity Common Ground hurriedly found another unlikely London home for Nash’s Welsh sods: in the lawns of Kenwood House on Hampstead Heath.
Clifford and King also had the bright idea of convening ecologists to count the species in each turf circle. The Welsh sods held 28 different species, including grasses, wildflowers, brambles and even nettles, while the manicured sods cut from Kensington Gardens were made up of a meagre three different species of grass. Suddenly, Nash’s little challenge to the art world held an ecological message, highlighting the biodiversity to be found in rural meadowlands and the sterile quality of urban parks.
While Nash’s little piece of Wales acclimatised to Hampstead Heath, the artist conscientiously watered the London turf at Cae’ny Coed, even buying a secondhand mower so he could keep it in the condition to which it was accustomed. The original plan was to return it to Kensington Gardens, but Nash says the Arts Council told him they had run out of project money and couldn’t afford to transport it back. Sod Swap became permanent.
Eventually, after 10 years at Kenwood House, English Heritage removed the Welsh sods. “The London turf stayed in Wales,” remembers Nash. “Chestnut trees I planted grew and grew and shaded the turf, and moss came in. There were daisies from London which came up for about five years but then disappeared. I kept up mowing it as if it was in London for 20 years until it was virtually all moss and then I thought I would let it go.” Over the years, artists, curators and students made a pilgrimage to visit it.
Reverse Sod Swap was “a kind of biographical piece for me,” says Perry. He lived in London for 20 years before moving to an old farm by the sea in north Pembrokeshire. “My parents retired down here so I’ve always been going between east London and west Wales,” he says. The landscape and seascape of the Pembrokeshire Coast national park still looks gorgeous but “it’s a very melancholy thing walking down to the sea because there’s nothing in the hedges. They’re stripped right back and the grass is just mown 24/7 by so many sheep. The chair of the RSPB [Royal Society for the Protection of Birds] said national parks are where wildlife goes to die.”
Perry had hoped Reverse Sod Swap would be an ecological statement, but he couldn’t have anticipated just how much of a statement it would make. In Wales, he took the turf from pasture still heavily grazed by sheep belonging to a tenant farmer. At the London end, he was given “a really poor” plot in Springfield Park with “bad bits of soil from everywhere and a little bit of grass out of all sorts of rough material. But I quite liked it because there were giant burdocks and ‘weeds’ and thistles. I liked that mix.”
Perry’s first challenge was to replicate the dimensions. Nash couldn’t remember the exact size of his 1983 turf circles but Perry dug out the old catalogue statement, which noted that there were 83 sods measuring 90x30cm (35x12in) in size. He then followed Nash’s idea of making little wooden “stretchers” to carry each sod from the ground to the waiting lorry. On the journey to Wales, they twice stopped at motorway services to water the precious sods.
In the two-and-a-half years since Reverse Sod Swap, Perry has been surprised by how the project has continued to transfix him. “David put his hand on my shoulder and looked me in the eye and said: ‘Mike, when you make work outside, things happen.’ I didn’t really know what he meant. But what’s amazing is that the work is living and changing all the time – it keeps giving me new images and new findings.”
After the reverse transplant, botanists surveyed the transplanted turfs and, strikingly, found the reverse of Nash’s 1983 swap. The turf taken from Springfield Park contained 39 species in total, whereas the Welsh sheep-grazed turf contained just four species. And so, across four decades, the two works starkly illustrate the loss of rural biodiversity – a loss often disguised by the superficially unchanging character of the British landscape, with its patchwork of hedges, fields and woods. But Reverse Sod Swap also reveals a more hopeful trend in London, where species have been revived by urban rewilding efforts, from creating wildflower areas in parks to building new sustainable urban drainage areas.
Perry is encouraged by what he sees when he returns to London and walks down the Grand Union canal. “It feels like there’s butterflies, there’s rough stuff. It’s not scientific because there are obviously areas in Wales that can’t be farmed and there’s amazing biodiversity, but I was just really trying to make a point through art.”
Nash is touched by the longevity of his Sod Swap, and the ecological message it has taken on. “What Mike has done is an amazing bonus,” he says. “My Sod Swap highlighted the paucity of plant species in London, not that that was my main intention. Reverse Sod Swap is much more pertinent environmentally because it’s highlighting the paucity of rural land. We artists put work out there and hope people will see it and make something of it – be stimulated or take it on as part of their awareness.”
- Reverse Sod Swap by Mike Perry and David Nash is published by Little Toller on 16 October (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Four decades later, Mike Perry’s reverse swap revealed a striking reversal in the fortunes of urban and rural nature In 1983, an open-topped truck unloaded an unusual cargo in Kensington Gardens: 83 hunks of turf cut from Cae’n y Coed, a wooded hillside in the Ffestiniog valley. title: They asked for 80 homes – she gave them 157! Council-housing miracle named Britain’s best new building
body:
If Andy Burnham is looking for inspiration for his great “council housebuilding comeback”, he would do well to visit Croydon. There, nestled into a steeply sloping site, sheltered by a canopy of mature trees, stands a cluster of crystalline pink and brown brick towers, where generous flats look on to a landscape of allotments, playgrounds and to the rolling hills of south London beyond. Designed by Mary Duggan Architects, with Ruff Architects, it is a model of council-led housebuilding – so much so that it has also been named this year’s best building in the UK, confounding the bookies’ outsider odds.
Only once before has the RIBA Stirling prize ever been awarded to a council housing project, when Goldsmith Street in Norwich scooped the gong in 2019, for its rows of low-energy brick terraces, designed by Mikhail Riches Architects and Cathy Hawley. This year’s winner, Lion Green Road in Coulsdon, is an entirely different animal, and it puts a welcome spotlight back on housing design at a time when the government plans to pump £39bn into the sector. It is also a bittersweet vindication of Croydon council’s erstwhile housebuilding company, Brick by Brick, a bold and sadly brief experiment by the previous Labour administration, which was halted in 2020 when the council went bankrupt, seeing numerous projects cancelled.
“At a time when we urgently need to deliver more homes,” says RIBA president, Chris Williamson, “Lion Green Road shows that density can be achieved without compromising the quality of the places we create. Through a consistent specification, with subtle variation in height and orientation, it offers housing at scale without uniformity.”
Burnham’s first allocation of £10bn, announced in August, is planned to kickstart 70,000 affordable homes across the country. Yet few people in Britain welcome the prospect of new housing in their backyards, even if it’s prize-winning. The planning application for Lion Green Road, submitted in 2017, received 18 letters of support and 257 objections, mostly about the loss of parking. Now built, almost a decade later, the project demonstrates how more homes than you might imagine can be constructed on the most unpromising of sites in a sympathetic way, without sacrificing greenery, views and public access – and keeping plenty of parking, too.
“We really pushed against the suburban model of terraces dominated by cars, with little front and back gardens,” says Duggan. The original brief asked for 80 homes, arranged as she describes, but Duggan proved she could fit 157 flats, distributed between five pavilion-like towers, retaining the mature trees and bluebell woodland on the site. The result feels like it has grown out of its woodland setting, with a public route that winds its way through the site, up to a historic railway embankment at the rear, and not a perimeter fence in sight.
“Brick by Brick was an amazing client,” says Duggan, who also had a small mews project in Crystal Palace on the drawing board for the council’s housebuilder, before the plug was pulled. “It was a refreshing change from how private developers think about affordable housing. Here, they weren’t talking about the land as a commodity, but as a genuinely public asset.”
The council cared about the interior spaces, too. Thanks to the “pinwheel” plan of the blocks, with flats radiating outwards from a central lift core, each home is dual aspect, maximising natural light, cross-ventilation and views. The flats all enjoy an inset loggia balcony, with a bulge at the base of the balustrades to accommodate plant pots, while cuts in the form (to preserve historic views) create some with larger roof terraces. In the interests of efficiency, the five towers all have the same star-shaped plan, but each is subtly rotated to reduce direct overlooking between neighbouring homes, enabling the buildings to stand close together without sacrificing privacy. Half of the flats are private rental, in two towers, while half are affordable, in three blocks retained by the council, rented at local housing allowance rates. Unlike the Norwich project, this is not true social housing.
The RIBA judges describe the project as a “new kind of garden neighbourhood”. The space between the blocks feels consciously planned, rather than a leftover afterthought, designed with landscape architecture practice Planit-IE to include a sensory garden, allotment plots and play areas. Walking around the development’s zig-zagging slopes and stepped pathways gives the feeling of exploring a bucolic hill town. Little bug hotels in the same faceted star-shaped form as the towers are a delightful touch; even the insects get a dignified dwelling.
Duggan says the project “expands the idea of the threshold”, and the arrival feels more welcoming than most. The entrance of each block is framed by a paved terrace, with seating and planting, while all have generous lobbies, no matter the tenure. It’s a far cry from the “poor door” apartheid of so much developer-built housing, where private owners get the hotel concierge treatment, while affordable tenants enter around the back by the bins. It all oozes quality on a budget, down to the choice of three dusty colours of brick, some projecting to create a textured, tweedy finish. The quality belies the tight construction budget of £2,500/sq metre – making it the cheapest project on the shortlist by far. Other Stirling Prize contenders this year included two exquisitely built projects for well-heeled Cambridge colleges, a large private house in Essex, an arts centre in Hertford, and an £825m office block in Paddington.
If there is a cloud hanging over Croydon’s triumph, it is the fate of Brick by Brick. It was established in 2015, as a wholly council-owned company, because the conventional development model was failing to deliver enough affordable homes. The idea was that Croydon would use its own land, often small leftover sites, and borrow against its own resources, to build a mix of private and affordable housing, while turning a profit for the public purse. But the sites often proved to be trickier than expected, adding additional costs, while the financial forecasts were overly optimistic, with Brexit and Covid introducing huge delays. Housing experts attribute its collapse to poor financial structuring, governance and risk management, rather than a failure in development expertise or quality of delivery.
Nonetheless, Brick by Brick built 751 homes, over half of which are affordable, of a design quality higher than most standard developer fare. With renewed housing cash from central government, might there be a chance for some of the halted schemes to be resurrected, and more of the imagination and innovation of Lion Green Road spread across the borough and beyond?

title: Calling the shots: what NAZA says about perpetrator cinema
body:
Are we still talking about the banality of evil? When that overworked phrase was first used by philosopher Hannah Arendt, it described the blank persona of Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann. Now, in NAZA, anonymised members of Israeli intelligence discuss their remote execution of the assault on Gaza. The comparison to Hitler’s Germany, while understandably controversial, is made by a subject themselves. If they are banal, it is a modern, oddly familiar kind. These are articulate, middle-class millennials. They say they are leftwing and non-racist. Put differently, they could be Guardian readers.
And yes, one remarks, they have been conducting a genocide.
The work of directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor is shattering. But we have been shattered before by the firsthand accounts of people who carry out atrocities – sometimes called perpetrator cinema. In 2013, director Joshua Oppenheimer released The Act of Killing, an astonishing film involving members of 1960s right-wing Indonesian death squads. It was lavishly acclaimed. Since then, it has only kept feeling painfully relevant.
Before that, documentary wild card Errol Morris made Standard Operating Procedure, interviewing US soldiers who abused Iraqis at the notorious Abu Ghraib jail. Edging into drama, you might even include Jonathan Glazer’s The Zone of Interest, where the commandant of Auschwitz lives happily with his wife and children. (Glazer is an executive producer of NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian.)
Questions gnaw through them all. To begin: who is it that commits crimes against humanity? The answer can feel inconclusive. NAZA is filled with Tel Aviv high-fliers, some citing as justification the horrific attacks of October 7. But the American troops of Standard Operating Procedure are ordinary grunts in the “war on terror”. Meanwhile, in The Act of Killing, ageing street thugs recreate their murders of trade unionists and teachers as the action movies they imagine them being. Flamboyance blooms in the abyss.
In every case, what we see won’t leave our heads, even as we flail for an adequate response. The late critic Roger Ebert famously called movies “empathy machines”. But these films short circuit the machinery. How can we empathise with people who seem to show no remorse?
For some, NAZA presents a bigger problem than that. The Israeli government has floated stripping Abraham and Szor of their citizenship, among other threats. But even for audiences far from the Middle East, the film is hard to deal with. We may feel anguished just as we are reminded how safe our anguish is. We might even think about that most unfriendly word: complicity.
But perpetrator cinema is about more than complicity. It is about the attempt to fathom the perpetrator. Discussing NAZA on the Jewish Currents podcast, Oppenheimer spoke to that task. “To understand a crime as a human activity, we have to look at the human beings who undertake that activity.”
Or do we understand mass murderers enough through what they do? In 2013, The Act of Killing also met pungent criticism. One influential figure in British documentary publicly called it a “snuff film”. (Oppenheimer next made The Look of Silence, about the victims.) And NAZA has faced pre-emptive criticism from Palestinians, including poet Mosab Abu Toha, arguing that the last three years in Gaza have already been documented by Gazans. “It’s all there,” he posted on social media. “So what will this film add?”
In this reading, NAZA is accused of privileging the perpetrator – giving literal voice to those for who the best platform, perhaps, would be a trial at the Hague. And yet another question is both obvious and uncomfortable. What’s in it for them anyway?
In this year’s documentary Killing Anna, former Syrian army officers were catfished into discussing civilian massacres by an academic posing as a loyalist of Bashar al-Assad. But most perpetrators are wholly aware they are being recorded. As such, we might expect a sobbing confessional. Not quite.
The torturers of Standard Operating Procedure came close now and then, but only amid a lot of evasion. As further ethical complication, they were also paid for their interviews. With The Act of Killing, though, Oppenheimer found a still more disturbing truth – his butchers were gleefully unrepentant. (They also believed that, as an American, he would approve of garrotting leftists.) And in NAZA, Yuval Abraham has said some of his interviewees spoke from “the opposite of shame”. That word complicity comes up again. Should a film-maker be doing this?
The thing is, though, lack of shame has a price. “War crimes are defined by the winners,” an Indonesian gangster says in The Act of Killing. “I’m a winner, so I can make my own definition.” In these films, that definition changes hands. Brilliantly, Oppenheimer did it by granting his subjects the freedom to reveal their nightmare psyches. In NAZA, journalism of the highest quality draws out a guilty plea with a seemingly howling lack of conscience.
Palestinian accounts of the assault on Gaza have been wrongly ignored. The response, to this Israeli version, of the Netanyahu government is telling. Aside from menacing the directors, a mimicking rebuttal, Naza: The Real Story was recently launched, desperately trying to reclaim control of the story.
And a director’s “complicity” is often indispensable. In 2017, the scalding Adriana’s Pact saw Chilean documentary maker Lissette Orozco interview her aunt, rumoured to have worked for the secret police of dictator Augusto Pinochet. When it turned out she had, the aunt’s berserk response to what she saw as a family betrayal was crucial to the story. Now the exposures of NAZA come from interviewees who would presumably never have talked to Abraham and Szor were they not Israeli too.
But more than that – the fact they are is also proof that Israelis can still say no to this Israel. Vital as they are elsewhere, the real power of these films is in the societies they portray. Official Indonesian history echoed the gangsters’ tales of bravely ridding the country of communists. Oppenheimer made the film available free there. Now NAZA confronts the belief that atrocities are only ever down to far-right “bad apples”. In perpetrator cinema, a common thread is directing us to unseen hierarchies – the politicians and generals whose lies to their own people are now laid bare.
Put like that, hope almost glimmers. Still. These films advise caution. Hollywood movies are delivery systems for catharsis. Here, it is elusive. Near the end of The Act of Killing, the most naggingly sympathetic of the subjects starts to retch, as if his body is trying to expel his own past. But nothing comes up. And now we watch NAZA, and know what has happened in Gaza still happens today.
No, what hope perpetrator cinema gives us is specific. Appearing with Oppenheimer on the Jewish Currents pod, Palestinian film-maker Rami Younis recalled meeting a giant of his country’s cinema, director Hany Abu-Assad, whose movies had been accused of humanising Israeli police. “What do you think happens when you keep demonising your enemy?” Abu-Assad said. “What happens to you?”
Usually “humanising” implies a soft focus. But NAZA and The Act of Killing remind us being human involves being capable of evil. They also offer the chance to fight back. The perpetrator of genocide refuses to see their enemy as like themselves – to truly look at them. With perpetrator cinema, though, we can look hard at people with whom we would like to share nothing – and say we are both human, however monstrous that also makes us.
brief: The documentary detailing Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza is the latest film to give a voice to those who carry out atrocities – confronting viewers with some of the most difficult questions of all Are we still talking about the banality of evil? title: Severe drought declared in six areas of England as reservoirs run low
body:
A severe drought has been declared in six areas of England, with some reservoirs at critically low levels, threatening public supplies.
Parts of Devon, Cornwall, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex have moved into severe drought, and urgent measures are being taken to secure public supplies of water after the UK experienced its hottest summer on record.
Despite the crisis, the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, has yet to approve requests from three water companies, two in areas now in severe drought, to extend restrictions on water use to businesses such as golf clubs and commercial car washes.
Emma Hardy, the water minister, indicated on Thursday that the environment could suffer in the continuing drought.
Hardy instructed the Environment Agency to prioritise protecting public water supplies in areas affected by severe drought where there is an unavoidable trade-off between environmental rules and water supplies.
After a meeting of the national drought group, Eagle, said: “This level of drought is something we have not experienced for decades, so this government is stepping up our support and planning.
“We are working closely with water companies to protect public supplies in the areas affected, and I’d continue to urge everyone to think about how they can use water wisely over the coming weeks.”
South East Water, South West Water and Southern Water want to impose non-essential user bans on businesses to protect supplies. This would affect golf clubs, private schools and commercial properties. But while Eagle called on water companies to step up their drought planning, she did not announce approval for the non-essential user bans.
The south-east and south-west of England have experienced their driest April to September in more than a century, fuelled by the climate crisis, affecting reservoir levels in those areas.
Levels at two reservoirs are critically low. Ardingly reservoir, which serves about 95,000 properties in Haywards Heath, Uckfield and surrounding areas, is only 19% full.
Storage at Wimbleball, which supplies South West Water customers in East Devon, North Devon, Somerset and West Dorset and Wessex Water customers in West Somerset, is at 16%.
The Environment Agency (EA) would expect reservoir storage to be about 75% at this time of year.
There are also concerns for several smaller South West Water reservoirs serving homes in Devon and Cornwall; these include Drift and Stithians which supply 56,000 households in Cornwall, and the Tottiford and Venford group which supplies 47,000 households in Devon.
The National Drought Group said the government and the EA would move to daily monitoring of reservoir and river levels and run heightened water quality monitoring because of the lower dilution levels of sewage, raising the risks for water quality and environmental pollution.
Businesses that abstract water will be put through more compliance checks to make sure they are taking only what they are allowed.
Philip Duffy, the chief executive of the EA, said: “We cannot change the weather, but water companies can act now. We expect them to follow their drought plans and take the steps needed to secure public water supplies.
“We are also asking everyone to use less water. That will leave more in our rivers and the environment, helping farmers and protecting wildlife and nature.”

title: Plan unveiled to increase share of land farmed organically in England to 10%
body:
The government has set an ambition to increase the share of English land farmed organically to 10% by 2036, but concerns remain over how the transition will be funded.
Currently, just 3.4% of England’s agricultural land is farmed organically, one of the smallest shares in Europe. France, for example, farms 10.4% of its land organically, and aims to increase this to 18% by 2027.
Rob Haward, the chief executive of organic veg box company Riverford, said it was a reflection of organic farming having political backing in the EU. Whereas in England, the last organic farming plan was published more than two decades ago.
The government’s new plan, which has been more than three years in the making, sets out a vision for growth in the organic sector, with public procurement – in schools and hospitals, for example – cited as a significant opportunity. The government already has a long-term ambition for 10% of public sector food spend to meet higher environmental production standards. The plan states that the organic sector can play a vital role in achieving this.
The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, said the plan was about “opening up opportunities across the sector, from backing farmers already producing organic food to helping others decide whether it could work for their businesses”.
She added: “Organic farming should not be treated as a niche. More people are looking closely at where their food comes from, how it is produced and whether it meets standards they value.”
Haward said public procurement was “impenetrable” for small organic farms, but hoped the plan would be a “catalyst for growth”. However, he said the sector now needed proper backing from the government, including grant funding.
In September, thousands of farmers were left empty-handed after the government’s sustainable farming incentive 2026 (SFI) funding was spent in just six hours. This meant that some farmers who might have been planning to use the funding to transition to organic farming may have missed out.
“SFI needs to be reliable, successful and secure to enable this transition,” said Haward. “It’s hard for any farm to invest in their business if things change, we need some consistency.”
Gareth Morgan, the head of farming policy at the Soil Association, said there had been a lot of discussions with Defra about funding, but in the end “there has been a compromise”.
“There is now an urgent need to reopen SFI to enable farms to move to organic farming,” he said.
Morgan added that increasing the share of land farmed organically could bring down the price of organic food for consumers. “Currently the price of food is subsidised and we don’t pay for the environmental impact. If organic food becomes more mainstream, the price difference will become less,” he said.
Martin Lines, the chief executive of the Nature Friendly Farming Network, said farmers could not rely on government funding alone to make this transition, and said there needed to be “real investment from the supply chain and the private sector, along with fairer prices for farmers for their goods and stronger domestic markets for homegrown produce”.
The National Farmers’ Union, whose members include organic and non-organic farms, said the plan signified a “really positive step forward … for the wider supply chain”.
“Supporting domestic production will strengthen the resilience of our food supply chains and ensure British farmers and growers benefit from opportunities, rather than increasing our reliance on imports,” said Paul Tompkins, the deputy president of the union.
In the plan’s foreword, Eagle said: “Across England, organic farmers, growers and food businesses play an important role in producing high-quality food while caring for soils, wildlife and the rural communities they are part of. In doing so, they also help advance wider goals for nature recovery, cleaner water and greater climate resilience.”
This year has been challenging for farmers because of crop-destroying heat and drought alongside soaring fertiliser costs tied to the war in Iran. Organic farms have been found to be more resilient in the face of these extreme weather conditions and are also not affected by rising fertiliser costs.
“Organic farmers are much less exposed to these risks,” Morgan said, adding that the plan was a sign that the government was thinking hard about the pathway for food security.

title: Indonesia wildfire fuelled by El Niño razes almost 300 homes
body:
A forest fire on Indonesia’s Sumatra island fuelled by El Niño has razed nearly 300 homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, an official has said, as the country battles devastating blazes and haze.
Residents first spotted the fire approaching their village in Bangka Belitung province on Saturday and tried to put it out themselves with portable water pumps, said the head of South Bangka regency, Riza Herdavid.
“They thought it was taken care of. But it’s peatland, and there was still a fire smouldering underneath. So, when they assumed it was over, the wind shifted and quickly drove the fire toward the settlement.”
The local disaster agency said nearly 1,000 people had fled the village.
“My house is gone,” said Leni, a 55-year-old woman staying at a shelter with her family.
“There’s nothing left. I could only save myself and take my kids with me … I panicked and didn’t have the time to grab anything.”
Riza said the village had been built on what used to be peatland in a protected area, but which was converted into a housing complex last year.
This year’s fires have created severe haze locally, with tens of thousands of cases of respiratory illnesses, and caused increased air pollution in Singapore and Malaysia.
Indonesia is among the countries worst affected by heat, drought and fire in El Niño years. The government says the current conditions are the worst in a decade.
Analysts indicate the area burned and emissions are on track to match the record blazes of 2015, which charred an area of 2.6m hectares and generated 333 megatonnes of carbon.
Wildlife has also been devastated as fires have spread around the country.
Earlier this week, a group of eight orangutans had to be relocated to the Batu Nyambu protected forest by car and boat. At least 46 of the critically endangered primates have been rescued since August, according to the West Kalimantan Natural Resources Conservation Agency.
How many have been killed is unclear, but experts have warned the toll is likely to be huge. The International Union for Conservation of Nature said fire had affected habitats containing 52% of Borneo’s orangutan population.
Even when the blazes are finally extinguished, many animals will face shortages of habitat, prey and water as a result of fire damage and drought.
Silvered langurs, long-tailed macaques and proboscis monkeys have been found dead in the ashes or by dried-up ponds. Elephants, gibbons, pangolins and turtles are also among the species likely to be affected.
The authorities have warned the fires could continue until November, when the El Niño is expected to peak.
Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto, ordered the government on Monday to mobilise maximum efforts to extinguish wildfires that have been raging for three months in some places.
Thick smoke in a province of Borneo has grounded water-bombing aircraft, according to the disaster agency. The cabinet secretary, Teddy Indra Wijaya, said the government had deployed more than 60,000 personnel on the ground.
- Agence-France Presse contributed to this report

title: Coastal erosion in England has claimed at least 183 homes in past 16 years
body:
Seaside communities along the east coast of England have lost at least 183 homes to coastal erosion and landslides over the past 16 years, figures obtained by the Guardian reveal.
After councils judged properties across the Yorkshire and East Anglian coasts too vulnerable to remain safely occupied, the homes were proactively demolished.
The demolitions cost £1.1m, with the Environment Agency contributing about £482,000 towards clearing 61 homes at risk of collapsing and the rest paid for by councils and at times by homeowners themselves.
Coastal erosion is the gradual wearing away and retreat of the sea shoreline, which can destabilise cliffs and eventually force homes and infrastructure to be demolished before they collapse. While it is a natural process, scientists said the climate crisis was accelerating the retreat of the UK’s shores.
The Guardian requested data from nine councils noted in a House of Commons environment, food and rural affairs committee (EFRA) report as being some of the most vulnerable to coastal erosion.
East Riding of Yorkshire council, which includes vulnerable communities in Skipsea, Aldbrough and Mappleton, has demolished 66 homes since 2010 – the most of these nine local authorities.
Great Yarmouth borough council (GYBC) has demolished 64 homes since 2010, with all the houses located in the village of Hemsby. Since December 2025, the council has removed 41 properties in the seaside resort.
A GYBC spokesperson said: “Last winter, the dunes in Hemsby saw about 50% of the erosion predicted for the entirety of the next 30 years. More than 10 metres of land was lost in just over 12 months.
“Council staff continue to liaise with people to make sure residents and the public are safe and work closely with people to offer support and advice and explain the options available.”
North Norfolk council has proactively demolished 21 homes over the same period.
East Suffolk council, which only held data for the past six years, recorded a sharp rise in demolitions last year. Eight homes were demolished between 2020 and 2024, and 16 between May last year and April this year.
Most of East Suffolk’s homes demolished this year are understood to be in Thorpeness. Hilary Lightfoot’s home, in which she lived and raised a family for 20 years, was demolished this year. “I’ve lost £650,000 – that was what my flat was worth,” she said. “I’ve had to dig into my pension savings to buy a house, of which I still owe money on. I’ve borrowed money. It’s just disastrous.”
The Environment Agency estimates that 3,500 properties in England are at risk from coastal erosion by 2055, increasing to more than 10,000 properties by 2105.
More than 6 miles (10km) of major roads, 107 miles of minor roads and 3.5 miles of railway – many serving small, coastal communities – are also at risk from erosion over the next 80 years, according to the EA.
Unlike flood damage, which can be covered by the Flood Re scheme, there is no UK insurance product for coastal erosion because insurers treat coastal retreat as a “virtual certainty” for some seaside homes rather than an accidental risk, according to the EFRA committee’s report.
East Suffolk council said that although some government funding was available towards demolition, “there are currently limited mechanisms to support the wider costs of adaptation and relocation” for residents.
The authority said it had invested about £1.5m in short-term measures designed to slow erosion and give residents more time to prepare, while also testing new approaches through the government’s flood and coastal innovation programme.
Sophie Day, senior research associate at the University of East Anglia, said because the east coast was made up of “very sandy, gravelly, silty material”, it was more vulnerable to erosion.
She said wetter winters, made more likely by the climate crisis, would saturate and destabilise soft cliffs such as those on the east coast, while increased storminess and rising sea levels would worsen the impact of high tides and leave beaches with less time to recover between storms.
While councils have increased spending on sea defences over the decades, Day said these protections have created an “illusion of permanence” for what is an accelerating issue. The scale of the threat from coastal erosion meant “we are going to have to shift to more of an acceptance of not intervening any more and enabling retreat”, she added.
Day said adapting to a retreating coastline meant planning for the loss of homes and infrastructure before the next emergency, while working more closely with communities.
“Having skilled people who are able to engage, who have the time, the training, the skills, to go and sit at somebody’s kitchen table and talk to them about the fact that, in a year, even five months’ time, their home may not be livable. What are the options? How can we find ways of giving people choices and support?”
North Norfolk district council (NNDC) said: “Households in all 21 homes were supported by NNDC. Nineteen of these properties were proactively demolished before they reached the cliff edge and became an emergency.
“NNDC continues to work with the Environment Agency and Defra … to better prepare communities. A number of pilot opportunities are under development. It is hoped that through this work, more targeted support for those impacted can become part of the business as usual and supported by government for the whole coast into the future.”
A spokesperson for East Riding council said: “East Riding of Yorkshire has some of the fastest eroding coastlines in Europe, resulting in the loss of homes, businesses and roads. Through the Changing Coasts East Riding project, the council is working directly with residents, businesses and communities to find out the full economic, environmental and social impacts of these losses.”
An Environment Agency spokesperson said it was “very aware” of how erosion was affecting coastal homeowners and communities.
They said: “While local authorities are best placed to support affected residents, we’re backing them with £36m for coastal erosion adaptation pilots, slashing planning regulation red tape in vulnerable areas and offering £10,000 grants to fund the safe demolition of affected properties – with scope to go further for more complex jobs.”
