title: Total fire ban for Sydney, with high temperatures and risk of bushfires from ‘dry lightning’
body:
A total fire ban was in place across greater Sydney on Monday with temperatures soaring above 35C in the city’s west.
The Bureau of Meteorology said Sydney faced extreme fire danger due to hot, dry conditions and the chance of thunderstorms, with little rainfall.
On Monday morning, the bureau said temperatures would be “well above average” on Monday, with areas including Mount Druitt predicted to hit 37C.
By Monday evening, the bureau confirmed Parramatta reached a high of 34.5C and Olympic Park in Homebush recorded a top of 35.2C.
“It definitely is one of the hottest days in several months,” Angus Hines, a senior meteorologist with the BoM, said.
Had Monday’s predicted maximum temperature been reached, it would have been 10 or 11C higher than average for this time in October in Sydney.
A peak of 37C would have been the hottest day in the city since February.
On Monday morning, the NSW Rural Fire Service said the total fire ban applied to the greater Sydney and greater Hunter regions. Outdoor fires, solid fuel barbecues and activities such as grinding and welding were all prohibited.
“Fire danger is going to be right up today, and so people need to take care right through the day to make sure that they’re not doing anything with flames out in the open,” Trent Curtin, the commissioner of the NSW RFS, told ABC radio.
“We’ve got some severe thunderstorms expected across large parts of NSW.
“We don’t think we’re going to see a whole lot of rain with that today, so that dry lightning starting fires out in the west and through the middle parts of NSW is going to be a real problem.”
Curtin said the RFS had made good progress this year with hazard reduction burning due to favourable conditions.
“We’ve been able to do a lot more this year than we have in prior years, because the conditions have been a little bit better and we’ve made sure we’ve taken every opportunity,” he said.
Kristy McBain, the federal emergency management minister, on Monday touted the rollout of the AusAlert system.
It means compatible phones sound an alarm and receive a text message if there’s an emergency situation nearby. Only two states – Victoria and Western Australia – have signed on to the system so far.
“That will get much better protection for communities who are experiencing disaster,” McBain told ABC TV.
“Near real-time message not [reliant] on any one telco provider is a real gamechanger for emergency management.”
Monday’s extreme heat comes on the back of Australia’s second-hottest September on record, spurred by a strengthening El Niño. The bureau said average temperatures ranked in the top five Septembers for every state.
“There’s only one clear driver of this and that’s climate change,” climate scientist Dr Linden Ashcroft said earlier this month.
Hines said El Niño was likely to really push up maximum and minimum temperatures over the next several months, with “lots of hot days ahead”.
“There’s plenty of summer left,” he said.
On Monday evening, a spokesperson for the bureau confirmed that while weather in Sydney had been “unusually hot”, it was not record-breaking.
“That doesn’t exclude the possibility that it reached 37C somewhere in Sydney, we only have finite temperature recording stations across the city”, they said.
In Sydney’s vicinity, Richmond and Gosford both reached highs of 37.7C, Cooranbong hit 36.4C and Maitland 36.3C.
The most recent record-breaking temperature for October in Sydney was a high of 39.5, recorded in Penrith on 22 October 2025. Before that, the highest Sydney temperature recorded for October was 39.1C in 2004 at Sydney airport, the spokesperson said.
Temperatures soared in the state’s north-west, with Walgett experiencing a high of 38.9C, while Bourke airport reached a top of 38.6C.

title: For the future of green politics, look beyond the Green party | Zoe Williams
body:
The future of Green politics is under constant discussion after the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, but a much heavier clash – in meaning, symbolism and portent – happened earlier this summer, in King’s Lynn and West Norfolk. The council declared a climate emergency in 2021, along with hundreds of others, and while it was under Conservative control. It is now controlled by independents, and a Reform UK councillor, Austen Moore, moved to scrap the declaration.
It was the end of June, and the meeting had to be called off, because of the extreme heat in the King’s Lynn council chamber. A lot of people paused to grimly remark on that irony, but not Moore, who simply rescheduled the motion for the following week, where it was voted down (by 33 to seven). A local scientist and member of Extinction Rebellion liveblogged that debate, adding helpful maps, such as how much of the county was already below the annual flood level – most of it, including King’s Lynn itself. If this all sounds like a cheerful take home, numerous other Reform-led councils have had the same debate and Reform has prevailed. Their arguments can be terrifyingly illiterate. In Kent, councillor Linden Kemkaran asserted that climate change is fine because the world was warmer in Roman times, and as “carbon dioxide … is a trace gas essential for life on Earth”, to try to cut carbon emissions would itself be dangerous.
If you’re waiting for reality to knock some sense into politics, you will wait too long. There is no heatwave, no flood, no El Niño, no omnicrisis, that will divert rightwing populism from its crusade against action on climate.
The question isn’t what the Green party alone could do to create an eco-populist wave of equal volume. A party that could single-handedly represent the 68% of people who want action on climate change doesn’t exist in modern British politics. The question is, how do you turn that strength of feeling into something more concrete, so it isn’t constantly being ram-raided by unshameable, unscientific chancers? Environmentalists in every party, leaders of every party (apart from the Conservatives, who seem hellbent on chasing Reform, despite the stated values of their supporters), need to find the language and ideas that turn passion for the environment into impetus.
In their recent report, Caroline Lucas and the green philosopher Rupert Read make the case for “eco-popularism” rather than eco-populism: a way of thinking that doesn’t try to hotwire its way into people’s emotional circuitry with invigorating binaries, but, rather, describes actions that would genuinely change lives for the better, and therefore be popular.
Rightwing populists have a set of arguments against climate action that are taking hold more generally and are self-fulfilling: the more they’re repeated, the more they win at local level, the more people come to believe that these views are generally held. Those narratives are that climate action of any sort – be it ultra-low emission zones, 15-minute cities or, most importantly, net zero – is too expensive at this time; that net zero itself is a luxury belief of the comfortable elite who don’t care about ordinary people’s living conditions (Lucas and Read paraphrase from a Nigel Farage column last year).
This so-called “Manichean” framing, the noble masses betrayed by a corrupt elite, is dog obvious, but to point to Farage and say “you, the guy in receipt of £5m from a non-domiciled crypto billionaire, you’re representing the masses against the elites?” is tempting but fruitless. No case for climate action will take hold unless it addresses the conditions that populists exploit – the cost of living, of course, but also the sense of precariousness and active fear of the future that climate events intensify.
A prime minister freezing bus fares or taking the VAT off heating doesn’t address those brute realities and deep anxieties: if anything, it shores up a sense that central government is no longer capable of building the resilience and adaptation a chaotic world demands. People need to know there’s a plan for cheaper, greener energy, food security and extreme weather events. Local, tangible actions should be supported, broadcast and celebrated, in political debate and in the media; a discussion held in abstract terms of global patterns and borderless looming disaster doesn’t just foster despair. It plays back into the hands of populists, whose incredibly proximal enemies – small boats, asylum seekers – and standing street armies create the opposite impression, of agency and might. It doesn’t matter that it’s specious and vindictive – it matters that it lands and there is no answering call to arms. One of the many paradoxes of the climate debate is that the far right talks as though disaster is not real, but acts as though it’s imminent. The left does the opposite, talking of catastrophe but acting as if there’s time to lose.
Without a change of direction, even those of us who are constitutionally not susceptible to rightwing populism will still give in to its echo, which is hopelessness. Coherence is desperately needed: to promise defence spending at the expense of heat pumps, or high-quality jobs with the downside of new fossil-fuel exploration, is simply to reinforce a sense of impotence, nationally and individually.
King’s Lynn and West Norfolk’s debate in July had an interesting pivot from Reform: they had started to magpie the language of “resilience building”, in place of climate action. But they didn’t mean it to describe peat and wildlife restoration, or food cooperatives, or retrofitted housing, or community-owned wind power. They weren’t interested in solar panels or sustainable drainage or civic infrastructure. It was the broadest possible false promise: spend less on climate, therefore less has been spent, therefore your community is more resilient. Councillors from all the other parties united to defeat them, and politics national and local can learn from that unity; but no party can afford to wait for an opponent to unite against.

title: Is it really ‘madness’ to account for emissions from fossil fuels burned overseas? The Coalition sure thinks so | Temperature Check
body:
The Coalition has come up with the perfect solution to deal with the climate pollution from when Australian fossil fuels are burned overseas.
We should either just pretend they don’t exist, or ignore the reason why people are concerned about them, even if those people include a majority of high court judges or the international court of justice.
This week the Coalition said it wanted to roll back new rules that ask fossil fuel producers to disclose the greenhouse gas emissions that come from burning their products overseas.
The step comes in response to a barrage of conservative outrage over a high court ruling last week that confirmed planners in New South Wales should have considered putting conditions on the overseas emissions from a coalmine.
The high court’s decision was “absurd” and “madness”, the Coalition said, with the Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, calling it “net zero on steroids”. Fossil fuel groups called it “utter madness” and warned it could spark a wave of legal challenges.
But none of those commentators tackle the reason why overseas emissions – known as scope 3 – are being counted and considered in the first place: they cause people harm.
Rules are being phased in that require companies – the largest first, followed by smaller companies up to a threshold – to report annually on these emissions which they are indirectly responsible for.
‘The quiet part out loud’
The Coalition wants these requirements gone, describing them as “absurd”. Another way to look at them is that they help corporations and the public to understand the full impact of their activities on the climate.
For fossil fuel exporters, these emissions make up the lion’s share of their climate impact.
What sparked that announcement was a high court judgment last week that also concerned scope 3 emissions.
The high court’s finding, by a majority of three judges to two, was clearly a victory for the retired NSW couple who had previously taken on the Mount Pleasant coalmine and won in the court of appeal.
In the cold light of the judgment, all that the high court judges said was that the NSW Independent Planning Commission had not followed the state’s existing laws properly.
“These requirements on the planning commission to consider scope 3 emissions have been part of the New South Wales planning system in one form or another for almost 20 years,” said Prof Jacqueline Peel, a leading international climate law expert at the University of Melbourne.
“The high court has really just said the quiet part out loud. The majority of the court looked at the law and saw that the decision-maker didn’t follow it.”
Peel said the provision that the high court had considered did not prevent the planning commission from approving a coal project.
All that it did, she said, was say the commission had to consider whether to impose conditions in relation to scope 3 emissions.
“Maybe [this decision] is construed as radical by some because if you do start to impose conditions on emissions generated overseas, then it could make coal production more expensive,” Peel said. “Whether you think that is good or bad depends on your views around climate change.”
Wrongful act?
The Coalition was angry with the decision because it said under the UN climate convention greenhouse gas emissions are assigned to the country where they are released.
Being able to wave away responsibility for these emissions by suggesting it is just an entry on a carbon accounting spreadsheet in a foreign land ignores the reason why they are being counted in the first place.
The emissions might occur somewhere else but they generate harms around the world that climate scientists are increasingly able to quantify. Those harms don’t stop at the NSW border.
As one of the judges to side against the mining company on the issue, Justice James Edelman wrote the “natural and irresistible interpretation” of the planning commission’s reasoning was that it was “distracted by the accounting concepts of the scopes into which greenhouse gas emissions are divided”.
What that meant, he wrote, was that the commission thought it didn’t need “to ensure that scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions are minimised to the greatest extent practicable.”
The Coalition claimed the issue with scope 3 emissions “turns on the wording of NSW planning law” – ignoring the harms that emissions cause around the world.
But the notion that a country should start mitigating scope 3 emissions has not appeared from out of the blue.
As well as it sitting on the NSW state planning rules for more than a decade (rules which the Coalition is pushing to have rescinded), the international court of justice declared last year that a failure of a state to protect the climate from greenhouse gas emissions “including through fossil fuel production” may “constitute an internationally wrongful act”.
At the UN, 141 countries voted to back the court’s opinion, against eight dissenters – Saudi Arabia, Russia, Israel, Iran, Yemen, Liberia, Belarus and, of course, the United States and its climate science-denying president.
Rather than these growing calls to manage fossil fuel production being “net zero on steroids” they should more accurately be understood as an attempt to cut the steroids driving the planet’s climate to ever deadlier extremes.
- Graham Readfearn is Guardian Australia’s environment and climate correspondent

title: I work for a major insurer. Much of my industry is fudging the numbers in the face of the climate crisis | Anonymous
body:
I work for a major insurer, assessing the risk posed by natural disasters on properties around the world, from family homes to schools, government offices and multibillion-dollar commercial centres. The world is facing greater risk than ever from extreme weather. We are not prepared – and that inaction could have profound consequences for the global financial system.
In the face of ever more extreme and unpredictable climate risks, I am coming under pressure to cut my forecasts for the losses that disasters will cause in order to make insurance more affordable – and get my employer more business. In some instances, the questioning of our numbers and models is justified. But too often, it is not being done to produce more accurate models, but to artificially lower prices. If this is happening at my firm, which is struggling to compete with rivals’ prices, it’s happening elsewhere.
Our sector is carrying more risk than we realise. The warming global climate has caused more frequent high-intensity storms, rising sea levels, flooding, wildfires and drought. While the immediate impact of these events is plain to see, the long-term effects will be compounded as insurers withdraw from affected areas, leaving the economy in freefall and people’s day-to-day lives in ruins.
As a modeller, it is my job to look objectively and scientifically at the data to calculate an expected loss from a natural disaster, which affects the price of the premium for a given policy. Our industry says it holds those numbers as sacrosanct, but as my analysis shows higher and more volatile risk, the price rises with it and we lose customers.
So modellers like me are coming under pressure to reduce their projected losses. In the most basic terms, we are collectively fudging the numbers and taking on more risk than we should for a lower price than the expected loss demands. Sometimes I will forecast losses that would normally be seen as much too risky for us to insure, but we offer the policies anyway. This will eventually lead to a sector built on “competitively priced” contracts that underestimate risk, leaving gaping holes in the safety net that insurance is supposed to provide.
For example, if subsidence – which is made worse by drought – damages a number of homes in your area, insurers may exclude this from your policy, so you won’t be covered if subsidence then hits your house.
When that happens to an entire community, businesses leave, investment dries up and the local economy tanks. Now imagine this happening in multiple towns around the country, at the same time. And subsidence is just one such issue, alongside wildfires, coastal erosion, wind and floods – and that’s just in the UK.
I have respect for underwriters who are just doing their jobs, and I know that no single individual is responsible. My concern lies with the attitude of much of the industry towards modellers, actuaries and researchers: there is a sense that we are an inconvenience to the deal-making process, rather than an essential part of risk management. We are the failsafe that stops our industry from reckless gambling.
At the largest scale, misquoted insurance can damage insurers, companies, their employees and the communities that rely on them. The upshot is that our customers are likely to be much more exposed to climate-related risks than they realise. People are not budgeting for a major increase in their insurance premiums or planning for their homes becoming uninsurable, but many of them absolutely should be.
If the worst happens, the insurance industry may not have the money to pay every claim when a major disaster hits. That would have profound consequences for the economy as a whole – businesses could go bankrupt, the housing market could seize up and, if people couldn’t pay their mortgages, banks would fail.
As natural catastrophes continue to become less predictable and more severe, the foundations of our entire economy will only become more fragile. Our customers deserve to know.
- The writer is a modeller working in the insurance industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism as part of their Secret Source series, a regular column featuring industry whistleblowers
